By integrating these two domains, this research develops a scalable and accurate approach to enhance real-time environmental monitoring. Hydrometeorological data often exhibit complex, non-linear relationships that conventional statistical models struggle to capture. This study employs advanced machine learning models, including Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and the Prophet model,to enhance real-time anomaly detection and forecasting. Additionally, statistical models and machine learning models such as Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA),Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA), Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Recurrent Nerural Network-Gated Recurrent Unit (RNN-GRU) are utilized to provide a comparative assessment of traditional forecasting techniques against machine learning-based approaches. The methodological framework significantly improves predictive capabilities, with broad applications in disaster preparedness, water resource management, and climate change adaptation. The research methodology follows a structured approach, beginning with data collection from temperature sensors in Ticino, and piezometers in Mendatica and Triora. The acquired data undergo preprocessing to remove inconsistencies, ensuring high-quality input for analysis. A machine learning-driven anomaly detection framework is implemented to identify outliers in time-series data. papers.title: From the mountains to the sky: Aerial Cable-Cars lifting social inclusion and transport equity in Latin America
papers.summary: Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) is a region with deep transport and spatial inequalities, producing differences in travel behaviour and transport supply across communities, as people living in the peripheries experience longer travel times and costs to access essential amenities. Topography is another important factor exacerbating these inequalities, as many LAC settlements are located near the Andes Mountains. Disadvantaged communities (DC) in the region are usually located in hilly terrain, often in areas at risk of landslides, and are characterised by informal development. In this context, Aerial Cable-Cars (ACC) presents a mode of public transport that provides high-quality service and infrastructure in LAC cities with the potential to improve social inclusion and accessibility for vulnerable communities. ACC have been rapidly adopted throughout LAC since their first introduction in Medellín in 2004. And particularly after 2010, when more than 90% of operational ACCs were inaugurated. This thesis seeks to contribute to the understanding of ACC technology as a mode of transport in LAC urban settlements, along with its implications for activity participation and transport-related social exclusion (TRSE), accessibility and transport equity, and mode choice. To do so, the study first conducted a literature review of empirical evidence on ACC transport projects in LAC. Then, the thesis focused on two case studies in Colombia: Bogotá and Manizales. In Bogotá, the first ACC (TransMiCable) was inaugurated in 2018, connecting Ciudad Bolívar’s residents to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system and primarily serving as a feeder. In Manizales, the ACC system (Cable Aéreo) comprises three interconnected lines, inaugurated in 2009, 2014, and 2025.

papers.title: Research on the Optimized 3D DEM‒SPH Algorithm and Impact Parameters of Surge Wave Amplitude for Granular Landslides
papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: ObjectiveMesh-based and Eulerian-Lagrangian methods cannot adequately simulate large deformations, free-surface fragmentation, and fluid-solid interaction during granular landslide-induced surges. A three-dimensional meshless semi-resolved Discrete Element Method (DEM) and Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) coupling algorithm was developed, incorporating a multiphase flow model to optimize the volume fraction distribution at the coupling interface. The key parameters controlling the maximum surge wave amplitude were systematically investigated to support hazard prediction in reservoir areas.MethodsDEM with a nonlinear contact force model and rolling resistance simulated granular landslides. Each DEM particle obeyed Newton's second law. Normal and tangential contact forces were computed using a nonlinear model with damping. SPH solved the Navier-Stokes equations for the fluid phase using a Wendland C2 kernel with a compact support radius of 2h. A δ‒SPH density diffusion term (coefficient δ=0.1) was added to the continuity equation to reduce pressure noise. The multiphase flow model optimized the volume fraction calculation at the solid-liquid interface using a density-gradient-based control equation. Buoyancy, drag, and reaction forces between DEM and SPH particles were computed using a semi-resolved scheme. Buoyancy was calculated via pressure interpolation from surrounding fluid particles. Drag forces were computed using the Ergun correlation for void fractions below 0.8 and the Wen-Yu correlation for void fractions of 0.8 or above, based on local void fraction and relative velocity. Physical experiments were conducted in a three-dimensional wave tank. The granular landslide material was quartz sand with a mean diameter of 8 mm, density of 2 600 kg/m³, and porosity of 0.23. papers.title: GeoAI for Sustainable Futures: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Earth Observation and GIS for Environmental Resilience
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), the integration of artificial intelligence with Earth Observation (EO) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS), is reshaping how environmental resilience is monitored and managed. This paper reviews GeoAI as both a technical practice and a geographical problem, arguing that its value for resilience planning depends on respecting the spatial properties — dependence, heterogeneity and scale — that distinguish geographic data from ordinary tabular data. The paper synthesises published evidence across four resilience-relevant domains: land use/land cover (LULC) change detection, drought risk assessment, landslide hazard zonation and groundwater potential mapping and situates this evidence within the Deccan Plateau and Western Ghats margin of Maharashtra, a terrain that compresses escarpment landslide risk, valley land-use change and rain-shadow drought within a single administrative region. The review finds consistent but bounded accuracy gains from machine-learning methods over conventional GIS overlay, with the largest gains reported where training and validation data are collected locally rather than transferred from elsewhere. The paper closes with a phased adoption roadmap for a teaching-and-research college operating in this terrain, arguing that institutional investment in ground-truth data collection should precede investment in more elaborate models.

papers.title: Evaluating The Impact of Climate Change On Landslide Susceptibility: An Electre Method Approach
papers.source: Journal on Applied and Chemical Physics
papers.summary: Climate Change Impact on Landslides Rising global temperatures contribute to more extreme weather patterns, including intense rainfall events that increase soil saturation and slope instability. Additionally, the melting of permafrost in colder regions due to warming temperatures weakens mountain slopes, heightening the risk of landslides. Deforestation and land-use changes further exacerbate these conditions by reducing natural vegetation that stabilizes soil. Research significance Researching climate change’s impact on landslides is critical as rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events intensify landslide risks globally. Increased rainfall and rapid snowmelt contribute to soil saturation and instability on slopes, while droughts can dry soils, leading to heightened erosion and landslide susceptibility. Methodology Climate models project changes in temperature, precipitation, and extreme weather, which can trigger landslides. Landslide susceptibility maps, created using GIS tools and machine learning algorithms, help identify high-risk zones based on topography, soil type, and vegetation. Historical landslide records are analyzed alongside climate data to detect trends and correlations. papers.title: Landslides and the Impacts on the Geological Heritage: A Case Study in Quang Binh, Vietnam
papers.summary: Landslide is a common geohazard that often occurs in mountainous areas. In recent years, this phenomenon has caused socio-economic losses and raised concerns regarding the conservation of geological heritage sites. In this study, field investigations, laboratory experiments, mapping, and analysis were conducted to assess landslides, causes, influencing factors, and their impact on geological heritage in former Quang Binh province, Vietnam. The synthetic results indicate that landslides occur frequently along cut roads in mountainous areas of Quang Binh and are triggered by various factors. In which, geological conditions, topography, and rainfall, are the primary contributors. Landslides not only affect road infrastructure but also affect accessibility and tourism activities on geological heritage sites. However, no significant direct damage to the heritage sites themselves was observed. The research results suggest that landslide risk management should be integrated into transportation planning and geotourism development to ensure the sustainable exploitation of geological heritage values.

papers.title: AI-powered sub-seasonal forecasting of monsoon-triggered landslide impacts in Nepal
papers.summary: Abstract Monsoon-triggered landslides result in perennial losses in Nepal, but we lack the capacity to anticipate their occurrence and subsequent impacts with sufficient lead time to take anticipatory or mitigating action. To address this challenge, here we describe an AI framework to forecast the occurrence of impacts from monsoon-triggered landslides across Nepal, using a combination of topographic data, antecedent rainfall observations, and sub-seasonal rainfall forecasts from dynamical forecast models. Responding directly to humanitarian planning needs, we create a first-of-its-kind method at national spatial scale and sub-seasonal temporal scale that provides district-wise landslide impact forecasting over a 14-day window for Nepal. We validate our approach by training our models on landslide impact records from 2016 to 2022 and highlight model performance during the 2023 and 2024 monsoon seasons, when the models consistently achieve an F1 score of 0.7 or greater. We detail the creation of a satellite embedding dataset with our tool, LandslideNet, which assists in capturing landslide impacts early in the monsoon season. Our framework is specifically designed to complement existing landslide susceptibility approaches and support operational decision-making needs of local government and humanitarian organisations by providing estimates of areas likely to experience landslide impacts over an upcoming two-week period, aiding in both preparedness and anticipatory action.

papers.title: Mapping landslide change and volume with repeat airborne LiDAR after the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna event: slope-dependent detection limits and lowered areas
papers.summary: Landslide inventories are validated against repeat topography by comparing the ground that changes beyond a detection limit inside mapped polygons with the same fraction on stable ground. Stable ground is gentler than landslides, and LiDAR noise grows with slope. We measure the consequence for the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna event, Italy, with four pairs of 0.5 m airborne LiDAR on 919 river-corridor tiles, the only ground where pre- and post-event surveys overlap, and the 80,997-polygon RER2023 inventory. Stable ground exceeds a tile's 95th-percentile limit on 4% of flat ground and 27% of slopes above 40°, so the rate that applies to the landslides is 13.7%, not 5.9%, and the usual comparison doubles the apparent signal. A fifth pair spanning the first post-event year is consistent with the slope-matched floor in aggregate (14.5% against 14.2%, where all stable ground predicts 6.1%), although gentle and steep ground depart from it in opposite directions. With the corrected floor, 36% of mapped landslide ground changed by more than about 0.5 m. Only 20% of the mapped area of debris and earth landslides was lowered beyond the limit, mostly in the upper half of each polygon, and the same estimator finds no lowering in the post-event year. Area–volume scaling applied to the outlines overstates the measured lowering 8 to 11 times, and on the lowered area the exponent is about 1.1 to 1.3 rather than 1.45. Inventory validation needs slope-matched floors, and inventory-based volumes need lowered or source areas.

papers.title: Data supporting “Engineering-Geological Architecture Governs Inherited-State Evolution and Reactivation-Threshold Erosion of Loess Landslides under Successive Earthquakes”
papers.summary: This dataset provides the supporting case-level data for the manuscript “Engineering-Geological Architecture Governs Inherited-State Evolution and Reactivation-Threshold Erosion of Loess Landslides under Successive Earthquakes.” The dataset contains the case-level registry and associated numerical outputs from 528 successive-earthquake simulations representing three contrasting engineering-geological endmembers (A, B, and C). The archived files document the simulation-case structure, prescribed resistance-state protocol, principal loading and state variables, response classifications, A/B reactivation-threshold brackets, data-field definitions, and file-integrity checks. The dataset supports the analyses of inherited mechanical-state evolution, architecture-conditioned reactivation resistance, mechanically distinct State 0/1/2 response pathways, and cross-architecture transfer presented in the manuscript and Supplementary Material. A data dictionary and dataset-structure file are included to facilitate interpretation and reuse.

papers.title: Numerical simulations of landslide generated tsunamis in Montagne Pelée, Martinique
papers.summary: I modelli numerici sono uno strumento fondamentale per comprendere e prevedere l'impatto degli tsunami generati da frane. Nel contesto dell'attuale fase di unrest sismico e idrotermale del vulcano Montagne Pelée (Martinica, Piccole Antille), questa tesi indaga la dinamica dei flussi granulari e l'ampiezza delle onde generate da due potenziali scenari di collasso di fianco. Per riprodurre la complessità di questi fenomeni, abbiamo utilizzato il codice numerico HySEA. Questo modello shallow-water (per acque basse) mediato sulla profondità incorpora una struttura multistrato e gestisce la pressione non idrostatica, consentendo di catturare i moti verticali essenziali e gli effetti di dispersione. Il confronto tra simulazioni con diverse stratificazioni rivela che la discretizzazione della colonna d'acqua in tre strati verticali fornisce un compromesso ottimale tra accuratezza fisica e costo computazionale. Poiché la dinamica delle frane subaeree che entrano in mare dipende fortemente dai parametri di attrito scelti, abbiamo testato diversi approcci di calibrazione, dimostrando che le incertezze nelle variabili di input possono alterare drasticamente le previsioni sull'elevazione massima della superficie libera e sulla profondità di inondazione. Applicando i vincoli di attrito più robusti, la valutazione finale della pericolosità rivela una minaccia costiera fortemente asimmetrica. Mentre il collasso parziale di 0,0095 km³ non rappresenta un pericolo significativo, il collasso totale di 0,0602 km³ del Domo del 1929 genera un'onda distruttiva diretta con forza verso sud. Questo scenario peggiore provoca un estremo effetto di shoaling e inondazioni catastrofiche che si spingono per oltre 120 metri nell'entroterra a Saint-Pierre e Le Carbet, evidenziando la necessità critica di strategie mirate di allerta rapida lungo la costa meridionale.

papers.title: Integrated Geotechnical and Seismic Stability Assessment of Tropical Residual Slopes in Sitinjau Lauik, West Sumatra, Indonesia
papers.summary: Sitinjau Lauik, a national road corridor in West Sumatra, Indonesia, is one of the most landslide-prone segments of the Bukit Barisan volcanic belt. This study assesses the geotechnical and seismic stability of three tropical residual soil slopes at this location by combining cone penetration testing (CPT), laboratory index testing, consolidated-drained direct shear testing (DST), and Morgenstern–Price limit-equilibrium analysis under static and pseudo-static seismic loading. CPT profiles revealed a weak layer (qc = 0.4–0.6 MPa) at 1.2–2.8 m depth in Slope 1. This slope also has a high plasticity index (PI = 39.7%), a high void ratio (e = 1.50), and a low dry density (γd = 10.06 kN/m³), resulting in lower shear-strength parameters (c' = 17.8 kPa, φ' = 19.2°) than Slopes 2 and 3 (PI < 10%). Static factors of safety (FS) were 1.08, 1.54, and 1.49 for Slopes 1, 2, and 3, respectively. A pseudo-static coefficient of kh = 0.15, consistent with regional peak ground acceleration zoning, reduced the FS values to 0.77, 1.23, and 1.17, making Slope 1 unstable during earthquakes. At kh = 0.20, none of the slopes met the minimum FS of 1.1 required by the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) 8460:2017. High plasticity, a high void ratio, and low CPT resistance distinguished the critical Slope 1 from the other slopes. Because only three slopes were examined, these findings are site-specific; nevertheless, they provide a basis for prioritizing slope remediation and early warning along this corridor.

papers.title: Integrating erosion susceptibility, topographic wetness, and short-duration rainfall intensity thresholds for landslide initiation: A process-oriented framework for the Black Sea Region of Türkiye
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Rainfall-triggered landslides result from the interaction between long-term preparatory terrain conditions and short-duration triggering rainfall events. However, most regional susceptibility studies either treat these components separately or represent rainfall using cumulative precipitation metrics that inadequately capture the intensity characteristics of triggering storms. This study proposes a process-oriented monthly framework integrating terrain susceptibility indicators with rainfall erosivity-derived short-duration rainfall intensity metrics to improve representation of landslide initiation processes in the Black Sea Region of Türkiye. Preparatory conditions were characterized using erosion susceptibility indicators derived from the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), representing terrain instability and moisture accumulation potential. Triggering conditions were quantified using monthly maximum 30-minute rainfall intensity (I30) values extracted from erosive rainfall events identified through the RUSLE rainfall erosivity framework. Because this methodology selectively identifies rainfall events with sufficient intensity and energy to generate significant surface responses, the derived I30 metric provides a physically interpretable representation of rainfall conditions associated with slope destabilization. Seven predictor scenarios combining preparatory and triggering variables were evaluated using four machine-learning algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM). Monthly rainfall-triggering thresholds were independently estimated using probabilistic, ROC-based (Youden index), and percentile-based approaches. Results indicate that scenarios integrating continuous I30 values with erosion susceptibility and wetness indicators consistently achieved the highest predictive performance, with monthly ROC–AUC values frequently exceeding 0.85. Threshold-based representations yielded slight

papers.title: Modelled active-mining and observed post-closure deformation in a mountainous coal mine: a 3DEC-InSAR case study from Xinjiang, China
papers.source: Geomechanics and Geophysics for Geo-Energy and Geo-Resources
papers.summary: Active mining and post-closure ground deformation are often examined separately, and their linkage remains poorly constrained in loess-covered mountainous terrain, where topography can amplify geohazards. We integrate 3DEC discrete-element simulations, SBAS-InSAR monitoring, and field investigations at a closed coal mine in Xinjiang, China. The analysis combines a simulated active-mining phase with a separate post-closure observation period beginning approximately two years after mine closure, characterizing two distinct stages rather than a continuous field-observed lifecycle. Three site-specific patterns emerge. Residual settlement continues after reclamation, supporting long-term monitoring. Deformation also varies with landform and material conditions: simulations show greater vertical movement in gullies and thicker loess, whereas slopes exhibit stronger lateral movement, step-like fissures, and landslide morphology in the field. The spatial correspondence between subsidence features and slope failures is consistent with a conceptual subsidence-slope-instability pathway, while the observations cannot resolve temporal precedence, infiltration-driven acceleration, or landslide probability. During excavation, simulations indicate stress redistribution, asymmetric bending, and upward deformation through the layered materials. These results provide case-specific evidence for deformation assessment and post-mining land-restoration planning.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Multimodal Graph-Temporal Network with Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Verification for Dynamic Slope Stability Prediction under Rainfall-Vegetation-Soil Coupling
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Overview Rainfall-induced shallow landslides on vegetated slopes are governed by nonlinear feedbacks among canopy interception, root water uptake, capillary hysteresis, and moisture-dependent root tensile reinforcement. Purely data-driven sequence models frequently violate water mass conservation and matric suction monotonicity during convective cloudbursts, whereas static soft-penalty physics-informed neural networks overlook drying-wetting retention loops, near-saturation root-soil slippage, and preferential macropore bypass. We present PIM-RVSNet, a physics-informed multimodal graph-temporal network coupled with an agentic hydro-mechanical equilibrium verifier for dynamic Factor of Safety (F_s(t)) and instability lead-time prediction. PIM-RVSNet integrates three irreducible mechanisms: a Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE) using multi-head Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention (DEH-CA) and vertical soil-horizon graph-recurrent message passing to align atmospheric forcing, depth-specific canopy-root traits, and four-layer soil profiles; a Differentiable Richards-Wu-Mohr-Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op) embedding scanning-curve van Genuchten hysteresis and saturation-attenuated root cohesion; and an Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Verifier (AHM-Verifier) that audits mass-balance drift, preferential bypass, and stress admissibility to iteratively recalibrate upper-boundary infiltration partitioning within at most three reflexion steps. Across 48 monitored slope units and 240 storm episodes (2,880 space-time states across four eco-geomorphic zones), PIM-RVSNet achieves a test coefficient of determination R^2 of 0.9514 ± 0.0028, RMSE_F_s of 0.1106 ± 0.0032, critical instability F1_crit of 0.8967 ± 0.0168, and a physical violation rate of 1.42 ± 0.41%, outperforming the strongest physics-informed baseline (R^2 = 0.9158 ± 0.0032, p_Holm = 1.24 × 10^-13) and extending mean pre-onset early-warning lead time from 2.15 h to 3.98 h. Cont

papers.title: A GeoAI framework for landslide susceptibility mapping using Google Earth Engine, ensemble machine learning, and SHAP explainable AI
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, yet susceptibility mapping in data-scarce areas remains challenging. This study proposes a reproducible Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) framework that integrates Google Earth Engine (GEE), ensemble machine learning, and explainable AI (XAI) for landslide susceptibility mapping in central Nepal. Using a balanced dataset of 9,479 observations from 4,743 landslide and 4,736 non-landslide locations, extracted seven conditioning factors: topographic (elevation, slope, aspect), climatic (rainfall), ecological (NDVI, land cover), and anthropogenic (population density) within the GEE cloud computing environment. Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models using stratified train-test splitting and 10-fold cross-validation. Both models showed strong predictive performance, with XGBoost achieving superior results (Accuracy: 88.3%, ROC-AUC: 0.952) compared to RF (Accuracy: 87.9%, ROC-AUC: 0.945). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified slope as the most influential predictor associated with model predictions followed by rainfall (16%) and elevation (15%), while lower NDVI values consistently correlated with higher susceptibility. The susceptibility map identified high-risk zones concentrated in Sindhupalchok, Dolakha, Dhading, Rasuwa, Gorkha, and Nuwakot districts. This framework reveals that freely available satellite data, cloud computing, and explainable machine learning can be effectively integrated for susceptibility mapping and community resilience initiatives.

papers.title: Reliability analysis of soil-rock composite slopes based on dimensionality reduction response surface method
papers.summary: To address the “curse of dimensionality” caused by high-dimensional parameters and the computational bottlenecks of 3D numerical simulations in the reliability evaluation of “overlying silty clay and underlying weathered mylonite” composite strata slopes, a reliability analysis framework combining 2D limit-equilibrium screening and a response-surface surrogate constructed from quasi-3D FLAC3D simulations is proposed. First, by combining the limit equilibrium method with an orthogonal experiment and multivariate analysis of variance (ANOVA), the 9-dimensional random variable space is reduced, identifying the cohesion, internal friction angle, and unit weight of the moderately weathered mylonite as the dominant parameters. Secondly, based on the equivalent continuum assumption for the fractured weathered rock mass, a quasi-3D finite-difference model implemented in FLAC3D is constructed, which demonstrates the progressive development of a deep-seated rotational failure mechanism in the composite slope. According to this, a second-order response surface surrogate model with a coefficient of determination R 2 = 0.9990 is developed using the Box–Behnken Design (BBD), which effectively captures the nonlinear coupling effects among the controlling parameters. Lastly, 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations using truncated-normal input distributions yield a baseline slope failure probability of 2.767% and an equivalent reliability index of 1.916. A Gaussian-Copula sensitivity analysis further shows that the estimated failure probability is influenced by the assumed dependence between cohesion and internal friction angle. The results demonstrate that probabilistic parameter variability can produce a non-negligible failure risk even when the deterministic mean - value condition gives F o S > 1.0 . This dimensionality-reduction response-surface framework provides an efficient approach for the probabilistic reliability assessment of heterogeneous Soil-Rock composite slopes.

papers.title: A real-time visual monitoring method for landslide creep using platform attitude self-calibration
papers.summary: High-frequency, high-precision, real-time displacement monitoring is essential for early warning of landslide creep, a key precursor to slope failure. However, platform attitude disturbances, such as wind-induced vibration and foundation settlement, can introduce spurious displacement into image sequences and reduce the accuracy of conventional vision-based monitoring. This study proposes a real-time visual monitoring technique for landslide creep based on platform attitude self-calibration. An optical tracker and an inertial measurement unit were integrated to acquire target images and attitude data simultaneously. A displacement decomposition model incorporating attitude fluctuations was developed to separate true slope movement from attitude-induced spurious displacement. Subpixel target localization used gradient-direction voting and weighted elliptical fitting, and real-time attitude estimation used an error-state Kalman filter. Indoor vibration tests at 40 m achieved an RMSE below 0.7 mm, with reductions of 0.955 and 0.846 compared with vision-only and vision-plus-reference-point correction approaches, respectively. During a 93-day field campaign at the Dayangshan landslide, Suzhou, the approach achieved a data capture rate of 0.986, an RMSE of 0.28–0.36 mm, and a correlation coefficient above 0.91 versus GNSS data. The approach provides a practical option for early warning of slope failure by accurately and continuously monitoring landslide creep under unstable platform conditions and unfavorable weather.

papers.title: Research on Displacement Prediction Model of Reservoir Slope Based on LRMA , LSTM, and GA ‐ BP
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurately predicting slope displacement is critical for slope stability assessment and geological disaster early‐warning. Most existing studies focus on single‐model improvement for slope displacement forecasting, lacking fair benchmark comparison between different models under identical engineering datasets, which restricts clear definition of model application boundaries. Taking nearly 500‐day monitoring displacement data of a reservoir bank slope as input, this paper comparatively investigated one statistical‐decomposition‐based data‐driven LRMA (Local Regression Moving Average) model and two other data‐driven models (LSTM, GA‐BP neural network) under a unified input–output framework and evaluation metrics. The LRMA model decomposes the displacement sequence into trend and periodic components, which are extracted by LOESS and adaptive moving average respectively. The LSTM and GA‐BP take the displacement of consecutive 5 days as input to predict the 6th‐day displacement. The test results indicate that the optimal LRMA, LSTM, and GA‐BP models have R 2 values of 0.5238, 0.8388, and 0.9628 in the test set, respectively. The core innovation lies in quantitatively revealing the respective applicable scenarios of two types of data‐driven models (statistical‐decomposition‐based and neural‐network‐based) for reservoir‐slope displacement prediction via parallel comparison. The LRMA with clear physical interpretation fits mechanism‐analysis scenarios; GA‐BP achieves the highest prediction accuracy and outperforms LSTM in prediction precision and stability for strong‐nonlinear displacement prediction, while LSTM is competent for nonlinear prediction tasks as well. This work provides a quantitative reference for reservoir bank slope stability evaluation and landslide disaster warning.

papers.title: Uzaktan Algılama ve Yapay Zekâ Entegrasyonu ile Afetlerin Analizi
papers.summary: "Monitoring and managing natural and human-induced disasters is vital for mitigating disaster risks and impacts due to increasing global climate variability, population growth, and rapid urbanization. Disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, and forest fires cause severe damage to human life and the natural environment. Their ability to spread over large areas and evolve rapidly often renders conventional field observation methods inadequate. In this context, remote sensing technologies offer significant advantages for disaster monitoring and analysis due to their capability to cover vast spatial areas and provide periodic data. Multispectral and high-resolution data obtained from satellite systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and LiDAR technologies are effectively utilized for disaster detection, damage assessment, monitoring spatial-temporal dynamics, and the generation of risk maps. Furthermore, the increasing volume and complexity of remote sensing data have accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and machine learning methods, into data analysis workflows. Convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory, and recently developed transformer-based models offer advanced solutions for the automated detection, classification, and mapping of disasters from remotely sensed data. Through the integration of these technologies, applications such as post-earthquake damage assessment, landslide susceptibility mapping, early detection and monitoring of forest fires, and mucilage formation detection can be performed rapidly and effectively. The convergence of remote sensing and artificial intelligence, commonly referred to as Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), further facilitates the development of risk prediction and decision support systems for potential disasters. This study provides a comprehensive review of the applications of these technologies across different types of disasters, highli

papers.title: Reproducibility materials for Terrain inputs and area filtering in landslide annotation recovery
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Analysis code, frozen protocols, split IDs, shared training-sample coordinates, source-data checksums, derived statistics, and execution instructions supporting the manuscript “Terrain inputs and area filtering in landslide annotation recovery.” The study compares multispectral inputs, slope, DEM, and area filtering on 3,799 Landslide4Sense patches, using random forests and histogram gradient boosting. Evaluation uses random whole-patch splits from the same dataset, with overlapping test sets. Component sizes refer to labeled annotation geometry. The package includes one source image patch and its annotation as a reproducibility sample. The full source dataset, fitted models, and large probability arrays are omitted; the supplied scripts document downloading the public data and regenerating the analysis. Source imagery and labels: https://zenodo.org/records/10463239 (CC BY 4.0). The package includes an English README_REPRODUCE.md and a SHA-256 member manifest. Funding: Open Research Project of the State Key Laboratory of Disaster Prevention and Reduction for Power Grid (SGHNFZ00JCJS2400037); National Key Research and Development Program of China (2024YFC3211201).

papers.title: Yıkıntı Atıklarının Yönetiminde Saha Değerlendirmesi ve Önceliklendirme Yaklaşımı
papers.summary: "Natural disasters have the potential to generate large amounts of debris. The amount of waste generated in an instant can far exceed the amount that would have accumulated over years, overwhelming local waste management facilities beyond their capacity. This waste leads to deterioration of water and air quality, noise pollution, negative impacts on flora and fauna, visual pollution, and negative socioeconomic effects. If managed effectively, disaster waste can become a valuable resource in the recycling and reconstruction process, contributing to social and economic improvement. Following the two earthquakes on February 6, 2023, with epicenters in Pazarcık and Elbistan (Kahramanmaraş), field visits and various meetings with relevant institutions were conducted in Kahramanmaraş and Hatay provinces to support the development of disaster/waste management plans, and the data obtained was evaluated. Within the scope of this evaluation, the existing dumping sites in both provinces were also examined separately regarding the storage and recycling of demolition waste that is currently present and may be generated from future demolitions. These examinations, along with criteria such as dumping site area, distance to the nearest settlement, distance to pasture land, distance to forest land, distance to a stream, presence of landslide risk, topographical condition of the site, quality, geological structure, and vegetation, were used to prioritize the sites using a multicriteria decision-making method. As a result of the study, an alternative model was developed that can be used to determine the most suitable sites for the storage and recycling of demolition waste."

papers.title: Soil erosion susceptibility modeling using stacking ensemble machine learning, Kangra District, north-western Himalaya, India
papers.summary: The present study aims to predict soil erosion-prone regions in Kangra District using ML algorithms; Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost and CatBoost and their stacking ensembles. Additionally, the study also utilizes the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) model to enhance the interpretability of the best-performing RF algorithm. For this, a comprehensive soil erosion point dataset was developed using empirical field survey integrated with visual interpretation of Google Earth historical images. The results show RF as the best-performing model, predicting 14.7% of the area into the very high susceptibility zone, followed by XGBoost (27.1%), SVM (24.4%) and CatBoost (16.4%), whereas the stacking ensemble predicted 25.2%. The SHAP analysis of the best-performing model (RF) indicates NDVI, slope and LULC as the primary governing factors influencing soil erosion in the region. This study also provides a scientific base for policy formulation and strategic planning to mitigate soil erosion in Kangra District.

papers.title: IoT-Based Smart Rock Fall Detection and Early Warning System for Mining and Hilly Regions: A Review
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Rockfalls are a recurring hazard in mining areas, road corridors, and hilly regions. They are difficult to predict because they usually show very little pre-failure deformation and collapse within a short time. Internet of Things (IoT) technology, which combines low-cost field sensors, wireless communication, cloud processing, and automated alerting, offers a practical way to monitor such slopes continuously. This review synthesizes five selected scholarly works that cover vibration-based stability assessment of falling-type rock masses, 5G-IoT monitoring with a tangent-angle warning criterion, micro-seismic rockfall detection with failure forecasting, a multi-sensor rockfall early warning system in the Himalaya, and an IoT-based landslide early warning framework deployed in India. The literature suggests that displacement alone is a weak indicator for brittle rock failure, and that dynamic indicators such as dominant frequency and acceleration amplitude ratio, or event-based indicators such as accumulated seismic energy, can show instability earlier. Field deployments also show that communication reliability, power supply, seasonal environmental effects, and the absence of validated alert thresholds are major practical constraints. The paper compares the studies’ methods and contributions, identifies cross-cutting challenges, and proposes directions for future investigation. Because the review is based on five selected papers rather than an exhaustive database search, it is presented as a focused narrative review and not as a systematic review.

papers.title: When anticipation fails: A forensic analysis of Tropical Cyclone Ditwah reveals whole-system performance limits in a small-island flood-risk system
papers.summary: Abstract. Tropical Cyclone (TC) Ditwah, which impacted Sri Lanka in November 2025, was one of the most damaging hydrometeorological disasters in the country's recent history, affecting more than two million people through widespread flooding and landslides. Early explanations attributed the disaster to failures in forecasting, reservoir operations, or institutional response. We argue instead that TC Ditwah revealed a breakdown in whole-system performance under extreme temporal stress. Using a forensic reconstruction spanning atmospheric evolution, hydrological response, reservoir operations, warning dissemination, institutional coordination, and community experience, we examine how multiple interconnected subsystems interacted during the event. Rapid cyclogenesis unusually close to Sri Lanka compressed forecast lead times, while the island's steep, rainfall-dominated catchments translated extreme rainfall into rapid flood responses across multiple basins. Reservoir preparedness, warning escalation, institutional decision processes, and community response operated on slower timescales, reducing the time available to convert anticipation into protective action. The resulting mismatch between fast physical processes and slower institutional and societal response generated an anticipation–action gap, despite the availability of hazard information. Rather than revealing isolated component failures, TC Ditwah exposed structural limitations in the design and operation of coupled flood-risk systems. We argue that improving forecasts alone is unlikely to substantially reduce future disaster risk unless forecasting, reservoir management, emergency governance, and community response are explicitly integrated into coordinated operational frameworks. More broadly, TC Ditwah illustrates the need to complement advances in prediction with simulation-based training, pre-defined decision protocols, and whole-system emergency operating modes capable of functioning under rapidly evolvi

papers.title: Comparative performance of maximum entropy, frequency ratio, and logistic regression models for landslide susceptibility mapping in Semarang Regency, Indonesia
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility mapping in many regions must rely on inventories compiled from community reporting, which provide presence data only and no field-verified non-occurrence points.Which modelling approach best suits such data remains unclear.This study compares Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), Frequency Ratio (FR), and logistic regression (LR) for landslide susceptibility mapping in Semarang Regency, Indonesia, using an identical set of conditioning factors and an identical validation scheme so that differences in performance reflect the methods themselves.An inventory of 445 landslide points, compiled from the records of the Regional Disaster Management Agency for 2021-2025 and from field survey, was modelled against 13 continuous conditioning factors at 30 m resolution and evaluated through spatial-block cross-validation (5 km blocks, five folds, ten random block assignments), with random five-fold cross-validation as a comparison.Discrimination was assessed with AUC, TSS at a threshold fixed on the training data, and McClish-standardised partial AUC restricted to the high-specificity range (0.8-1.0), with differences tested using the DeLong test and a paired bootstrap.MaxEnt and FR performed equivalently on the full AUC (0.688 and 0.691, mean of the ten block assignments; DeLong p < 0.05 in one of ten) and on TSS (0.278 and 0.269), both within the range of moderate discrimination.LR scored lower (AUC 0.653; TSS 0.222) and differed significantly from both, a gap that persisted across 1,000 pseudo-absence datasets and when pseudo-absences were kept at least 500 m or 1000 m from landslide points.MaxEnt outperformed FR only over the high-specificity range (pAUC 0.610 against 0.578; bootstrap p < 0.005 in all ten block assignments) and in the most susceptible class, where it captured 57.5% of events against 52.4% for FR and 45.6% for LR.The ranking of the models was unchanged when the inventory was thinned to a minimum of 100 m or 250 m between points.Slope was the str
