papers.title: Enerji Altyapılarının İklim Kaynaklı Afetlere Karşı Dayanıklılığı
papers.summary: "This study examines the vulnerability and resilience of energy infrastructures to climate changeinduced disasters from the perspectives of energy security, supply continuity, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. It addresses, within an integrated framework, the impacts of major climate hazards such as extreme heat, drought, heavy precipitation and flooding, storms, landslides, wildfires and icing on the energy system. In this context, the study evaluates heat stress and cooling-water constraints in thermal power plants, drought and changes in flow regimes in hydropower plants, temperature-related efficiency losses and site damage in solar power plants, and storm, icing and automatic shutdown mechanisms in wind power plants. It also discusses the risks posed by extreme heat, wind, floods and wildfires to transmission and distribution grids, as well as the climate-related impacts on natural gas, oil and storage infrastructures. The study shows that climate risks do not only cause physical damage, but also disrupt the functioning of the energy system through efficiency losses, capacity reductions, operational interruptions, supply chain disruptions, access constraints and service continuity problems. Therefore, location-based mapping of climate-related vulnerabilities and risks at the level of neighbourhoods, streets, facilities, line routes and critical infrastructure points is essential for identifying which infrastructure assets are exposed to which hazards and to what extent. In addition, institutionalizing data sharing through the protocols envisaged under Climate Law No. 7552 will enable reliable risk monitoring, systematic measurement of vulnerabilities and the timely prioritization of resilience investments. In light of Türkiye’s energy system characteristics and climate policy documents, the study identifies priority areas of sensitivity and develops resilienceoriented policy recommendations, including the updating of design standards, strengthenin

papers.title: Chapter 4: Glaciogenic sediments and structures in the Port Askaig Formation on the Garvellachs and Islay
authors: J. Hans Braakm Bruce K. Levell
papers.summary: In this chapter, we conduct a thorough reappraisal of evidence for glaciation in the Port Askaig Formation (PAF) based on comprehensive documentation of all exposures on the Garvellachs and parts of Islay. Diamictites and associated facies record a range of terrestrial, lacustrine and marine environments. Most massive diamictites on the Garvellachs contain structures indicating shear beneath grounded ice, including 'stoss-lee' clasts, strong preferred a-axis orientations, glaciotectonism of subjacent sediments, and streamlined and folded rafts, and are interpreted as subglacial traction tills and glaciotectonites. The Great Breccia on the Garvellachs and the Persabus Complex on Islay consist of folded and thrust megablocks and diamictite, interpreted as the product of proglacial glaciotectonic deformation in which permafrozen foreland materials were excavated and upthrust before being over-ridden. The PAF also contains intervals of laminated mudstones with dropstones, stratified diamictites, and interbeds of sandstone and conglomerate, interpreted as the products of subaqueous deposition in glaciolacustrine and glaciomarine environments. Glaciomarine deposition is most spectacularly recorded in the 'Disrupted Beds', including subaqueous fans, submarine landslides and rain-out of ice-rafted debris. Glaciogenic facies associations exhibit systematic evolution through time, revealing the interplay of climate, glacier advance–retreat cycles and sea-level change over the course of the Sturtian panglaciation.

papers.title: A strength reduction method for stochastic stability evaluation of landslide dams
papers.source: International Conference on Material Science and Environmental Engineering (MSEE)
papers.summary: In the context of emergency management, obtaining rapid and reliable stability evaluation of landslide dams is the primary task of disaster mitigation, because partial slope failure often accelerates dams failure shortly after formation. This paper takes a typical landslide dam as a practical case, adopts stochastic finite element method, nested under Monte Carlo framework, and generates a full‑domain random field model. In this paper, the effect of spatial variation of shear strength in different material regions on safety factor and failure possibility is systematically studied by using shear strength reduction technique. In addition, a random field model of slip region based on the concept of local strength reduction is introduced. Through strict comparison with the full‑domain random field model, the feasibility of the model and the improvement of computational efficiency are verified. Therefore, this study provides scientific basis and technical support for the stability evaluation of landslide dam slope.

papers.title: Desafios e perspectivas para o fortalecimento da infraestrutura hospitalar diante das mudanças climáticas
authors: Maria do Carmo de Rezende Teixeira Guerra
papers.summary: Climate change has intensified the occurrence of extreme hydrological events, such as floods, inundations, and landslides, generating significant impacts on urban infrastructure and healthcare systems. In this context, this study analyzes the challenges and prospects for adapting hospitals located in areas exposed to water-related disasters, considering the effects of climate change on healthcare capacity and hospital infrastructure. The research is characterized as exploratory and descriptive, using a qualitative approach based on a bibliographic and documentary review of scientific articles, institutional reports, and official documents related to climate change, public health, and risk management. The findings indicate that hydrological disasters compromise hospital physical structures, cause operational disruptions, reduce bed availability, and increase demand for emergency healthcare services. Emergency departments, diagnostic imaging units, and surgical centers were identified as the most vulnerable sectors during extreme events. The analysis also demonstrated that the lack of preventive planning, deficiencies in drainage systems, and the location of hospitals in flood-prone areas increase institutional risks. On the other hand, strategies such as contingency planning, workforce training, integration between healthcare services and civil defense agencies, resilient infrastructure, and nature-based solutions, including green areas and hospital gardens, contribute to strengthening the response capacity of healthcare institutions. It is concluded that the development of resilient hospitals requires integrated actions involving planning, management, infrastructure, and public policies aligned with the guidelines discussed within the framework of COP30, aiming to ensure continuity of care and population protection in the face of contemporary climate challenges.

papers.title: Numerical Forensic Analysis of Brittle Failure of Cantilever Sheet Pile Walls due to Point Infiltration in Soft Clay
papers.summary: The collapse of cantilevered sheet pile walls on very soft clay layers in urban areas is often exacerbated by overlooked anthropogenic factors, such as drainage system leaks. Conventional geotechnical analysis is generally biased toward short-term undrained parameters ( ) without considering the hazard of continuous saturation. This study aims to conduct an investigation using a 2D Finite Element Method (FEM) to evaluate the impact of drainage channel infiltration on the transition of soil hydromechanical behavior from the undrained to the drained phase based on a field case study. The analysis results indicate that seepage flow reduces the soil’s effective stress, lowering the Safety Factor (SF) from the existing critical limit of 1.07 and contributing to a simulated soil body collapse. Furthermore, a potential change in the landslide mechanisms was numerically observed; from a ductile global rotational failure (deformation 0.244 m) to a brittle failure and strain localization at the pinning depth (deformation 0.035 m). The simulated loss of soil shear strength, coupled with lateral hydrostatic pressure, contributed to structural over-stressing, marked by a surge in bending moment values exceeding 320% (from 129.0 to 421.2 kN·m/m) and a shift of the critical point toward the center of the span. As a practical implication, this study recommends the integration of proactive hydrological mitigation measures and the reactive installation of weep holes to prevent the failure of geotechnical infrastructure due to anthropogenic factors.

papers.title: Case studies in machine learning for geotechnical engineering: Applications, challenges, and future directions
papers.summary: No abstract available

papers.title: Integrating soil erosion modelling and field verification for spatial assessment of critical land
papers.summary: Land degradation is a global environmental issue that affects the ecological functions and sustainability of land resources.In Indonesia, degraded land conditions are commonly addressed through the concept of critical land, particularly in watershed assessment, management, and rehabilitation.Spatial approaches have been widely applied to identify critical land over large areas; however, their representativeness is strongly influenced by input data quality and may not fully reflect site-level degradation conditions.This study assessed critical land using a spatial approach that integrated key biophysical parameters with field-based verification in part of the Serang Watershed.Critical land was identified using a multicriteria spatial approach based on P.3/PDASHL/SET/KUM.1/7/2018.Land cover was derived from Sentinel-2A imagery using Random Forest and quantitatively assessed using 45 field reference points.Soil erosion was estimated using USLE, with soil erodibility determined through laboratory analysis of 18 soil samples representing different land units.Five criticality classes were identified, with Slightly Critical land dominating 58.45% of the study area, while Critical and Highly Critical land accounted for 6.27%.Field-based verification of areas classified as Critical and Highly Critical revealed diverse degradation characteristics, including rill and gully erosion, topsoil loss, shallow soil, slope failure, and anthropogenic disturbances.These findings indicate that integrating spatial modelling with field-based verification can provide site-level information to support the interpretation of critical-land conditions and the development of site-specific soil conservation and land rehabilitation measures.

papers.title: An AutoML and GeoAI workflow for comparative landslide susceptibility assessment in high-relief mountain terrain
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility mapping in complex mountain terrain demands modeling frameworks capable of resolving non-linear, high-dimensional conditioning factor relationships while maintaining spatial referencing integrity. This study applies and comparatively evaluates the AutoML and GeoAI tools implemented in ArcGIS Pro 3.5 for comparative LSM in Choman District, Kurdistan Region using LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, Random Trees, Extremely Randomized Trees, and a weighted Ensemble model. A spatially balanced training dataset of 2,384 samples was intersected with thirteen conditioning factors and partitioned into 75% training and 25% independent test subsets. On an independent holdout set the Ensemble model returned the lowest log-loss (0.0809) together with an accuracy of 97.15% (95% CI 95.48–98.21%), ROC-AUC of 0.9965, and KS of 0.943; its margin over the leading individual learners was not statistically significant, though it exceeded both bagging-based ensembles on every metric. Under five-fold spatial block cross-validation, adopted as the primary estimate of generalization performance, mean ROC-AUC was 0.993 ± 0.003 and mean accuracy 95.56 ± 1.20%. The three gradient boosting algorithms formed a coherent high-performance cluster, while Tree algorithms showed substantially higher log-loss and compressed probability distributions. Feature importance analysis identified NDVI, land cover, LS factor, and lithostratigraphic units as the four dominant predictors. Hot-spot stability analysis, perturbing the susceptibility index at 10%, 20%, and 30%, showed that 96.84%, 93.70%, and 88.90% of 1,373,610 terrain features respectively retained their original cluster classification, with interquartile ranges of 0 at the two lower magnitudes, indicating that the mapped clustering structure is robust to imprecision in the susceptibility values. This workflow provides a reproducible and uncertainty-aware methodology for similar mountain geohazard situations.

papers.title: Landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in high-consequence areas of the oilfield based on multi-band InSAR and machine learning
papers.summary: Loess landslides pose a serious threat to energy infrastructure on the Loess Plateau; however, studies on landslide identification and monitoring in high-consequence areas of oil and gas facilities remain limited. This study investigates landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in a high-consequence area of the Changqing Oilfield in Qingyang City, Gansu Province, China, using Lutan-1 and Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar data and machine learning. Combining optical remote sensing images and applying the Minimum Covariance Determinant method and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to the InSAR derived deformation results, 65 potential landslides are identified. A random forest model, incorporating 13 conditioning factors, is constructed to generate a susceptibility map, with Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP) analysis used to interpret factor contributions. The results indicate that high susceptibility zones are predominantly controlled by surface roughness, distance to streams, and land surface temperature, and contain the majority of identified landslide points. 21.7% of oilfield facilities fall within these high-risk zones, highlighting the urgent need for continuous monitoring. This integrated framework provides a practical approach for geological hazard prevention in loess areas with critical energy infrastructure.

papers.title: Data and code for: Embodied carbon of landslide remediation on a tropical national road: as-built retaining walls versus alternatives at least as safe
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Anonymised life cycle inventory (modules A1–A5 plus replacement within 50 years, B4), parameter ranges and pedigree scores, design checks, limit-equilibrium stability results, paired Monte Carlo results and the Python code (Bishop simplified slope stability, retaining wall checks, carbon and cost model) supporting a manuscript submitted to Transportation Geotechnics on two landslide repairs on a national road in East Kalimantan, Indonesia. Contract names, contractor, contract numbers and road names are anonymised.Files: Supplementary_material_S1.pdf (supplementary methods and results); Supplementary_material_S2_data_workbook.xlsx (data workbook); Supplementary_material_S2_code.zip (code, README_code.md and MIT LICENSE).Licences: data and documents CC BY 4.0; code MIT (see LICENSE in the zip). Funding: Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education (LPDP), grant 2025061124802886.

papers.title: Insights of the Effects of Rainfall Variability and Climate Change on Landslide Risk in the Road Infrastructure of the Colombian Andean Region
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This repository contains the R and Python code developed in this thesis. It includes scripts for (i) landslide susceptibility modelling with generalized additive models (GAMs) and machine- and deep-learning algorithms; (ii) wavelet analysis; (iii) bibliometric analysis; (iv) computation of extreme rainfall indices; (v) estimation of landslide magnitude probability; and (vi) Bayesian estimation of rainfall thresholds for landslide triggering. Third-party data (e.g., SGC–SIMMA landslide inventory, CMIP6 projections, INVÍAS road network) are not redistributed where their licences do not allow it; instead, the thesis cites their original sources and access conditions.

papers.title: Estimating soil water retention curves from co‐located in situ water content and matric potential sensors
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract The soil water retention curve (SWRC) governs water storage and redistribution in the vadose zone and is a key input for hydrologic and agroecosystem models. Laboratory evaporation methods provide high‐quality SWRCs but are destructive and represent static conditions that may not reflect in situ soil behavior under natural field conditions. Co‐located field sensors measuring volumetric water content ( θ ) and matric potential ( h ) offer a continuous, nondestructive alternative for estimating field‐based SWRCs. In this study, the extent to which SWRCs can be derived from field‐installed sensors by directly comparing in situ θ – h relationships with laboratory evaporation measurements was evaluated. Six parametric retention models (Brooks–Corey, Fredlund–Xing, Kosugi, van Genuchten‐mnvar, van Genuchten [ m = 1 − 1/ n ], and van Genuchten‐PDI) were fitted to laboratory and field datasets in silt‐loam soil. Model performance and parameter stability were assessed using root mean square error of water content (RMSE_ θ ), and corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc). Field capacity (FC), permanent wilting point (PWP), and plant‐available water (PAW) were also calculated. Field‐derived θ s was consistently lower than laboratory‐derived θ s , indicating effective saturation in field conditions than complete saturation in laboratory conditions. No single retention model consistently provided the best fit across all laboratory and field datasets. The FC was relatively consistent across models, but PWP and PAW were more sensitive to model structure and extrapolation for θ r . These results indicate that co‐located θ–h sensors can help field‐based SWRC estimation when model selection accounts for the limited suction domain. Additional high‐suction observations would improve constraint of dry‐end parameters and derived hydraulic indicators.

papers.title: Extreme precipitation events: a comprehensive catalog for northern Chile (17.5° S to 30.0° S)
papers.summary: Abstract. This study presents a comprehensive catalog of the extreme seasonal rainfall events of northern Chile between 1979 and 2019. We analyzed its meteorological patterns across three latitudinal bands (17.5° S–23.5° S, 23.5° S–27° S, and 27° S–30° S) using daily precipitation and mean daily temperature from the CR2METv2.5 product, and vertically integrated water vapor transport (IVT) data from ERA5 reanalysis. These events were classified into three main precipitation categories: Stratiform, Coastal, and Andes Mountain. The Andes Mountain category was further subdivided into five subcategories based on IVT patterns and precipitation location: north Andes, south Andes, along Andes, Convergence, and Westerly IVT. The catalog includes meteorological descriptors for each seasonal extreme event, such as: date, precipitation category, maximum precipitation within the latitudinal band, average storm temperature, and average snowline elevation determined using empirical method and MODIS remote sensing imagery. Additionally, we included the IVT and spatial snowcover derived from MODIS images for each event. To test the applicability of this catalog, we characterized extreme events composite results for the Austral summer between 27° S–30° S (latitudinal band 3). Additionally, we contrasted our catalog to existing landslide inventory and estimated approximate debris flow volumes for the March 2015 Atacama event. These findings can enhance the understanding of extreme precipitation events in arid and semiarid zones in Chile and provide a valuable resource for storyline analysis and precipitation pattern identification. The catalog can be accessed through the Zenodo platform at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14342936.

papers.title: Teachers' Creativity In Developing Kamishibai Media To Enhance Disaster Awareness Among Elementary School Students
papers.summary: Both Indonesia and Japan are situated in the Pacific Ring of Fire, characterized by high vulnerability to natural disasters. However, the implementation of disaster education in Indonesian elementary schools continues to face challenges, including the scarcity of contextual visual aids and the prevalence of one-way lecture methods. Kamishibai, a traditional Japanese visual storytelling art, offers substantial potential as an alternative instructional medium that synthesizes visual power, oral narration, and interactive theatrical expression to concretize abstract hazard concepts for young learners. This study aims to analyze teachers' creativity in designing Kamishibai media and to evaluate its effectiveness in disaster mitigation instruction. This research employed a quantitative descriptive evaluative survey approach. The study involved 36 educators across various educational levels, including elementary schools, kindergartens, junior high schools, and special education schools in West Java. Data collection utilized a Kamishibai media evaluation questionnaire comprising 12 items on a 1–5 Likert scale, open-ended questions regarding prior mitigation teaching practices, and visual documentation of the Kamishibai media produced by the teachers. Data were analyzed using univariate descriptive statistics to determine frequency distributions, satisfaction percentages, and mean scores. Results: The evaluation of Kamishibai media implementation yielded an overall grand mean score of 4.54 out of 5.00 (90.7% satisfaction rate). The highest ratings were achieved for the medium's capacity to concretize abstract disaster concepts (mean = 4.78; 100% positive response) and to facilitate structured content delivery (mean = 4.72; 100% positive response). The instructional materials developed by teachers during the workshop demonstrated diverse contextual mitigation themes, such as a flood scenario entitled "When the Flood Comes," earthquake simulations emphasizing the "drop, cover

papers.title: A receptor-based framework for comparing multi-hazard aggregation operators in forest ecosystem exposure assessment
papers.summary: Forest ecosystems in mountainous regions are increasingly exposed to interacting natural hazards, yet multi-hazard assessments commonly rely on single aggregation approaches that overlook how methodological choices influence ecosystem exposure patterns. This study proposes a receptor-based framework for comparing multi-hazard aggregation operators and demonstrates its application for forest ecosystem exposure assessment in Ilam Province, located in the Zagros Mountains of western Iran. The framework integrates hazard susceptibility modeling, aggregation operator comparison, and receptor-specific spatial analyses to systematically examine how different aggregation logics influence the magnitude and spatial configuration of ecosystem exposure. Four hazards, i.e., flood, landslide, wildfire, and drought, were modeled to generate susceptibility layers for forest exposure assessment using Random Forest models for flood, landslide, and wildfire, and the standardized precipitation index (SPI) for drought. Hazard layers were spatially harmonized and aggregated using five operators: Sum, Maximum, Fuzzy OR, Fuzzy AND, and Overlap. Forest ecosystems were treated as explicit receptors, enabling quantitative exposure evaluation through hazard dominance analysis, coincidence patterns, hotspot fragmentation metrics, and edge-to-core gradients. Wildfires (50.82%) and landslides (32.86%) dominated forest exposure, and 59.57% of forest areas were simultaneously exposed to two or more hazards, indicating widespread multi-hazard conditions. Aggregation choice substantially influenced both exposure magnitude and spatial configuration. Additive and union-based operators (Sum, Maximum, and Fuzzy OR) produced large, spatially continuous hotspot zones (largest patch index (LPI) >82%), highlighting broad forest areas subject to cumulative hazard pressure. In contrast, restrictive operators (Fuzzy AND and Overlap) generated smaller and more fragmented clusters, identifying localized sites of

papers.title: Revision of the Australian Geomechanics Society Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management
papers.summary: The Australian Geomechanics Society Guidelines for landslide risk management developed in 2007 (AGS 2007), provide guidance on best practice in landslide risk management within Australia and have since established international recognition and standing. They present a framework for landslide risk management, guidance on landslide zoning for land use planning and guidance on assessing risk from landslides. In 2023 the Australian Geomechanics Society jointly with the New Zealand Geotechnical Society commenced a process of updating the guidelines. This process involved contribution from a broad range of experts and sought to develop new guidelines that present state-of-the-art practice in landslide risk management. This paper sets out key updates made to the guidelines which include partitioning the guidelines into three separate guidelines: landslide risk assessment, landslide mapping and principles of landslide risk management. Whilst the purpose of the first 2 documents is to provide guidance to landslide specialists, the third is written in a less technical style and is intended to inform a range of stakeholders, for example land managers and regulators about the principles of landslide risk management, their role in the process and what to expect from landslide specialists.

papers.title: Runoff Interception Characteristics of a Y-Shaped Bamboo Structure for Slope Protection
papers.summary: Abstract Conventional slope protection systems are susceptible to runoff-induced erosion, surface-soil loss, and shallow soil deformation under rainfall conditions. This study developed a Y-shaped bamboo structure integrating runoff interception and seepage drainage functions. Model tests and theoretical analysis were conducted to investigate the runoff interception efficiency of the structure under simulated rainfall conditions. The results showed that the Y-shaped bamboo structure exhibited effective runoff interception performance, with the cumulative intercepted runoff increasing approximately linearly with rainfall duration. The included angle between the two wings had the greatest effect on runoff interception efficiency, followed by wing length and wing diameter, with these three parameters collectively accounting for 93.04% of the total variance. Furthermore, a theoretical runoff interception model coupling weir flow theory with Darcy's law was developed and validated against laboratory model tests, showing good agreement with the experimental results. The findings provide a theoretical basis for geometric optimization and support the potential application of Y-shaped bamboo structures in ecological slope protection.

papers.title: Kinematic Analysis of the Slopes of the Mutirão Quarry, in Seropédica, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
papers.summary: Kinematic analysis is one of the methods employed in rock mass stability studies. A detailed analysis was conducted on the slopes of Mutirão Quarry, a decommissioned unit in Seropédica, Rio de Janeiro. The site is used as a “training outcrop” for practical training of geology students at the UFRRJ – Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro. The rock mass consists of Neoproterozoic orthogneisses with low-angle dip banding, which does not influence slope stability. For this study, 204 discontinuity measurements collected between 2023 and 2025 were used, and ten slope segments were defined and analyzed, and the results were compared to field observations for validation. Structural analysis indicated four main discontinuity families, and kinematic analysis indicated higher probability of planar sliding and toppling (flexural and direct). However, the analysis revealed a significant discrepancy in wedge failure assessment; the software indicated significant failure probability percentages that were not confirmed in the field. This occurs because the last version of the program does not apply lateral limits to wedges, treating laterally limited planar failures as if they were actual wedges. However, for other processes, the analysis showed high adherence to observed reality.

papers.title: Typology of Landslides in the Himalaya
papers.summary: The Himalayas are among the most landslide-prone regions in the world. This region's diversity of landslide types reflects the complex interplay of micro-climatic conditions, active tectonics, geological weaknesses, high relief, and steep slopes. The specific typologies of landslides in the Himalayas, in general, consider factors like material type and movement style, with common landslide types that include debris slides, debris flows triggered by heavy rainfall or glacial melt; rockslides caused by steep slopes, the interplay of slope and geological discontinuity surfaces; and tectonic activity triggered by rainfall and seismic activities. The Himalayas have almost all types of slides, of all dimensions and proportions, from huge tectonic slides to ubiquitous shallow debris slides in deep overburden mass or old landslide debris mass. However, in cryosphere regions and around, the mass movements are influenced by climate change, extreme precipitation, glacial retreat, and permafrost degradation. In the trans-Himalayan region, where cold desert conditions occur, the landslides are distinctively different types, such as huge talus, slope wash and rockfall or rock avalanche on steeper slopes. Creep and subsidence in the Himalaya occur at an extremely slow, continuous, and often imperceptible pace. Yet, the downslope movement of soil and weathered rock remains widespread. Climatic shifts—particularly increased snowmelt and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)-are projected to intensify landslide activity and may even transform their typologies. This paper presents a comprehensive spectrum of landslide typology, highlighting how climatically driven triggers interact with diverse geomaterials across different Himalayan regions.

papers.title: Geotechnical Investigation and Process Interpretation of aLandslide-Prone Area in Medellín, Colombia
papers.summary: The project Inform@Risk has been developing a landslide early warning system in the informal settlement Bello Oriente on the north-eastern slope of the city of Medellín, Colombia, the subsurface of which is made up entirely of the ultramafic ‘Medellín Dunite’. The geotechnical investigations carried out in the project to determine the requirements of that system included multiple mappings, drillings, and laboratory tests. All these investigations discovered highly heterogeneous subsurface conditions, created by a combination of fracturing, weathering, serpentinization, and pseudokarst. This highly landslide-prone block-in-matrix structure, already influenced by past landslides, reaches a depth of at least 50 m, and shows no correlation between degree of weathering and depth. The shear parameters vary to a high degree, making the determination of a critical slope angle very difficult. All these factors make it challenging to predict the exact size, depth, velocity, and location of a possible landslide and are a great challenge for the layout of the early warning system. This study emphasizes the importance of detailed geological investigation and the collection of field data for a hazard analysis as basis for the development of landslide early warning systems.

papers.title: Integrating Satellite Surface Reflectance and Field Measurements to Predict Moisture Content Profiles in Bare-Soil Conditions
papers.summary: Landslides triggered by rainfall infiltration pose significant geotechnical hazards, yet predictive modeling remains limited by the lack of scalable, high-resolution soil moisture data. This study develops a machine learning-based Hydro/Spectral (H/S) model to predict volumetric water content (VWC) at multiple soil depths using Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery and in-situ soil temperature measurements from ten Kentucky Mesonet stations. Over 500 cloud-free images were processed within 160 m × 160 m bare-soil buffers, an area of interest significantly finer than the kilometer-scale resolutions typical of most satellite-based soil moisture predictions. For each image, statistical descriptors such as skewness, variance, and covariance eigenvalues were extracted from reflectance data in visible, near infrared, and shortwave infrared bands. These features were paired with daily in-situ measurements to train and validate multiple regression models. Random Forest outperformed other models, achieving the highest R² and lowest RMSE across all depths. Soil temperature and spectral indices such as the Normalized Difference Soil Index (NDSI) were identified as key predictors. Results demonstrate that reflectance and climate data can predict shallow soil moisture with moderate accuracy at fine spatial scales. This approach supports the development of scalable, non-invasive tools for monitoring unsaturated soil conditions and improving slope stability assessments under changing climate conditions.

papers.title: Exploring the Applicability of Three-Dimensional Limit Equilibrium Models for Landslide Susceptibility Analysis at the Reservoir Basin Scale
papers.summary: Landslides affecting slopes delimiting reservoir impoundments and the surrounding areas are a common hazard that can occur at different stages of a reservoir's operational life, due to factors like heavy rainfall, earthquakes, and impoundment level changes. Their occurrence significantly undermines the safe operation of reservoirs; hence, developing efficient techniques to assess landslide susceptibility is vital. This study is aimed at extending the application of 3D limit equilibrium (LE) slope stability analysis technique to the entire reservoir scale to generate landslide susceptibility maps under different groundwater conditions at San Pietro Dam, Southern Italy. The 3D LE assessment of landslide susceptibility, which is commonly performed at a single-slope scale, was implemented for the examined reservoir basin by using Slide3 software. All calculations were carried out on a geotechnical model with representative strength parameters built on a 3D geometry generated from a 10-m DEM. Results show that the approach can detect landslide-prone areas around the reservoir, characterized by low safety factor values. The accuracy increases from the assumption of dry slopes to scenarios of shallow groundwater levels. A general overestimation or an underestimation of the landslide susceptibility is observed when residual strength or peak strength parameters are respectively used. This implies that landslides in the area probably occurred under post-peak strength parameters, i.e., intermediate between peak and residual. Basically, the results shed light on the possibility of extending 3D LE analysis for slope stability analysis at the reservoir scale, even for deep landslides and complex geological contexts.

papers.title: Integrating Geoethics into Disaster Risk Management: a Framework for Resilience in Peru
papers.summary: Disaster risk management (DRM) in Peru remains constrained by fragmented governance, rapid informal urban expansion, and limited integration of geoscientific evidence into territorial planning. Recurrent impacts from earthquakes, landslides, floods, and debris flows demonstrate that predominantly technocratic and response-oriented approaches are insufficient to reduce risk in complex geodynamic settings. This paper proposes a geoethics-based framework for disaster risk management that strengthens engineering practices by embedding ethical principles, responsibility, transparency, equity, and prevention into decision-making processes. Building on the IAEG–IAPG Peru White Paper and the Sendai Framework Midterm Review, the study analyses structural, institutional, and technical gaps that hinder the effective use of hazard and risk information in Peru. The analysis shows that risk is not solely driven by natural hazards, but by cumulative interactions between geological processes, land-use decisions, and governance failures. Inconsistent methodologies, limited data interoperability, and weak enforcement of planning regulations contribute to the siting of settlements and infrastructure in high-hazard areas. From an engineering perspective, geoethics functions as a quality-control mechanism, reinforcing the obligation to apply scientifically robust methods, communicate uncertainty, and uphold duty of care in public safety–critical decisions. The proposed framework integrates geoethical principles with strategic actions in governance, territorial planning, geoscience education, and stakeholder engagement. Its implementation supports a shift toward prevention-oriented, socially accountable, and resilience-focused DRM. While grounded in the Peruvian context, the framework can be applied to other high-risk regions in Latin America and beyond, facing similar governance and geodynamic challenges.

papers.title: Understanding the Geohazard Characteristics of the Bobonaro Mélange Lithology and Its Implications for Sustainable Infrastructure in Timor-Leste
papers.summary: Geological hazards like landslides and slope failures have a major impact on the infrastructural development in Timor-Leste due to the geological complexity and the widespread occurrences of synorogenic deposits of Bobonaro Mélange lithology across Timor Island and the Banda Arc, with approximately 40% of Timor-Leste’s surface geology. This study presents an understanding of the geohazard characteristics of this lithology from a mineralogical and geotechnical framework across three study locations: Suai Expressway, Bee-Mean Road, and Balibo-Leolima Road. This study demonstrates the variability in concentrations of smectite clay (0.8-20%), with a clay content range up to 96.5%, a high plasticity index of up to 53.1%, and a low coefficient of permeability (in the 10⁻⁴ cm/sec range); these factors contribute directly and significantly to geological hazards. These values also determine the swelling-shrinking behavior with progressive and retrogressive landslide evolution, which revealed a high susceptibility to deformation under natural factors such as rainfall as well as anthropogenic influences, including deforestation and man-made slope cuts. Based on these characteristics, this study designates the Bobonaro mélange lithology as “Bobonaro problematic clay.” These findings provide an understanding for sustainable development in complex geological conditions through fostering a more resilient and sustainable infrastructure in Timor-Leste as well as contributing to safety and economic productivity. It also proposes transferable insights for geological hazard assessment that are applicable to the Bobonaro problematic clay found within the Banda Arc collision zone, as well as similar tectonic settings globally.

papers.title: Greenfield Finite Element Modelling for Damage Assessment of Axially Rigid Buildings Under Groundwater-Driven Slope Movements
papers.summary: This study presents the results of a numerical analysis aimed to investigate the ground movements induced by groundwater table rise in drained soil conditions on slopes and the deformation patterns associated with axially rigid, shallow-founded buildings located along the slope for a preliminary assessment of the potential induced damage. Slope geometry is examined using a multi-step elastoplastic finite element approach. The numerical simulations reproduce progressive groundwater rise, generating incremental greenfield displacements and strains with the progressive reduction of the factor of safety. The deformation parameters are quantified through greenfield displacements and strains evaluated at different positions along the slope. Damage categories (e.g., slight, moderate, severe) are inferred by correlating computed deformation parameters with established limiting-strain thresholds consistent with an axially rigid structural model. Results demonstrate that increasing pore water pressures significantly amplifies ground displacements whereas the spatial distribution of damage-related strains is primarily controlled by the evolving kinematics of the slope. The modelled ground displacements indicate a predominantly translational response in the central portion of the slope, combined with finite-slope and rotational components near the crest and toe. These kinematic differences control the spatial distribution of greenfield strain distribution, with the highest values mainly concentrated in the upper part of the slope. The proposed approach should therefore be interpreted as a preliminary greenfield-based assessment of strain levels for idealised axially rigid, shallow-founded buildings, rather than as a direct prediction of observed building damage. The results represent an initial step towards a screening-level framework linking groundwater-induced slope deformation, stability reduction and potential building-related strain levels.

papers.title: Enhancing Operational Resilience in Delivering Clean and Renewable Energy: Integrating Multidisciplinary Approaches to Mitigate Flood and Landslide Hazards in Geothermal Production Fields
papers.summary: Climate change is increasingly affecting the Philippines, bringing more intense and frequent hydro-meteorological events in recent years. With the country being highly vulnerable to natural hazards, it is imperative that proactive hazard mitigation strategies be employed to ensure the stability and continuous operation of geothermal power facilities despite adverse weather conditions. This study presents three case studies from geothermal production fields in the Philippines, where cascading geohazards—including earthquake-induced slope weakening, prolonged rainfall-triggered landslides, and flooding associated with landslide dam breaches—have caused significant operational disruptions and infrastructure damage. In one case, a breached landslide dam upstream triggered debris-laden flow that obstructed a critical drainage structure, resulting in unexpected flooding despite relatively low recorded rainfall at the facility. A multidisciplinary approach was employed, integrating hydrologic and hydraulic modeling, landslide inventory mapping, and geotechnical assessment to evaluate hazard interactions and identify vulnerable areas. The results highlight how initial triggering events can initiate a series of interrelated processes, where slope instability, sediment transport, and drainage blockage collectively amplify the impacts on geothermal infrastructure. Risk-based assessments were conducted to support the prioritization of mitigation measures, enabling more efficient allocation of resources. The findings underscore the importance of adopting a systems-based approach to geohazard assessment, supported by collaborative efforts among technical disciplines and stakeholders. Such approaches are essential in enhancing the operational resilience of geothermal facilities and ensuring the sustained delivery of clean and renewable energy under increasing climate variability.

papers.title: Which Geo-Auxiliary Information Improves Landslide Segmentation? A Systematic Study Using a Residual Dual-Branch SegFormer
papers.summary: Rapid post-event landslide mapping is essential for emergency response and disaster management; however, accurately delineating rainfall-induced landslides remains challenging because of their fragmented morphology, heterogeneous landscapes, and the complementary nature of Earth Observation data. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance using optical imagery, the contribution of different geo-auxiliary information to landslide segmentation and its transferability across regions remain insufficiently understood. This study proposes a Residual Dual-Branch SegFormer that integrates heterogeneous geospatial information through a lightweight residual Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) encoder and a novel Multi-Scale Geo-Auxiliary Gated Fusion Module (MGFM), enabling adaptive feature fusion while preserving the original SegFormer architecture. Using a multimodal dataset constructed from the March 2023 Tropical Cyclone Freddy event in southern Malawi, we systematically evaluate RGB imagery combined with optical, terrain, and Sentinel-1 SAR-derived auxiliary layers. The framework is assessed on a geographically independent test area and further validated through zero-shot transfer on the public Landslide4Scene and Lushan datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the following: (1) Integrating pre- and post-event SAR coherence with RGB imagery achieves the best overall performance when applied to areas that match the training data, reaching a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 80.56% and an F1-score of 78.03% in the independent Malawi test area. (2) RGB combined with slope represents the most effective among the evaluated static topographic configurations in zero-shot transfer to the two external datasets, consistently outperforming the RGB baseline. (3) The proposed framework exhibits strong cross-region generalization, achieving the highest transfer performance on both external datasets while demonstrating that SAR coherence pro

papers.title: Numerical investigation of progressive submarine landslides and the resulting wave response using a two-phase two-layer SPFEM
papers.summary: No abstract available

papers.title: Stakeholder Perspectives on Landslide Susceptibility Models in Nepal
papers.summary: Landslides are a recurring and fatal hazard in the Nepal Himalaya, leading to widespread development of landslide susceptibility maps to support planning and disaster risk management. Despite advances in modelling techniques, their practical uptake in governance remains inconsistent. This study explores how decision-makers and technical experts conceptualize and apply landslide susceptibility models in Nepal. Ten semi-structured interviews were conducted with stakeholders involved in landslide risk reduction and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Findings indicate a divergence in interpretation: participants with technical backgrounds tended to frame susceptibility maps as advisory or awareness-raising tools, whereas non-technical decision-makers expected more definitive information to guide regulatory action. Field verification was considered essential for decision legitimacy, particularly where model resolution, outdated data, or terrain complexity limited confidence. Scale mismatches, prediction errors, and ambiguity in terminology and color-coded classifications further influenced trust and practical application. The study reinforces international evidence that challenges in susceptibility mapping stem less from technical sophistication and more from clarity of scope, uncertainty communication, and alignment with governance needs. Strengthening this interface is critical to improving the real-world value of landslide models in Nepal as well as providing direction for the application of susceptibility maps elsewhere.

papers.title: Evolution of Shear Zone Materials in a Slowly Deforming Rock Slope: Mechanical Implications for Gámanjunni-3, Northern Norway
papers.summary: Rockslides with basal shear zones often creep with periodic accelerations controlled by shear-zone material properties. These properties influence hydraulic conductivity, residual friction angle, and rate dependence. We present mineralogical, grain-size distribution, and ring-shear data from a shear-band soil at the Gámanjunni-3 rockslide Northern Norway. X-ray diffraction indicates phyllosilicate-rich assemblages (>70 wt.% clay minerals) dominated by illite/mica and illite–vermiculite, with minor illite–smectite. Grain-size distributions at outcrop scale are sandy–gravelly. Ring-shear tests on a representative sample give apparent residual friction angle of ≈19–24° and predominantly rate-strengthening behavior from 0.01 to 2 mm/min, with a tentative drop in apparent friction at 10 mm/min. These results are consistent with a model in which deformation localizes along inherited foliation-parallel ductile shear zones, with comminution-driven clay enrichment reducing frictional strength and leading to steady deformation without rapid acceleration periods (the precursor to failure). Gámanjunni-3 is sensitive to external forcing, with implications for seasonal acceleration and climate-driven changes in slope stability in an area where increased rainfall intensity and duration is expected.

papers.title: Influence of Giant-Particle Content on Reservoir-Induced Deformation of Soil–Rock Mixed Bank Slopes: A Physical Simulation Study
papers.summary: Periodic reservoir water level fluctuations significantly affect the stability of soil–rock mixed bank slopes. To investigate the influence of giant-particle content on bank slope deformation during impoundment, physical model tests were conducted using the Zhugangshan Tunnel accumulation body in Tianquan County, Ya'an, as a prototype. Three slope models with different giant-particle contents (10%, 30%, and 50%) were tested under cyclic reservoir water level fluctuations. The results demonstrate that slope deformation mainly occurs during the first impoundment cycle. The deformation process includes soil softening, consolidation settlement, internal erosion, particle loss, and shallow surface sliding. As giant-particle content increases, the heterogeneity of the soil–rock mixture initially weakens slope stability. However, when a stable giant-particle skeleton forms, deformation resistance and overall stability improve significantly. The findings provide a reference for stability assessment and treatment of giant-particle soil–rock bank slopes in reservoir areas.

papers.title: Lake Biwa, Japan: A Valuable Case Study for Investigating Geological Conditions Vulnerable to Ground Failure
papers.summary: Historical cases worldwide show that coastal settlements can be rapidly submerged by earthquake-induced ground failure. The 1692 Port Royal earthquake in Jamaica, the 1999 İzmit earthquake in Turkey, and the 2018 Sulawesi earthquake in Indonesia all illustrate how seismic shaking, liquefaction and subaqueous landslides produce large-scale submergence. Against this global background, the Shimosakahama Sengen submerged site in Lake Biwa, Japan, provides an important lacustrine example for understanding similar processes. This study presents integrated geological investigations using: (1) underwater acoustic bathymetry, (2) sub-bottom profiler imaging (SBP), (3) onshore and underwater surface-wave velocity profiling, (4) Swedish Weight Sounding (SWS), and (5) vibro-hammer core sampling. Bathymetric data reveal hummocky terrain, depressions, and arcuate scarps suggestive of possible subaqueous landslide headwalls. Sub-bottom profiles identify a disturbed sediment layer approximately 0.5–2 m below the lakebed, overlying intact stratigraphy. Surface-wave analysis delineates lagoonal or sandbar deposits and a laterally extensive soft, low-velocity layer at ~5 m depth, likely representing a mechanically weak horizon that may have acted as a rupture surface during sediment displacement. SWS measurements and core samples corroborate the presence of a fine-sand or silt horizon with low penetration resistance corresponding to the low s-wave velocity layer. These findings suggest that the Lake Biwa ruins may have been submerged by earthquake-related ground failure, consistent with global analogs. Future work should expand comparative studies across submerged ruins to better constrain geotechnical properties of the sediments and evaluate their associated seismic-hazard implications.

papers.title: Transition Dynamics of Geological Disaster Resilience and Network Structure Analysis in Mountain Cities: Evidence from County-Level Areas in Western Sichuan Province, China
papers.summary: Against the background of intensifying global climate change and the continued expansion of human activities into mountainous areas, geological hazards such as landslides, rockfalls, and debris flows have become increasingly frequent, posing serious challenges to urban safety and sustainable development in mountainous regions. From a resilience perspective, this study selects 19 cities in western Sichuan Province as the study area and develops a three-dimensional geological-hazard resilience framework comprising adaptation, resistance, and recovery capacities. The entropy weight–TOPSIS method is employed to assess geological-hazard resilience from 2018 to 2022, while kernel density estimation, Markov chains, an improved gravity model, and social network analysis are integrated to investigate spatiotemporal evolution and network structure. The results show that: (1) geological-hazard resilience generally increased across the study area, while regional disparities continued to widen; (2) the three resilience dimensions gradually shifted from imbalance toward greater coordination, with adaptation and recovery capacities improving markedly, whereas resistance capacity remained relatively weak and exhibited greater fluctuations; (3) temporally, the kernel density distribution evolved from a sharper to a flatter pattern, indicating some improvement among low-resilience areas while differentiation persisted; spatially, resilience exhibited an “east-high, west-low” pattern, together with evident path dependence and neighborhood effects. Low-resilience areas showed relatively high state persistence, and upward transition probabilities varied under different neighborhood conditions; and (4) the spatial network structure became progressively denser, with increasing intercity connections and network density, although diffusion toward western areas remained limited and regional development disparities persisted. These findings provide a basis for disaster risk reduction and coor

papers.title: SAHAY: AN INTEGRATED, KERALA-FOCUSED DISASTER MANAGEMENT, EARLY-WARNING AND RESCUE COORDINATION PLATFORM
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as floods, landslides, and extreme rainfall require timely prediction, reliable information, effective communication, and coordinated emergency response. Recent research has explored Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Internet of Things (IoT), crowdsourcing, and early-warning technologies for different aspects of disaster management. However, many existing approaches remain fragmented, focusing mainly on prediction, monitoring, mapping, or information collection rather than connecting these functions with practical emergency response. This review examines existing disastermanagement research and software technologies, with particular emphasis on Kerala-specific studies related to landslides, rainfall, floods, and real-time monitoring. Based on the identified research gaps, SAHAY is proposed as an integrated Keralafocused disaster-management and decisionsupport platform that combines real-time weather and location data, AI/ML-based risk assessment, GIS visualization, personalized alerts, citizen incident reporting, SOS, evacuation and shelter assistance, and rescue-team coordination. The proposed platform aims to bridge the gap between disaster prediction and emergency response through a unified, multi-role system.

papers.title: Code for: Deglacial runoff events did not simply track mean hydroclimatic state in a Tibetan Plateau catchment
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: How runoff hazards respond to hydroclimatic mean state and variability remains unclear. Here we reconstruct 28 preserved runoff events spanning 21.7–10.5 thousand years before present from a landslide-dammed lake on the eastern Tibetan Plateau. A Bayesian chronology constrained by 11 optically stimulated luminescence ages propagates dating uncertainty into event-rate estimates. The Younger Dryas has the highest posterior median rate of 7.17 events per thousand years. Higher rates than during Heinrich Stadial 1 persist across tested Bacon configurations, whereas the comparison with the Bølling–Allerød is more model-sensitive. Hulu and Dongshiya–Laomu speleothem oxygen-isotope means during the Younger Dryas lie between those of these two intervals, while submillennial variability persists after detrending. This combination is consistent with hydroclimatic fluctuations contributing to runoff-threshold exceedance, potentially through intense summer rainfall. Sediment supply and preservation provide alternative or interacting explanations. These findings highlight variability and sedimentary processes alongside mean hydroclimatic conditions.

papers.title: Influence of a Deep-Drainage System on the Dynamics of the Succiso Landslide (Northern Apennines, Italy)
papers.summary: Deepseated landslides in the clayrich formations of the Northern Apennines are strongly influenced by groundwater dynamics and climatic variability. The Succiso landslide provides a valuable case study due to longterm monitoring and the installation of a deep drainage system between 2014 and 2016. By combining multidecadal rainfall data with displacement time series, we assess the evolution of hydrological forcing and drainage effectiveness across different activity phases. Displacement rates, computed from cumulative displacement increments, show a marked and sustained reduction following drainage installation, particularly during 2015–2023, confirming the effectiveness of groundwater lowering in reducing deformation. From late 2023 onwards, a renewed increase in displacement is observed across both monitored sectors. The relationship between hydrological forcing and landslide kinematics varies over time. During the predrainage phase, velocity generally increases with precipitation, though variability indicates additional control by internal hydromechanical processes. In the postdrainage phase, velocities remain low and largely insensitive to rainfall. In the most recent phase, increased activity occurs under wetter conditions; however, the relationship with antecedent precipitation remains weak and highly variable, suggesting that landslide response cannot be explained by hydrological forcing alone. These results highlight a nonstationary landslide behaviour and emphasise the role of evolving hydromechanical conditions in modulating system response. Continuous monitoring and adaptive management are therefore essential to ensure the longterm effectiveness of mitigation measures.

papers.title: Efficient Finite Element Modeling of Initial K0 Geostress and Shear-Slide Stability in Sloping Ground
papers.summary: Abstract Reliable initialization of in situ $${K}_{0}$$ K 0 stresses and efficient stability analysis are fundamental to robust finite-element modeling of infinite slopes. Yet, existing modeling schemes either apply gravity loading with an indirect $${K}_{0}-\nu $$ K 0 - ν mapping that is not mechanics-consistent for sloping ground, or require large computational domains that are expensive for repeated analyses. In this study, an efficient FEM framework is developed that retains the gravity load procedure (GLP) and addresses its stress-initialization limitation for homogeneous infinite slopes. Specifically, a closed-form coupling of Poisson’s ratio components is derived within a transversely isotropic elastic formulation, in which slope cross-anisotropy arises from stress-induced anisotropy. This coupling enforces target $${K}_{0}$$ K 0 -type geostress states in sloping ground, without using the conventional horizontal-ground $${K}_{0}-\nu $$ K 0 - ν relation. The formulation is implemented in a compact periodic unit-block FEM model (Geometry I, L/H = 0.2). It is combined with strength-reduction using an elastic–perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb model for shear-slide factor-of-safety (FOS) assessment. Results are evaluated against analytical infinite-slope solutions and conventional large-domain FEM simulations (Geometry II, L/H = 32) performed using COMSOL Multiphysics and PLAXIS 2D. The proposed model reproduces analytical $${K}_{0}$$ K 0 stress profiles across tested slope angles and pore-pressure ratios. It avoids spurious yielding during geostress initialization and provides FOS predictions in close agreement with analytical solutions under both dry and seepage-parallel conditions. Compared with the large-domain approach, it delivers substantially improved efficiency (at least ~ 4 × shorter runtime in tested cases) with orders-of-magnitude fewer degrees of freedom, while preserving the expected slope-parallel failure mechanism. The effects of slope angle, pore-pre

papers.title: Coupled InSAR and Stability Index for Early Detection of Rainfall-Induced Landslides
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides triggered by short-duration intense precipitation frequently lack detectable precursory surface deformation in InSAR (Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar) time series, owing to geometric distortions (layover and shadow) and limited satellite revisit intervals. To overcome these constraints, this study proposes an integrated early identification framework that couples SBAS-InSAR (Small Baseline Subset)-InSAR deformation monitoring with a rainfall-driven time-series SINMAP (Stability Index MAPping) stability index. Using long-term Sentinel-1 data from the Xishancun and Huangnibazi landslides in Li County, Sichuan Province, InSAR applicability was first quantified through R-index visibility and measurement sensitivity analyses. In zones of poor InSAR performance, a spatio-temporal cross-validation approach was applied to fuse deformation trends with dynamic stability index evolution for enhanced hazard delineation. Results indicate that the Xishancun landslide remains largely stable, with instability confined to the toe under heavy rainfall, whereas the Huangnibazi landslide exhibits greater rainfall sensitivity but severe monitoring challenges due to geometric distortions. Retrospective application to the catastrophic 23 July 2019 Jichang Town landslide (Shuicheng, Guizhou) successfully captured progressive destabilisation signals—via sharp stability index declines preceding failure—that were undetectable by InSAR alone. This coupled deformation–stability index method substantially improves early detection of concealed, rainfall-triggered landslides and provides a practical, transferable tool for risk assessment and early warning in complex mountainous terrains.

papers.title: Enhancing Cross-Regional Landslide Susceptibility Assessment via a Conditional Domain Adversarial Network
papers.summary: Accurate landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA) is essential for regional disaster prevention and mitigation planning. Although machine learning and deep learning models have been widely adopted for LSA, their transferability across regions is often compromised by distributional discrepancies between source and target datasets. To address this challenge, we adapted the conditional domain adversarial network (CDAN) framework for cross-regional landslide susceptibility assessment to mitigate domain shift and improve cross-regional robustness. Two cross-regional transfer experiments were conducted to compare CDAN with conventional machine learning, direct-transfer deep learning, and representative domain adaptation methods. The results showed that CDAN achieved the highest mean Accuracy and F1 score among the benchmark models in both target domains, with Accuracy values of 0.77 and 0.80 and F1 scores of 0.78 and 0.80, respectively. The corresponding values of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were 0.837 and 0.836, respectively. Neighborhood-based spatial information also improved the direct-transfer performance of conventional machine learning models compared with single-pixel representations. These results indicate that the CDAN-based framework can reduce the reliance on labeled target-domain samples and support county-level cross-regional landslide susceptibility assessment under domain shift.

papers.title: A Predictive Debris Flow Warning System Using Saturation Modelling: Development at Scotland's A83 Rest and Be Thankful
papers.summary: The A83 at Rest and Be Thankful (RaBT), Scotland, is a strategic transport corridor affected by frequent rainfall-triggered debris flows. Following two large landslide events in 2020 and the recognition of evolving slope behavior, a need emerged for an operational tool to support proportionate exposure risk management of hazards, while longer-term resilience options are progressed. A Saturation Hazard Matrix (SHM) was developed to provide daily hazard levels derived from a simplified soil saturation index and forecast rainfall totals, calibrated against a landslide inventory supported by rainfall records and time-lapse monitoring. The SHM expresses hazard in five levels linked to predefined operational actions, including enhanced inspection and diversion via the Old Military Road. Performance assessment against events reaching the A83 or protection measures indicates that higher hazard levels correspond to increased event likelihood, while maintaining a practicable balance between false alarms and missed events. The approach demonstrates how simplified saturation modelling can translate complex processes into a transparent decision framework for managing debris-flow hazard on transport infrastructure under conditions of uncertainty.

papers.title: Development Suitability on Mountainous Region in Kundasang, Malaysia
papers.summary: In line with Malaysia’s rapid advancement and urbanization, mountainous areas particularly those prone to active soil movement and landslides are no longer excluded from development and have increasingly become focal zones for infrastructure and urban expansion. This study aims to determine appropriate development suitability approach based on the physical and environmental characteristic of the area. Terrain mapping approach is implemented to provide a comprehensive conceptual evaluation for determining development suitability levels in mountainous region. Whereas, a landslide susceptibility assessment was conducted using the Susceptibility method (Information Value method) to quantify the influence of slope instability towards development suitability. The results were further correlated with elements at risk, particularly building materials and structural types, in order to identify the dominant construction materials and evaluate whether the existing structural systems are suitable and resilient under landslide-prone conditions. This approach is applied to Kundasang area in Sabah, Malaysia due to the topographic factor of hilly terrain, growing population and tourism demands. The findings of the study indicate that only 6.41% of the study area is classified suitable (Class I) for development and urban growth, reflecting the limited presence of stable terrain within this mountainous and landslide-prone environment. In contrast, the remaining 92.39% falls within the moderately suitable (Class II), less suitable (Class III) and unsuitable (Class IV) categories. Hence, this approach has demonstrated a reliable interpretation of development suitability in mountainous areas by incorporating key terrain and landslide-related factors, while also evaluating building materials and structural characteristics, thereby supporting sustainable, structurally resilient, and well-planned development.

papers.title: Heating-Induced Variation in Soil Strength and Its Mapping Using SWIR Spectroscopy
papers.summary: Temperature-dependent changes in residual shear strength are important for slope stability, landslide reactivation, and thermally loaded geotechnical structures. Although this response is controlled by mineral composition, there is no clear method for extending laboratory results to larger areas. This study combines temperature-controlled ring shear testing with short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectroscopy for eight mixtures of quartz-rich sand, kaolin, and bentonite. The specimens were tested at normal stresses of 50, 100, and 150 kPa and subjected to heating-cooling cycles between 20 and 80 °C. Sand and kaolin rich mixtures showed little change, whereas mixtures containing at least 50% bentonite showed clear heating-induced strengthening. For pure bentonite, the residual friction angle increased from 6.18° to 9.02°, corresponding to Δϕr=+2.84°. The SWIR spectra distinguished clay-bearing from clay-free mixtures using the absorption feature near 2209 nm and differentiated high-activity from low-activity clays using the feature near 1912 nm. Partial least-squares regression was then used to relate the spectra to residual friction angle. Finally, the spectral data were interpolated across a sand–kaolin–bentonite ternary space and combined with the laboratory results to map Δϕr. The study provides a first step toward mapping mineral-dependent thermal changes in soil strength.

papers.title: Mineralogy-Controlled Thermal Sensitivity of Residual Shear Strength: Evidence from Illitic Landslide Clay and Reconstituted Kaolin
papers.summary: The residual shear strength governs the long-term stability of slow-moving landslides and reactivated clayey shear zones. Temperature variations, driven by seasonal fluctuations, geothermal gradients, or climate change, can alter interparticle interactions and change the soil’s resistance to shearing. While the thermal response of soils has been studied with respect to various soil properties, its specific impact on residual shear strength remains poorly understood, particularly with respect to the coupled effects of mineralogy, normal stress, and shear rate. This study investigates the thermal sensitivity of residual shear strength in two fine-grained soils: (i) a natural illitic clay from the Dubičná landslide (Czechia) and (ii) a commercial Malaysian kaolin. Multi-rate ring shear tests were conducted at normal stresses of 50, 100, and 150 kPa under controlled temperatures of 20 °C and 70 °C. To capture varying structural states (apparent overconsolidated, transitional, and normally consolidated), specimens were prepared at initial water contents ranging from 55% to 100%. Shearing rates were varied from 0.018 to 1.8 mm/min to evaluate potential rate-dependence under residual conditions. Statistical analyses, including Welch’s t-test with defined significance thresholds, were employed to isolate systematic thermal effects from experimental scatter. The results reveal stress-dependent, mineralogy-controlled thermal responses. At a high normal stress of 150 kPa, the illitic Dubičná clay exhibits thermal strengthening, whereas the Malaysian kaolin demonstrates systematic thermal weakening. At a low normal stress of 50 kPa, temperature effects remain within experimental variability for both soils. These findings highlight that normal stress and clay mineralogy are primary drivers of thermal sensitivity under residual shear conditions, offering insights for the stability assessment of reactivated clay shear zones under changing environmental conditions.

papers.title: Pre-Event DEM-Based Deep-Seated Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using a Vision Transformer in the Kii Mountains, Japan
papers.summary: This study evaluates deep-seated landslide susceptibility using pre-event LiDAR-derived DEM data from the 2011 Kii Peninsula heavy rainfall disaster. Terrain parameters representing gravitational deformation were calculated and used as inputs to compare a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Vision Transformer (ViT). Validation results show that ViT achieved higher classification accuracy (0.867) than CNN (0.837), with recall for the landslide class exceeding 95%. ViT effectively captured broader geomorphological context, whereas CNN emphasized local terrain features. Both models showed difficulty in distinguishing DSGSD, reflecting its intermediate geomorphic characteristics. Tests in unseen areas indicate the potential to identify terrain prone to future failure using pre-event topography alone.

papers.title: Multi-Temporal Assessment of Slope Reactivation and Dormancy in a Himalayan Catchment Using Rainfall Patterns
papers.summary: The Mandakini catchment in the central Himalayas experienced widespread landslides during the 2013 North Indian Floods, particularly due to the Chorabari glacial lake outburst. The landslide activity within this catchment has been monitored for a period of over 10 years, from 2013 to 2023, during which time many landslides show reactivation and new ones are initiated. This study analyses decadal rainfall patterns (2013–2023) using reanalysis precipitation data to investigate the hydro-meteorological conditions associated with landslide recurrence and slope behaviour over time. We analyse seasonal rainfall distribution, interannual variability, and trends, including those of extreme rainfall events, to explore potential links between monsoonal dynamics and the reactivation of mapped landslides. The temporal correlation between rainfall anomalies and landslide activity provides insights into how slopes transition between active, dormant, and reactivated states. This analysis identifies indicative hydro-meteorological controls that contribute to the initiation of slope failures in such settings. This work highlights the need to consider long-term rainfall trends and seasonal thresholds in landslide-prone regions, especially with more frequent extreme rainfall events. The findings improve and support hazard assessment and the development of adaptive early warning strategies for Himalayan environments increasingly exposed to extreme hydroclimatic events.

papers.title: Risk Reduction Municipal Plan of João Monlevade, Brazil – a Social Perspective on Methods and Results
papers.summary: This paper presents some of the results of a risk reduction plan developed for a city located in Southeast Brazil, in which both mass movements and hydrological frequently occur and have already resulted in some life, houses and infrastructure losses. The methodology was based on the one developed by Ministry of Cities in 2006, updated and modified to encompass both the processes observed in urban areas and the socioeconomic vulnerability of the population. Risk areas were identified based on historical data and field mapping, during which the following activities were performed: evidence identification, geological-geotechnical and hydrological conditioning and occupational conditions. Based on this, the following processes were identified: landslides (translational and rotational), rock fall, creep, erosion (including margin undermining) and flooding. The study has identified 18 sectors with Moderate risk (R2), with 67 buildings; 21 sectors classified as High risk (R3), encompassing 599 buildings; and 17 sectors classified as Very High risk (R4), with 216 buildings. In total, 3204 people live in these risk areas, the majority living in areas subjected to flooding.

papers.title: Rainfall Induced Landslide Behaviour and the Implications of Climate Change on the Undercliff, Isle of Wight, UK
papers.summary: The Undercliff, on the south coast of the Isle of Wight UK, is a complex deep-seated mass movement, the origins of which date back to the Late Quaternary, when sea level and climate conditions were different than today. Development of urban infrastructure upon the Undercliff expanded rapidly from the 1850s which has since been subject to repeated damage from ground movement and landslides. The sustainability of development within the Undercliff is at risk from the impacts of future landslide-driven climate change and sea level rise. Forecasting the effects of climate and sea level change on land stability requires long-term empirical data and landslide ground model to show the relationships between weather (rainfall), groundwater, ground movement rates and landslide frequency. The likelihood and severity of the landslide behaviour scenarios range from the present day i.e. progressive slope creep to those that require pre-cursor initiating events i.e. failure of coastal defences, and others that cause a step change i.e. new landslide mechanism. Linking the landslide behaviour response to climate change, threshold events and mitigation using quantitative methods provides an objective basis to inform strategies to manage the risk, including planning and development control, engineering measures, in situ monitoring and engagement of the local community to share information and homeowner guidance.

papers.title: Data for: Deglacial runoff events did not simply track mean hydroclimatic state in a Tibetan Plateau catchment
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: How runoff hazards respond to hydroclimatic mean state and variability remains unclear. Hulu and Dongshiya–Laomu speleothem oxygen-isotope means during the Younger Dryas lie between those of these two intervals, while submillennial variability persists after detrending.
