papers.title: Recent Experiences with the Slope Stability Probability Classification (SSPC)
papers.summary: The Slope Stability Probability Classification (SSPC) is a classification system designed for estimating stability of slopes. The classification system is based on probabilities for individual failure mechanisms acting in slopes. Failure mechanisms considered are sliding, plane and wedge sliding, toppling, and groundmass failure. The SSPC works with weighting factors for method of excavation and weathering to compensate for past and future damage and changes due to method of excavation and weathering. The SSPC system may forecast major slides or failure of masses but also includes smaller but still devastating effects on the stability of a slope, such as loss of structure, raveling, and erosion of a slope. The SSPC system was developed on mainly rock slopes but also works for groundmasses with a more soil-type character. The system was developed in the early 1990’s and has been used throughout the world since thereafter. Some of the slopes that were classified in the 1990’s have been revisited in recent years to see whether the SSPC system still holds. In addition, a couple of other slopes have been assessed. The slopes are located in the Falset region in Catalunya, Spain, and in Germany. The results show the SSPC system is still very much useful and forecasts stability to a high degree of reliability.

papers.title: Effects of Root–Crack Dynamics on Soil Infiltration During the Growth Period Across Seasons
papers.summary: Reliable measurement of soil infiltration is fundamental in geotechnical engineering, especially when evaluating slope stability. Although vegetation is widely recognised for enhancing environmental resilience, the impact of plant roots on soil permeability remains debated in the literature. In addition, desiccation cracks play a critical role in modifying infiltration behaviour, particularly under seasonal changes. This study explores the coupled effects of root development and crack formation on infiltration rates across different seasons. Infiltration rates were measured directly in both bare and vegetated plots over a six-month observation period using the double-ring infiltrometer method. The interaction mechanisms between root development and crack dynamics were quantified through the Root Area Ratio (RAR) and Crack Identification Factor (CIF), assessed using a minirhizotron imaging system. The results demonstrate that as vetiver roots developed, they substantially altered crack characteristics, reducing 2 times lower CIF and producing a more irregular crack network compared to bare soil. Statistical analysis revealed positive correlations between both RAR and CIF with infiltration rate, suggesting that root proliferation and crack presence jointly facilitate water entry into the soil. Compared with the bare zone, the vegetated area exhibited markedly higher final infiltration rates, approximately 2.7 times greater in the summer dry period. The results indicate that infiltration was controlled by both surface cracking and vegetation-induced soil structure. Although bare soil exhibited higher CIF, vegetated plots showed higher infiltration rates, particularly during the dry summer period. This suggests that root-induced macropores and improved pore connectivity enhanced infiltration independently of visible surface crack.

papers.title: Geohazard-Induced Landslide: Stability Analysis and Engineering Perspectives, Case Study Applications, and Insights
papers.summary: This study investigates a landslide that occurred downstream of the Zemkan Dam in western Iran, damaging an irrigation canal located approximately 550 m downstream of the dam axis. The landslide developed along the interface between colluvial overburden materials and the underlying Taleh Zang Formation, composed of alternating limestone, calcareous marl, and thin shale layers. Field investigations and geotechnical studies identified extensive cracking, ground displacement, and deformation of the canal structure. The instability was primarily triggered by the 2018 Sarpol-e Zahab earthquake and was further aggravated by heavy rainfall infiltration and surcharge loading from spillway excavation materials deposited on the slope. Slope stability analyses were performed using Phase2 (v.08) under static and pseudo-static loading conditions. Based on the modeling results, a stabilization system consisting of reinforced in-situ concrete piles, cable anchors, slope correction, and surface drainage measures was designed. The analysis indicates that the proposed remedial system provides acceptable safety factors under both static and seismic conditions while effectively reducing slope displacement and pile loading. The study demonstrates the combined influence of geological, hydrological, and seismic factors on slope instability and highlights the effectiveness of integrated stabilization measures for landslide risk mitigation in dam-related infrastructure.

papers.title: The Infinite Slope Length: Investigating the Length-to-Depth Ratio Threshold
papers.summary: The Infinite Slope Method (ISM) is a standard tool in geotechnical engineering for rapid slope stability assessment, yet its validity depends on the geometric assumption that landslide length (L) greatly exceeds thickness (H). This research investigates the precise limits of this assumption by defining the minimum dimensions required for a slope to be characterized as "infinite." We present an innovative extension of the ISM that incorporates internal stress evaluation to quantify the stabilizing influence of the landslide toe on the Factor of Safety (FS). Following validation against empirical field data, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to determine the critical Length-to-Depth (L/H) threshold. Results indicate a clear quantitative boundary: for landslides with an L/H ratio below 30, the stabilizing effects of finite length are significant, and the conventional infinite slope assumption may no longer be considered negligible.

papers.title: Numerical Analysis of the Ngouache IV Landslide (Bafoussam, Cameroon) Using ABAQUS: Influence of Geotechnical Parameters
papers.summary: Over the past 25 years, landslides have caused substantial loss of life and damage to infrastructure in Cameroon. Among the most devastating events are the Ngouache IV landslide, which claimed more than 40 lives in October 2019, and the Mawoh landslide in Limbe, which resulted in 21 fatalities in 2001. More recently, the Dschang Cliff landslide caused multiple fatalities and severely disrupted national road traffic, underscoring the growing landslide hazard in the country. This study focuses on the Ngouache IV landslide and aims to model its failure mechanism to improve the understanding and mitigation of landslide hazards in similar geological and geomorphological settings across the country. Slope stability was evaluated through a numerical analysis that assessed the influence of key geotechnical parameters on slope behavior. The analysis was conducted using the finite element software ABAQUS. The investigated parameters include Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, cohesion, angle of internal friction, pore-water pressure, and void ratio. Results from this parametric study indicate that besides the pore-water pressure, the Young’s modulus exerts the greatest influence on slope deformation, leading to the largest predicted ground displacement and volume of mobilized material. These findings highlight the critical role of geotechnical parameters in slope stability modeling and provide valuable insights for landslide risk assessment and mitigation strategies in landslide-prone regions of Cameroon.

papers.title: Digital Transition and Artificial Intelligence for Early Warning and Risk Assessment in Engineering Geology
papers.summary: Digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming engineering geology by enabling more robust monitoring, risk assessment, and early warning for geohazards. This paper presents insights and practical results from two large-scale, EU-supported projects: 4G-MONITOR and CRISAFE. Both projects address the increasing complexity and frequency of geological hazards due to climate change and urbanization, focusing on the integration of sensor technologies, digital platforms, and AI analytics. The 4G-MONITOR project develops and validates a modular IoT sensor network—using magnetic, gravity, and geodetic sensors—combined with AI algorithms for real-time detection of ground deformations and hazardous movements. Data fusion and edge computing approaches support early warnings in remote areas, with applications in landslide and infrastructure monitoring. The CRISAFE project advances digital risk assessment and early warning for cascading multi-hazard scenarios (floods, earthquakes, liquefaction) in critical urban infrastructure. It applies harmonized, quantified methodologies for vulnerability analysis and integrates real-time sensor data with advanced visualization on IT platforms for infrastructure managers and first responders. AI-driven tools enhance risk communication and public awareness. Combined, these projects demonstrate the transformative potential of digital transition and AI to deliver holistic, interoperable, and actionable solutions in engineering geology, supporting both scientific innovation and civil protection across Europe.

papers.title: Stability Analysis of the Dubičná Landslide: The Role of Temperature-Dependent Friction in a Warming Ground
papers.summary: The role of ground temperature in slope stability remains under-researched outside of permafrost contexts, despite experimental evidence that residual shear strength varies measurably with temperature in clay-rich soils. Here, we present a preliminary thermo-mechanical stability analysis of the 5.5 m-thick Dubičná landslide in the Czech Republic, occurring in high-plasticity marlstones of the Březno Formation. Using a modified ring-shear apparatus, we quantified the thermal sensitivity of the residual shear strength of the shear-zone material, revealing measurable thermal strengthening during slow shearing. To evaluate potential slope-scale impacts, we developed a transient heat-flow model and calibrated it against historical data and in situ monitoring. This thermal history, combined with future projections to 2100, was used in combination with temperature-dependent Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion for slope stability determination. The model captured the phase lag and depth-dependent amplitude attenuation of temperature, allowing the factor of safety's sensitivity to surface temperature changes to be quantified. Transient stability analyses yield seasonal FS oscillations of ΔFS = 0.003 and a net thermally induced strengthening of ΔFS = 0.011 under the IPCC SSP5-8.5 projection (2015–2100) from pre-warming period to 2100.

papers.title: A Method for Estimating the Potential Damage Zone of Debris Flow using a Random Walk Model
papers.summary: A random walk model was applied to predict debris flow potential damage zones induced by landslide occurrences. The volume of failed material was estimated using the empirical relationship proposed by Guzzetti et al. (2009), and the runout distance corresponding to the failed material volume was predicted using the empirical relationship suggested by Corominas (1996). Debris flow runout trajectories were simulated using a random walk model, in which flow and deposition characteristics were simplified as a function of slope angle. The applicability of the proposed method was evaluated using landslide inventory data from the Cheonwangbong area of Mt. Jiri. The results indicate that the proposed approach can estimate debris flow potential damage zones with reasonable accuracy, and that a 10 m × 10 m cell resolution allows realistic reproduction of the observed damage zones.

papers.title: Mechanical and Microstructural Characterization of Deformed Volcaniclastic Rocks from the Lower Comondú, Baja California Sur, Mexico
papers.summary: Volcaniclastic rocks are widespread in tectonically deformed regions and play a key role in slope stability and hazard mitigation. However, their mechanical behavior remains poorly understood, particularly in weakly lithified, porous rock masses. This study examines the deformation mechanisms of pyroclastic and volcanoclastic rocks of the Lower Comondú Group in southern Baja California, Mexico. Field mapping reveals Miocene compressional deformation, characterized by folding, faulting, and injection features related to crustal shortening. Uniaxial and triaxial compressive tests were conducted on rock specimens. Unconfined and confined tests (30 MPa) were performed using a servo-hydraulic MTS 815 system with cyclic loading protocols. In addition, micro-CT scans were performed before and after these mechanical tests to monitor microstructural changes. Ignimbrites samples exhibit unconfined compressive strength (UCS) values of 16.5–17.5 MPa and elastic moduli of 0.8– 1 GPa, while sandstones range from 13.2 to 18.8 MPa and 0.78–1.6 GPa, respectively. Poisson’s ratios range from 0.1 to 0.3. The results indicate that porosity, mineralogy, and pumice-rich textures strongly control the brittle–ductile transition. Cyclic loading experiments also reveal progressive fracture development, stiffness degradation, and dilatancy. Micro-CT image analysis confirms that the internal damage zones are aligned with fractures existing in the non-deformed specimen. These results improve the geomechanical characterization of volcanosedimentary successions in compressive tectonic settings relevant for slope stability analysis, engineering design, and the assessment of geohazards in volcanic terrains such as those in some places in Baja California, México.

papers.title: Quantitative Assessment of Weathered Slope Soil Strength during Rainfall-Runoff Processes
papers.summary: In high-intensity rainstorms, weathered soil performance deteriorates with changes in soil mechanical properties caused by soil erosion, which will result in landslides. However, evaluation of weathered slope soil strength during rainfall-runoff processes is difficult. We proposed a temporal and spatial evaluation method of soil erosion and strength based on surface wave tests and three-dimensional (3-D) laser scanning. A rainfall experiment and a surface wave test were set up in a completely decomposed migmatitic granite slope of a highway. Shear wave velocity and rill distribution of slope during rainfall were obtained. With the increasing influence of infiltration and erosion, the shear wave velocity decreased from 105.8 m/s to 102.4 m/s, while the erosion rate increased slowly from 0% to 3.5%. The shear wave velocity decreased from 102.4 m/s to 97.3 m/s with an increase in erosion degree in the later stage, while the erosion rate increased rapidly from 3.5% to 7.1%. A correlation model between the erosion rate and shear wave velocity was obtained. With an increase in the erosion rate, the shear wave velocity decreased, which is related to the shear strength. A nonlinear decrease in soil shear strength at a certain depth increases the risk of sudden local collapse. Based on that, we can evaluate slope erosion degree by surface wave method and analyze the slope stability under rainfall erosion.

papers.title: Geotechnical and Hydrogeological Conditions of Subsidence Sites Detected by InSAR of Sentinel-1 Images from 2015 to 2020 in the Area of Barcelona
papers.summary: Sentinel-1 InSAR processing was conducted to monitor ground deformation in the area of Barcelona during 2015-2020 associated with the dewatering of a construction site for road tunnels beneath Glòries square. These data revealed the existence of 56 additional sites with significant subsidence across the city and its surroundings, including the Llobregat river lower valley and delta, and the Vallès graben North of Barcelona, between the cities of Rubí and La Llagosta. These subsiding locations generally exhibited displacement rates ranging from 1 to 10 cm*yr⁻¹. In order to explain the observed ground settlements, geotechnical logs, piezometric data, land use, construction works history, and field observations of damage in infrastructure were reviewed. The proposed subsidence mechanisms include the compaction of old landfills, landslides in steep terrain, recent construction of railway embankments, as well as the consolidation of thick clay layers. Despite the limited availability of data, fine-grained soils and anthropogenic fill materials were described for 35 sites, and subsidence was correlated with groundwater withdrawals in 3 sites. The results of this analysis show the potential of InSAR data as an efficient ground monitoring tool for hazard management.

papers.title: Geotechnical and Rheological Characteristics of Fine-Grained Sediments and Influencing Factors for Debris Flow Mobility
papers.summary: Fine-grained sediments that are remolded after slope failure may transform into debris flows; therefore, their post-failure mobility is better described by rheological parameters than by conventional intact-soil strength alone. This study evaluates the geotechnical and rheological behavior of natural fine-grained sediments collected in the Republic of Korea, using fall cone tests, steady-state shear tests, and oscillatory shear tests. The fall cone test was used to determine the remolded undrained shear strength, whereas the rheometer tests were used to estimate Bingham yield stress, Bingham viscosity, and dynamic yield points derived from storage and loss moduli. The results show shear-thinning behavior over the tested shear-rate range and indicate that rheological yield stresses are generally higher than the remolded undrained shear strength. In oscillatory shear, the fall cone strength lies between the first yield point, associated with the elastic or static regime, and the second yield point, associated with the onset of flow. These results suggest that undrained shear strength can be used as a simplified input when yield stress cannot be measured directly, but it should be interpreted as the maximum resistance of fully remolded soil rather than as a direct substitute for rheological yield stress.

papers.title: Advancing Remote Sensing for Semantic Landslide Hazard Mapping and Monitoring
papers.summary: Landslide hazard assessment and monitoring have traditionally relied on visual interpretation and heuristic classification methods, often limiting the spatial and temporal resolution of actionable insights. Recent advances in remote sensing technologies and machine learning offer new opportunities to automate and enhance the semantic understanding of landslide processes across diverse terrains. This study proposes a novel framework that integrates very high-resolution remote sensing data with semantic segmentation and classification algorithms to improve the accuracy, consistency, and interpretability of landslide hazard. Using a multi-sensor fusion approach, the framework applies deep learning-based semantic classification to differentiate landslide-prone areas from stable terrain and to identify geomorphic features, including scarp zones, depositional zones, and tension cracks. Time-series analysis enables continuous monitoring and detection of precursory signals, supporting dynamic hazard assessment and monitoring. The method is validated in complex coastal and mountainous environments with diverse lithologies and land cover, demonstrating robust performance in both detecting active landslides and mapping specific zones. This research highlights the potential of semantic remote sensing approaches for scalable, data-driven landslide hazard mapping and monitoring. The results support more informed decision-making for early warning systems, infrastructure planning, and disaster risk reduction in landslide-prone regions.

papers.title: Role of Topo-Climatic Factors in Landslide Susceptibility Mapping: A Machine Learning Perspective
papers.summary: With the rapid growth of machine learning (ML) applications in landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM), many studies have relied on large and diverse datasets to improve predictive performance. However, in data-scarce regions, model transferability becomes challenging, and not all input variables contribute meaningful information to landslide prediction, leading to the well-known problem of “garbage in, garbage out”. Therefore, careful selection of physically meaningful predictors is essential. In this study, we develop a Random Forest–based framework for landslide mapping using topographic and climatic factors only as inputs. Notably, the model incorporates effective rainfall (ER), derived from a process-based hydrological model, and a recently proposed topographic metric, topographic source density (D_ts), that were not used in previous LSM studies. Results demonstrate that incorporating these predictors substantially improves model performance, achieving a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.972. Overall, the findings suggest that a physically meaningful machine learning approach can reliably predict regional landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: Impact of Climate Change on Sediment Transfer and Associated Debris Flow Management: A Case Study in the Swiss Alps
papers.summary: In recent decades, the Swiss Alps have been affected by climate change at a much higher rate than the global average. Several signs, including hydrological modifications and changes in the frequency or magnitude of slope instabilities, are altering the landscape. Rock glaciers show very high melting rates that can lead to severe debris flow events and thus a change in both the associated risk and vulnerability of the population in affected areas. This leads public authorities to constantly increase the share of their budget allocated to natural hazards in order to maintain the risk at an acceptable level. In canton Wallis (Southwestern Swiss Alps), 200 sediment retention basins have been built since 1950, representing an average annual cost of roughly 75 million Swiss francs. In this paper, we want to expose with a case study, how climate change and geomorphological modifications can affect the management of natural hazards such as debris flow. The Péterey torrent is a stream flowing from the Bonnard rock glacier above the village of Zinal, and episodes of debris flow and slope erosion put the village under pressure. Previous geomorphological analysis and recorded environmental data show an increase in glacier movements and sediment transfer through debris flow. Here in Zinal, public authorities invested 4 million Swiss francs to increase the resilience of infrastructure and mitigate the risk for the local residents. Among other measures, the retention basin capacity was increased by 700% to reach 40,000 to 60,000 m3.

papers.title: Numerical Integration and Step-Size Sensitivity for a Coupled Hydro-Mechanical Constitutive Model of Root-Reinforced Unsaturated Soil
papers.summary: Increasing rainfall variability driven by climate change poses growing challenges to the stability of unsaturated slopes, where hydraulic and mechanical processes are highly coupled. Vegetation provides an effective nature-based solution, but its integration into quantitative geomechanical models remains limited. This study builds on a coupled hydro-mechanical constitutive model that incorporates root reinforcement effects within unsaturated soils. The formulation extends the Barcelona Basic Model by introducing root volume fraction as an internal variable, which modifies the critical state parameter, preconsolidation stress, and shear strength evolution. Both suction and biological reinforcement are treated as independent state variables that govern the yield surface geometry, hardening behaviour, and deformation response under environmental loading. The model is implemented using an implicit elastic predictor–plastic corrector stress update under strain control, and the numerical integration accuracy is evaluated through a step-size sensitivity study. Numerical results demonstrate convergence of the deviatoric and volumetric responses to a fine-increment benchmark and quantify relative errors as a function of strain increment. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting strain increments in subsequent parametric and finite-element simulations, where suction evolution and root-volume effects are activated and numerical artefacts must be distinguished from physical trends.

papers.title: Movement Mechanisms and Impact Range Assessment of High-Elevation Long-Runout Landslides in Southeastern Tibet
papers.summary: High-elevation long-runout landslides represent one of the most consequential hazard types in southeastern Tibet, posing significant threats to transportation corridors, settlements, river channels, and major engineering projects. The behavior of these landslides is controlled by coupled triggering factors including ancient landslide reactivation, structural preparation, hydroclimatic weakening, and involves complex physical mechanisms that influence their impact range, such as basal erosion, pore-pressure generation, and entrainment. This paper collects recent findings from several representative landslide cases, integrating fields investigations, physical experiments, and AI-based prediction methods to examine the movement mechanisms and assess potential impact ranges. The case studies show that high-elevation long-runout landslides may evolve through different pathways, ranging from localized creep of ancient landslide deposits to structurally prepared slope failure and rapid impact-entrainment cascades. Flume impact experiments reveal transient compression, high-frequency particle collisions, basal erosion, and entrainment, while ring shear tests indicate two major mechanical pathways: drained residual sliding in slow-moving ancient landslides and undrained impact-induced weakening in rapid long-runout failures. Based on these findings, a mechanism-informed assessment framework is proposed by linking landslide detection, activity diagnosis, mechanism interpretation, and rapid runout prediction. An AI-based landslide detector based on segment anything model (LSDSAM) supports regional landslide identification from remote-sensing imagery, while a physics-informed runout emulator enables fast prediction of potential impact ranges. This integrated pathway provides practical support for hazard assessment of high-elevation long-runout landslides in southeastern Tibet.

papers.title: Engineering Geological Assessment and Landslide Risk Mitigation along the famous Odontotos Railway in the Vouraikos Gorge, Greece
papers.summary: This study evaluates the engineering-geological conditions and landslide risks along the historic Odontotos Railway in the Vouraikos Gorge, Greece, an engineering feat completed in 1896. Connecting Diakopto to Kalavryta, this narrow-gauge railway traverses a tectonically active environment characterized by steep slopes and complex geological formations. The research focuses on mitigating risks from earthflows, debris flows, and rockfalls, which were significantly exacerbated following a devastating wildfire in 2023 that stripped the landscape of stabilizing vegetation. The methodological approach integrated detailed field mapping, on-site hazard identification, and the development of an Engineering Geological Map and a Rock and Earth Mass Movement Inventory Map. Slope gradients were classified to identify high-risk sectors, particularly those exceeding 65∘. Furthermore, 3D rockfall simulations were conducted using RocFall software to assess kinetic energy distributions and trajectory patterns. Results indicate that rock fragments of approximately 2.6 tonnes can generate kinetic energies up to 760 kJ, posing a direct threat to railway infrastructure. The study concludes by delineating critical locations and proposing technically substantiated protection measures—such as reinforced drainage and installation of specialized rock fall and debris flow barriers —to ensure the continued safety and functionality of this vital tourist corridor.

papers.title: Effects of DEM Resolution and Mapping Units and Their Interaction on Landslide Susceptibility Assessment: A Case Study from Shangyou County, Jiangxi, China
papers.summary: Abstract DEM resolution and mapping-unit selection influence terrain representation and landslide susceptibility assessment. However, the relative effects and interaction remain insufficiently understood in hilly regions dominated by shallow and small-scale landslides. Shangyou County, Jiangxi Province, China, was selected as the study area. The region is characterized by widespread shallow landslides and intensive slope-cutting activities. Two DEM datasets (5 m and 12.5 m) were combined with two mapping-unit types (grid cells and slope units) to establish four evaluation scenarios. Ten environmental factors, including elevation, slope, aspect, overburden thickness, engineering geological groups, distance to roads, distance to rivers, distance to faults, cut-slope density (CutDensity), and mean annual rainfall were used as model inputs. CutDensity was derived from 11912 mapped cut-slope polygons recorded irrespective of landslide occurrence and was used to represent anthropogenic disturbances. Model performance was assessed using repeated five-fold cross-validation and spatial block cross-validation, ROC-AUC, and feature-importance analysis. Differences between the original DEM products varied with mapping-unit type, with relatively small differences for grid-cell models but larger differences for slope-unit models. A significant DEM-mapping-unit interaction was observed for both RF and XGBoost. Controlled resampling showed generally small AUC differences between the original 5 m DEM and its 12.5 m resampled version, suggesting that differences between original DEM products cannot be attributed to nominal resolution alone. Feature-importance analysis showed that CutDensity ranked first in RF, whereas GeoGroup had the highest importance in XGBoost. Removing CutDensity reduced the mean AUC by 0.0293 for RF and 0.0240 for XGBoost. Map comparisons focused on spatial agreement, class transitions, and observed landslide proportions, recognizing the limitations of quantile

papers.title: Risk Assessment in Road Corridors: The Case of National Route 32, Costa Rica
papers.summary: A methodological guide was developed in Costa Rica to integrate risk assessment and management in road corridors exposed to earthquakes, slope instability, lahars, and floods, which was applied to a pilot study case on National Road 32. A multicriteria approach identifies hazards, quantifies vulnerability, and supports the formulation of mitigation and adaptation measures. Seismicity, landslides, and short-term climate variability, potentially altered by anthropogenic global warming, are the most significant hazards; combined with increasing vulnerability, they are the primary drivers of current and future structural and economic damage and losses. The accuracy of risk estimates depends on the availability and reliability of data on exposed elements, as well as access to software capable of detailed hazard and vulnerability assessments. Results with reduced epistemic uncertainties rely upon robust datasets and information, including digital elevation models, geological and geotechnical data, rainfall, and river flow records, as well as seismic acceleration and spectral data. This foundation supports rational recommendations for strengthening road infrastructure exposed to intense events in mountainous, piedmont, and lowland areas. The guidelines provide a framework for informed decision-making, design, planning, and operation of resilient investments and offer a replicable methodology for other lifelines to enhance the capacity to manage risk and adapt infrastructure to current and future climate, hydrometeorological, and geodynamic challenges.

papers.title: S/F and criticals for kaupuni stre, mailiili stream and the occurence at karston bridge wahiawa
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract: C.A.S.H-M Spatial Simulation & Structural Stress Analysis Across Oʻahu Watersheds This study establishes a rigorous spatial simulation and structural stress framework utilizing the custom C.A.S.H-M (Correlation and Ablation of Structured Hanging-Mass) model to evaluate flood hazards, landslides, and bridge integrity across critical Oʻahu drainage corridors. By integrating verified Google Earth coordinate anchors with a universal density-field power spectrum exponent (\bm{\beta = -1.3765}), scalar field amplifications were computed across three distinct hydrological incident zones: 1. Kaupuni Place, Waiʻanae (\bm{21.4479^\circ\text{ N}, -158.1906^\circ\text{ W}}): Modeled across a leeward transition zone with a camera range scale parameter of \bm{975.21\text{ m}}, yielding a baseline structural stress index of \bm{\sigma_{stress} = 12.2568}. 2. Māʻiliʻili Stream (\bm{21.4317^\circ\text{ N}, -158.1825^\circ\text{ W}}): Evaluated across high-energy coastal basalt and limestone transitions with a scale parameter of \bm{4,620.43\text{ m}}, producing a heightened stress concentration index of \bm{\sigma_{stress} = 58.0776}. 3. Kaukonahua Bridge & Wahiawā Dam Corridor (\bm{21.5034^\circ\text{ N}, -158.0251^\circ\text{ W}}): Analyzed under catastrophic peak discharge and debris-choke loading conditions with a range scale of \bm{5,910.12\text{ m}}, registering a critical structural stress peak of \bm{\sigma_{bridge} = 74.3120}. These computational metrics validate that structural stress localization scales predictably with localized topography and camera range parameters. The findings directly inform the deployment of off-grid telemetry networks—such as the 27-node SIAFI LoRaWAN self-healing mesh and WaiPolo sonar reference systems—providing early detection of scaled-invariant degradation 6 to 12 hours prior to failure. papers.title: Multi-source Data Analysis for Assessing Active Slow-moving Landslides Exhibiting Limited Geomorphic Evidence: the Santa Cecilia Case Study (Northern Apennines, Italy)
papers.summary: The detection and kinematic assessment of slow-moving landslides in geologically complex settings can be challenging, especially when the landslides exhibit limited geomorphic evidence despite being active. The Santa Cecilia landslide, located in the Piacenza Apennines (Northern Italy) is one of these cases. This study aims to a preliminary characterization of the landslide through the integrated analysis of geomorphological observations, subsurface investigations, and multi-temporal monitoring data. High-resolution UAV-LiDAR (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) data were used to support geomorphological mapping and the identification of surface features. Subsurface conditions were investigated through geophysical investigations, boreholes, and inclinometer monitoring, providing constraints on lithological heterogeneity and deformation depth. Multi-Temporal Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (MT-InSAR) analysis, based on Sentinel-1 data acquired between 2019 and 2024, was applied to detect and quantify surface displacements, from both ascending and descending orbits, allowing assessment of the influence of satellite line-of-sight geometry on displacement detection. The integration of MT-InSAR results with inclinometric measurements highlights spatial variability in deformation rates within the landslide body, with more active sectors showing coherent kinematic signals across independent datasets. Results suggest a transition from brittle deformation affecting competent lithologies in the upper slope to more distributed movement within fine-grained materials downslope. Although the proposed kinematic model is preliminary, it provides a coherent framework for interpreting landslide dynamics and for guiding future monitoring and investigation campaigns, aimed at defining the most appropriate rick mitigation strategies.

papers.title: The 2026 Rasuwa Disaster: A Transboundary Rock–Ice Avalanche, Himalayan Tsunami, and Cascading Hazards
papers.summary: The Himalaya is increasingly affected by high-mountain disasters driven by the interactions among cryospheric change since 1990, slope instability, thawing of glacial deposits and rock-mass permafrost, avalanches, and river systems. The 2026 Rasuwa disaster in the Nepal Himalaya highlights the destructive potential of these cascading processes, in which a massive rock–ice avalanche transformed into a devastating downstream flood and sediment-laden flow. This event is referred to as a “Himalayan tsunami” because the rapidly propagating flood and debris-flow wave resembled the destructive waves of an oceanic tsunami. Similar, although comparatively smaller, disasters have occurred across the Himalaya, including the Seti River disaster in Pokhara, Nepal, on 5 May 2012; the Bhotekoshi disaster in Sindhupalchowk, Nepal, in July 2016; the Chamoli disaster in India on 7 February 2021; the Melamchi disaster in Nepal on 15 June 2021; and the Sikkim disaster in India on 3 October 2023. Together, these events demonstrate how high-altitude mass movements and hydrological processes can propagate through mountain river systems, threatening downstream settlements and critical infrastructure. Based on satellite imagery, available field observations, photographs, and geomorphological interpretation, this study examines the source characteristics, cascading processes, and environmental implications of the Rasuwa disaster. Rapid fragmentation and movement, combined with river interaction and the entrainment of sediment and water, provide a reasonable mechanism for the destructive downstream flood and debris-flow wave. The event underscores the limitations of isolated, single-hazard assessments and downstream-focused monitoring. Effective risk reduction requires integrated source-to-sink (S2S) investigations, high-altitude slope materials and glacier monitoring, real-time river observation, transboundary data sharing, impact-based early-warning systems, and risk-sensitive infrastructur

papers.title: Landslide Hazard Mapping in Tbilisi (Georgia)
papers.summary: Geological hazards such as landslides, debris ﬂows, rock avalanches, rockfalls has always been and still represents a major threat for communities all over the world, causing extensive damage and often times the destruction of infrastructures and facilities. Geological-related, adverse phenomena are more frequent in mountainous countries with complicated geological, tectonic, climate and morphological settings. Tbilisi has a very convenient location and is not only the capital of the country, but also a hub of the transit corridor. However, in the conditions of complex morphological and geological environment, as well as high pressure of technogenic activities, geo-ecological complications have reached a critical level. Within the framework of a program led by Department of Geology of Georgia, landslide hazard assessment was done. Based on the analysis and generalization of produced (historical) materials, laboratory and field studies, the research evaluates the combination of factors that determine the tendencies of landslide hazards. Landslide processes are widespread, causing economic loss and damage to the city's infrastructure and, most tragically, often resulting in human casualties. Surveys in the study area revealed different type of landslides, based on that inventory map and GIS database was created/updated. Geological maps published in the last century were revised and updated, as well as various thematic (elevation, slope and aspect) maps were processed. Based on all this information, a hazard zoning map was compiled. Research classifies the protective adaptation measures, which are necessary to mitigate or completely eliminate the hazards, according to their type and genesis.

papers.title: Landslide Mitigation in Volumetric-Sensitive Soils: Integrated Stabilization Design for the Kalibeng Formation
papers.summary: Landslides and ground movements significantly threaten Semarang City, Indonesia, particularly in the Deliksari area. This region’s vulnerability stems from its location within the Kalibeng Formation, characterized by brownish-gray marly clay identified as montmorillonite. This expansive clay, combined with complex geological structures like joints and faults, creates high soil porosity and erosivity, leading to discontinuous layers prone to failure. This study conducts a geotechnical assessment and stability analysis. Field investigations via cone penetration tests (qc) yielded a cone resistance of 82 kg/cm² (8.04 MPa) at 20 m depth. Laboratory results showed a Liquid Limit (LL) of 148.12% and free swell of 425%. Using the Stark and Eid correlation, we determined the average friction angle (ϕAverage) to be 12.65°. Back-calculation via GeoStudio on the existing slope revealed a critical Safety Factor (SF) of 0.343. To mitigate instability, we modelled two reinforcement simulations. The first, utilizing a counterweight, gabions, bamboo piles, and one 600 mm diameter bore pile, yielded an SF of 0.684. The second simulation, which added a second bore pile, significantly increased stability to an SF of 1.611. Consequently, the recommended design features a 1V:5H slope counterweight supported by two bore piles, gabions, and 4 m deep bamboo piles. To manage pore water pressure, a 60 cm sand drain wrapped in non-woven geotextile is integrated between the embankment and original soil.

papers.title: LiDAR for Rapid Geomorphological Assessment, Examples in Relict Periglacial and Landslide Landsystems
papers.summary: Areas of relict periglacial (permafrost) landforms, including landslides, cambering, valley bulge and associated gulls are often challenging to delineate from ground mapping alone. This submission presents the advances in ground model assessment offered by airborne LiDAR (laser scanning) data sets for engineering geomorphology. High resolution digital elevation models derived from the LiDAR imagery can be utilized to interpret and visualize the on-ground geomorphology. The available LiDAR imagery is described, and examples of their use presented from classic case study sites.

papers.title: Influence of hydraulic conductivity variability on slope stability modelling in a first-order watershed
papers.summary: Abstract In landslide studies, the definition of geotechnical and hydrological parameters provides the basis for deterministic slope-stability modelling. However, their availability and spatial representativeness remain important limitations for watershed-scale applications. This study evaluated the influence of different saturated hydraulic conductivity (K sat ) spatialization approaches on Factor of Safety (FS) estimates using a deterministic slope-stability model in a first-order watershed. A Digital Terrain Model was used to derive morphometric and hydrological parameters, while field measurements of K sat supported three parameterization approaches: morphology-based, inverse distance weighting (IDW), and a single representative value. Instability scenarios were evaluated using a landslide scar inventory, and soil samples from six K sat measurement points were used to characterize particle-size distribution. Among the tested parameter configurations, maximum soil depth and initial groundwater-table depth produced greater differences in model results than K sat spatialization. K sat showed limited spatial variability, with measurements at 30 cm depth spanning from 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹, whereas those at 50 cm were concentrated around 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹. Higher clay contents with depth at some sampling points may have contributed to the observed decrease in K sat . Overall, within the observed range of K sat variability, a single representative value provided a practical alternative to spatially distributed parameterization in the studied first-order watershed. These findings are applicable to first-order watersheds where shallow landsliding is recurrent; broader applications involving greater geomorphological diversity and different predominant slope processes may require K sat characterization across a wider range of geomorphological compartments.

papers.title: Slowing a Large Landslide to Maintain a Highway
papers.summary: In August 2023, cracking across both lanes of State Highway 1 (‘SH1’) was observed near Utiku, New Zealand. The locations of the mapped cracks coincided with the headscarp of the existing Utiku Landslide, a large, deep-seated, slow-moving landslide that has intermittently impacted SH1 and the North Island Main Trunk railway, since at least the 1960s. The surface cracking and deformation resulted from renewed movement of the landslide along the basal failure plane some 55-75 m below SH1, caused by elevated groundwater levels resulting from many months of above-average rainfall. A remedial design involving four components was developed: (i) minor road realignment, as well as undercut and subgrade improvement; (ii) installation of fanned inclined drains to relieve groundwater pressure and improve landslide stability; (iii) surface water and pavement drainage improvements; (iv) ongoing instrumentation and monitoring. The fanned inclined drains almost immediately had significant impacts on groundwater levels, in places lowering them by close to 9 m. This paper addresses the geology and history of the Utiku Landslide, and how this informed the remedial design. The assessment of the 2023 landslide movement, the design of the fanned inclined drains, including the performance-based approach to optimising design and construction, as well as the monitoring results which show the beneficial impacts of the drains on groundwater levels and landslide stability are discussed in detail. We conclude by providing recommendations for the application of this approach to similar projects.

papers.title: Compaction Effect on Open-Pit Coal Mine Disposal Material: An Experimental Study, South Kalimantan, Indonesia
papers.summary: Disposal slope stability is a significant matter in open-pit coal mines. Mechanical compaction of disposal materials made of sand-clay mixtures is essential for regulating slope stability and total disposal capacity. This study investigates the effect of mechanical compaction using a 20-ton vibratory compactor on the compaction characteristics and dry density of disposal material. Field investigation was conducted at disposal Block K and Block G of an open-pit coal mine in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, where the materials consist of sandstone-claystone mixtures derived from the Warukin Formation. A large sampling tube (13.3 cm diameter) was used to collect undisturbed samples at depths of up to 1.5 m along multiple disposal lanes that were mechanically compacted. For validation, the measured density values were then compared to California Bearing Ratio estimates derived from Dynamic Cone Penetrometer tests. Field test results with a 2 m lift dumping layer indicate that additional compaction using a 20-ton compactor applied over 40 passes significantly increased dry density value of the disposal material. At a depth of 0.3 m, dry density increased from 1.56 g/cm³ to 1.90 g/cm³ in Block K and from 1.23 g/cm³ to 1.69 g/cm³ in Block G.

papers.title: Mechanical deterioration and damage evolution of coal specimens under drying–wetting cycles
papers.summary: Utilizing underground mine reservoirs for pumped hydroelectric storage (PHS) stations represents a highly promising approach for large-scale energy storage. However, the long-term exposure of coal pillar dams to drying-wetting cycles (DWC) poses a severe risk of structural instability. This study investigated the mechanical degradation and damage mechanisms of coal specimens, leveraging triaxial loading coupled with acoustic emission (AE) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) monitoring. The results indicated that the compressive strength and cohesion underwent non-uniform, multi-stage degradation with increasing DWC, with the most acute deterioration occurring after the first cycle. AE monitoring revealed that with increasing DWC, the frequency of high-amplitude AE events escalated, and their peaks shifted forward. Concurrently, the overall b -value exhibited a downward trend. RA-AF analysis showed an increasing fraction of shear-related AE signals with increasing DWC. NMR testing revealed predominantly unimodal T 2 spectra dominated by small pores. With increasing DWC, the relative fraction of small pores decreased, whereas those of medium and large pores increased, indicating a shift toward larger pore structures. These findings provide laboratory evidence of DWC-related coal deterioration relevant to further material assessments for underground reservoirs and potential PHS applications.

papers.title: A Three-Tier Evidence Hierarchy with Conditioned Generative Models for Discrete Fracture Network Reconstruction from Borehole Scanline Observations
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Fracture networks govern the mechanical behaviour of rock masses, and their accurate characterisation underpins slope stability, excavation design, and rock mass classification. Direct field observations sample only a small part of the fracture system, so much of the geometry remains unknown. This study presents an evidence-guided framework for reconstructing two-dimensional discrete fracture networks from sparse borehole scanline observations, organised as a three-tier hierarchy based on observational certainty. Measured traces are retained as Tier 1 anchors under a tolerance-based containment criterion, indicated traces are extended by a family-conditioned length predictor built around an Enhanced Variational Autoencoder, and inferred traces are generated for unobserved regions by a sequential transformer that learns the typical spatial layout of each joint family. All candidates pass through a multi-objective scorer that enforces seven geological constraints. The framework was validated on nine fully mapped bench faces of an open-pit mine, comprising 512 traces across three systematic joint families and random joints, at borehole spacings of 3 to 11 m. Relative to a Monte Carlo baseline, it reduced held-out per-family orientation error for all three joint families and improved the overall agreement with the mapped orientation and length distributions by about a third. Leave-one-bench-face-out testing confirmed that this performance reflects the framework rather than the particular faces held out. Reconstruction quality depended on a trade-off in observation spacing, with intermediate layouts giving the best overall balance across orientation accuracy, spatial fidelity, and network topology for the studied rock mass.

papers.title: Impact of high-volume steel slag with varying particle sizes on engineering properties of micro silica- modified concrete
papers.summary: Abstract The use of steel slag (SS) as partial replacement of natural fine and coarse aggregates and micro silica (MS) as partial replacement of cement was experimented with respect to engineering performance of concrete. In the present study, 0–70% of the natural sand and gravel, respectively, were replaced by fine steel slag (FSS) and coarse steel slag (CSS) as replacements on an absolute-volume basis. Also 10% MS was added to selected mixes in which 0%, 30%, 50%, and 70% SS was used. Workability, density, compressive strength, splitting tensile strength, flexural strength, sorptivity, ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) and performance in an adopted modified freeze–thaw exposure protocol were assessed. The SS-only mixtures showed the best compressive strength of 42.1 MPa which was obtained from the 40% SS mixture with no MS. However, when the SS replacement level increased, the compressive strength values decreased, even though the density of the concrete was increased, for example, to 70% SS, compressive strength was reduced to 31.8 MPa. The tested combinations of mixtures containing MS had 30% SS + 10% MS with the best overall combination of mechanical and durability related properties measured. The improvements observed herein are similar to those reported in literature for the filler and pozzolanic effects but were not directly ascertained in the present study by microstructural characterization, and thus specific changes in the interfacial transition zone, pore structure or C–S–H formation are not directly obtained. Likewise, the occurrence of possible volumetric instability and microcracking at high SS replacement levels are literature-supported interpretations, due to the absence of measurement of free CaO/free MgO contents and expansion. The results of the freeze-thaw test, based on the modified exposure protocol, are comparative in nature and do not represent standard performance. The results of a screening-level embodiment of carbon comparison showed that t

papers.title: Study on the sodium storage performance of zinc/sulfur co-doped hard carbon materials
papers.source: International Conference on Material Science and Environmental Engineering (MSEE)
papers.summary: To enhance sodium storage capacity, cycling stability, and rate performance in hard carbon (HC) materials, high-temperature pyrolysis was used to dope different heteroatoms (Zn, S, and Zn/S co-doping) into HC. The H-Zn/S-HC-1050 carbon material was obtained using a temperature-controlled strategy with acid treatment. Its composition and microstructure were characterized, and its electrochemical performance was evaluated. The results demonstrate that the Zn/S co-doped carbon material (Zn/S-HC) exhibited better rate performance than single-element doped counterparts (Zn- HC and S-HC), due to the formation of ZnS particles during pyrolysis that continuously etched the carbon skeleton and created porous rich pore structures, thereby increasing the number of active sites. In addition, the temperature regulation during the Zn/S co-doping process was optimized to optimize the synergy between dopants and microstructural features of HC. Acid washing prevented the introduction of excessive impurities that could deteriorate the electrochemical performance. At a current density of 50 mA g⁻¹,H-Zn/S-HC-1050 exhibited a reversible discharge capacity of 276.3 mAh g⁻¹, i.e., a 15.46% increase compared to the original Zn/S-HC material (239.3 mAh g⁻¹). After 100 charge–discharge cycles at 100 mA g⁻¹, it maintained a reversible capacity of 201.65 mAh g⁻¹. These results confirm that H-Zn/S-HC-1050 leverages the synergistic effects Zn/S co-doping by optimizing the degree of carbonization and reducing the impurity adhesion, which offers offering a viable route to designing high-performance hard carbon materials.

papers.title: Laboratory-scale LID infrastructure schemes for highly polluted urban stormwater runoff improvement: setup and initial testing
papers.summary: Urban stormwater runoff in highly polluted environments contains elevated concentrations of nutrients, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, as well as chemical oxygen demand (COD), posing significant challenges to environmental water quality. This study investigates the laboratory-scale setup and efficiency of three low-impact development (LID) systems, namely, rain gardens, filter strips, and vegetated swales, for treating synthetic stormwater mimicking highly polluted urban runoff. Experiments were conducted under controlled hydraulic loading rates (HLRs) and pollutant concentrations to evaluate pollutant removal efficiency. Rain gardens, constructed with layered engineered media, including sand, compost, and iron-enhanced biochar, achieved the highest pollutant removal, with average reductions of 70% for total phosphorus (TP), 65% for nitrate-N (NO₃⁻-N), and 85% for COD. Vegetated filter strips achieved moderate nutrient reductions of 45% for TP and 40% for NO₃⁻-N, and 60% for COD. Vegetated swales achieved average reductions of 60% for TP, 55% for NO₃⁻-N, and 65% for COD. The research compares the pollutant removal performance of three LID prototype types under controlled laboratory high-pollution conditions, while recognising that differences in media composition, vegetation, and hydraulic behaviour were not independently evaluated. The rain garden prototype demonstrated the highest overall pollutant removal efficiency, while the swale and filter strip showed comparatively lower performance under the tested conditions. These results suggest that combining different LID types in a treatment train may enhance overall system performance, particularly for pollutants such as dissolved organic nitrogen and COD in highly polluted runoff. The novelty of this study lies in the controlled laboratory comparison of multiple LID typologies under highly polluted conditions representative of poorly serviced urban environments, for which limited experimental data currently ex

papers.title: Enhancing spalling prevention of self‐compacting concrete at elevated temperatures: Incorporation of steel‐ PVA fibers
papers.summary: Abstract Self‐compacting concrete (SCC) is widely used for its excellent workability, but its dense internal structure causes spalling at elevated temperatures, which poses a critical risk to structural integrity and engineering safety. This study proposes a synergistic reinforcement scheme of steel and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fibers, with steel fiber volume fractions of 0, 0.4%, 0.8%, 1.2%, 1.4% and PVA fiber volume fractions of 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.3%. The effects of single‐doped and hybrid fibers on the high‐temperature spalling resistance of SCC were investigated via high‐temperature tests, gas permeability measurements, mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Results show that ≥0.1 vol.% PVA fibers completely prevent SCC spalling under engineering high‐temperature conditions, compared with 100% spalling of the reference group; 1.4% single‐doped steel fibers reduce the spalling degree to 4.32%, providing practical dosage references. SCC gas permeability remains acceptable below 400°C but degrades sharply above 600°C, and higher fiber content effectively retards this degradation to maintain steam‐release capacity. 400°C is the critical temperature for pore‐structure degradation, where thermal‐stress concentration accelerates interfacial microcracking and impairs structural performance. Microscopic analyses reveal that PVA fibers melt at ~230°C to form interconnected steam‐venting channels with slight pore coarsening, while steel fibers restrain crack propagation via three‐dimensional bridging for complementary interfacial protection. A temperature‐dependent two‐stage synergistic mechanism is proposed: steel fibers control cracks below 400°C, and PVA fibers realize steam‐pressure relief above 400°C. This greatly improves the high‐temperature spalling resistance of SCC and offers theoretical–experimental support for its fire‐resistant engineering design.

papers.title: Study on the expansion characteristics and semi-empirical damage model of cemented sulfur-containing tailings backfill
papers.summary: In cemented sulfur-containing tailings backfill (CSTB), secondary products from sulfide oxidation alter the internal pore structure, induce expansion cracking, and consequently degrade the mechanical strength. Laboratory experiments elucidated the evolution of the expansion rate ( ε ) with curing times (14–102 days) and sulfur content, and the influence of backfill microstructure on ε . The expansion rate exhibited a positive correlation with both curing times and sulfur content, showing a distinct inflection point at 28 days beyond which it accelerated. This accelerated expansion was concomitant with a sharp increase in the content of harmful pores, attributed to the formation of isolated pores within the backfill matrix. A time-dependent semi-empirical damage model for strength was established based on the Lemaitre strain equivalence hypothesis and the Weibull distribution. This model incorporates the expansion rate ( ε ) as its key state variable, which is itself a function of curing time ( T ) and sulfur content ( C ). The proposed semi-empirical damage model demonstrates strong agreement with the experimental data. The evolution laws of the key state variables are empirically derived from experimental data within the tested parameter ranges (sulfur content 8%–16%, curing time 14–102 days), and the model is therefore presented as a semi-empirical formulation for engineering applications. This model successfully delineates the evolution of total damage in the backfill under varying mix parameters and curing times. This study aims to forecast the long-term strength and damage evolution of cemented sulfur-containing tailings backfill under various curing times, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for backfill design in mining operations.

papers.title: Contrasting invasion risks of Pomacea canaliculata and Pontederia crassipes under future climate change in the middle and lower reaches of Yangtze River
papers.summary: The invasion and spread of alien aquatic organisms pose an increasing threat to ecosystem stability and functioning, biodiversity conservation, and socioeconomic development under ongoing climate change. However, limited attention has been given to the compound ecological risks of multi-species invasions driven by the combined effects of climate factors, topography, water quality, vegetation, and other environmental variables under future climate scenarios. Focusing on Pomacea canaliculata (P. canaliculata) and Pontederia crassipes ( P. crassipes ), this study employed the MaxEnt model and spatial analysis to identify key environmental determinants and to project current and future habitat suitability in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin under SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. The results show that the MaxEnt model performed with high accuracy for P. crassipes (AUC = 0.954) and good accuracy for P. canaliculata (AUC = 0.880). Temperature-related variables predominantly constrained the distribution of P. crassipes , with a cumulative contribution of 44.2%, particularly isothermality and temperature seasonality, whereas P. canaliculata was jointly influenced by terrain factors and thermal conditions, with contribution rates of 40.5% and 23.3%, respectively. In terms of current habitat distribution, P. canaliculata (28.23 × 10 4 km 2 ) occupies a larger range than P. crassipes (5.77 × 10 4 km 2 ), with P. canaliculata exhibiting a widespread distribution mainly concentrated in the Hanjiang Plain and the Jiangsu-Anhui coastal plains, whereas P. crassipes follows a belt-like distribution pattern, primarily spreading in Poyang Lake and the Yangtze River Delta. From 2021 to 2100, the suitable habitat of P. canaliculata is projected to expand under both SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios, with a more extensive and rapid expansion under the high-emission scenario (SSP585) (reaching 35.06 × 10 4 km 2 during 20 4 1–2060, an increase of 6.83 × 10 4 km 2 from present)

papers.title: Experimental investigation of suction flow enhancement in submerged jet pumps via perforated mixing chamber
papers.summary: Liquid–liquid jet pumps are essential in dredging, slurry transport, and submerged mixing applications, yet their suction performance remains constrained by the limited entrainment area in conventional solid-walled mixing chambers. This study experimentally investigates the geometric modification of using perforated mixing chambers that enable distributed radial suction driven by the hydrostatic pressure differential between the surrounding fluid and the low-pressure core induced by the motive jet. Seven perforated mixing chamber designs, differing in pore diameter, perforation density, spatial arrangement (aligned vs. staggered), and active perforated length, were tested against a non-perforated baseline in a fully submerged test rig. Performance was quantified primarily through the suction flow ratio ( M ) and specific energy consumption (SEC). All perforated configurations demonstrated superior entrainment compared to the conventional design. The optimal configuration was identified through parametric analysis and verified in a dedicated confirmation experiment. This configuration, at a dimensionless perforation ratio of τ ≈ 26.59 × 10 −3 , achieved a mean suction flow ratio of 6.97, corresponding to a 39.4% increase in the volumetric entrainment, while simultaneously reducing specific energy consumption by up to 39.45%. This configuration also shows a rise in the hydraulic efficiency from 7.8% (baseline) to 10.9% which overcomes the maximum theoretical efficiency value for conventional jet pump by 36.3%. A dimensionless perforation ratio ( τ , which is the ratio of the total open area of the perforations to the total surface area of the perforated section of the mixing chamber) was introduced to generalize the findings, revealing an optimal operating window. Below this range, suction is under-saturated; above it, excessive open area causes flow disturbances and pressure recovery that diminish returns. These results establish perforated mixing chambers as an effe

papers.title: Impact of the spatial layout of effective impervious area increments on urban stormwater peak flow and runoff volume
papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: To reveal the influence mechanism of the layout of effective impervious area (EIA) on urban stormwater processes，a refined stormwater model was constructed，and upstream and downstream sub-catchments were delineated. Taking the Shuangqiaobang runoff plot in Changzhou，Southern Jiangsu，China，as a typical study area，the impact on peak flow and runoff volume were systematically analyzed by setting different scenarios of EIA increments with different locations and scales. Results showed that the location of the EIA，infiltration capacity of the original pervious surface，and rainfall magnitude are key factors affecting the hydrological response. The spatial location effect of newly added EIA is significant，with the growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume in downstream areas being significantly higher than those in upstream areas，showing maximum difference of 18.48% and 7.70% under the moderate-infiltration scenario，respectively. Pervious areas with stronger original infiltration capacity exhibit a greater proportional increase in runoff after conversion to EIA. The growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume tend to decrease with increasing rainfall return period，exhibiting an amplification effect under low-return-period rainfall events. This study provides a scientific basis for optimizing the spatial patterns of underlying surfaces in urban settings and guiding the rational layout of stormwater facilities.

papers.title: Assessment of Fully Polarimetric Biomass Data for Soil Moisture Retrieval
papers.summary: Water management for irrigation is an essential activity especially in agricultural areas or where water is scarce. Water storage in the soil affects the vapour transpiration but also its heat storage capacity, its thermal conductivity and the energy separation between latent and sensible heat fluxes. From a hydrological perspective, soil moisture links the partitioning of rainfall into runoff and infiltration and therefore it has an important role in several ecological applications as flood forecasting, crop yield expectation, meteorological prediction, erosion and slope failure forecasting, water reservoir management, etc. Most of the soil moisture models describe only the bare soil response. In a real scenario, the presence of bare soil is not common as most of the time some kind of vegetation may be found on top. In order to reduce the amount of vegetation responses in addition to the soil moisture estimation longer wavelength can be used. In this study we like to explore the polarimetric and interferometric response of the BIOMASS mission, which operates in P band wavelength. Polarimetry can be used to define the scattering mechanisms and is able, when using decomposition methods to separate the ground and vegetation contribution. To perform this separation a physical model is employed and fully polarimetric data is needed in order to invert for the different involved parameters. It is worth mentioning that for extracting the ground response and the corresponding soil moisture, a significant degree of penetration into vegetation is required. For this reason, SAR soil moisture inversion has traditionally been investigated with L-band. In this study we use quad polarimetry in P band to investigate the sensitivity to bare soil and vegetated soil for soil moisture estimation [R1]. Differential SAR interferometry, a popular technique for measuring displacements of the Earth's surface, is potentially influenced by changes in soil moisture. Different mechanisms for th

papers.title: Spatial and vertical variability of soil physico‐hydraulic properties and subsurface lithology in the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan
papers.summary: Abstract Accurate characterization of soil physico‐hydraulic properties is critical for irrigation and drainage design, solute transport, soil–water–plant, and rainfall–runoff relationships. However, spatially representative datasets for these properties remain limited for the Indus Basin of Pakistan, where hydrological studies often rely on generalized parameters derived from other regions, introducing uncertainties in model‐based assessments. This study presents a basin‐scale integrated assessment of soil texture, bulk density, infiltration behavior, and soil moisture retention characteristics covering the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan. Field‐based in situ measurements were conducted at 66 spatially distributed sites across four doabs (area between the two rivers) at surface, 0.5‐m, and 1.0‐m depths. An integrated methodological framework was employed, combining hydrometer analysis for soil texture, improved double‐ring infiltrometer tests for infiltration, pressure‐plate extractor for soil water retention, oven‐dried weight for bulk density, and resistivity survey for subsurface lithological assessment. Infiltration datasets were analyzed using the Horton and Philip cumulative infiltration models, while soil water retention behavior was quantified using hanging water column and pressure plate methods and parameterized using the van Genuchten model. Results indicate that the Horton infiltration model outperformed the Philip model for estimation of cumulative infiltration. Silty clay loam, sandy loam, and silt loam are the dominant texture classes. The soil with infiltration rates up to 30 mm/h remain predominant across the study area. This study provides robust and accurate baseline datasets along with an integrated methodological framework to support basin‐scale improved hydrological modeling, flood simulations, recharge estimation, and effective water resource management.

papers.title: Modelling the Impact of Initial Water Content on Sorptivity and β Parameters of the Cumulative Infiltration Curve
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Cumulative infiltration is a key factor for the accurate determination of the soil water balance. The 1D QEI model, which incorporates the hydraulic conductivity, K , for initial ( θ i ) and saturated ( θ s ) volumetric water contents the sorptivity, S , and the β parameter, has become a popular formulation to simulate the cumulative infiltration curve. However, given the complexity of estimating S and β for variable values of the hydrological studies tend to rely on infiltration measurements conducted under dry initial soil conditions, often overlooking how initial water content affects the shape of the infiltration curve. To address this issue, this work proposes two simple empirical functions (PTF) relating both S and β to Δ θ . These PTF, which were developed based on the corresponding analytical solutions for S and β , were applied to different values of Δ θ and six synthetic soils with textures ranging from loamy sand to clay. Keeping θ s constant, increasing values of θ i , from the residual water content, θ r , to θ s , were evaluated. The numerical consistency of the new models was evaluated by comparing the cumulative infiltration curves generated by applying the analytical solutions and the proposed PTFs to the QEI function for different soil textural characteristics and Δ θ values against the corresponding simulations performed with HYDRUS‐1D. The results demonstrated that θ i significantly influences the cumulative infiltration curve. While linear relationships passing through the origin ( R 2 = 0.99; p < 0.001) were observed between S 2 and Δ θ , asymptotic growth functions characterized the relationships between β and Δ θ ( R 2 = 0.99, p < 0.001). Excellent fits were also found between the HYDRUS‐1D simulations for increasing values of Δ θ and those generated with the QEI model using both the analytical solutions and the proposed PTF approaches. The results suggest that θ i must be considered in infiltration models to ensure the accuracy of h

papers.summary: Overview Reference implementation and evaluation pipeline for PIM-RVSNet, a physics-informed multimodal graph-temporal network with agentic hydro-mechanical verification for dynamic slope stability prediction under rainfall–vegetation–soil coupling. The package implements all three components described in the article: the Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE, C1) with Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention and vertical soil-horizon graph-recurrent message passing; the Differentiable Richards–Wu–Mohr–Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op, C2) with van Genuchten scanning hysteresis and moisture-attenuated Wu–Waldron root cohesion; and the Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Verifier (AHM-Verifier, C3) built from MassBalanceAudit, MacroporeBypassDetector, and SuctionEquilibriumCheck. Reference implementations of all competing baselines and the full metric suite (R², RMSEFs, MAEFs, RMSEψ, F1crit, AUROC, failure warning lead time, physical consistency violation rate, water mass-balance error, and Holm–Bonferroni paired tests) are included.
