papers.title: X‐Ray CT Analysis of Soil Pore Structure, Connectivity and Hydraulic Responses to Micro‐Nanobubble Aerated Drip Irrigation
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Soil pore network architecture is fundamental to rhizosphere functioning. This study employed high‐resolution X‐ray computed tomography (CT) to quantify rhizosphere pore structure, spatial distribution, connectivity and hydraulic function in greenhouse tomato across two consecutive growing seasons (S1 and S2) under five micro‐nanobubble (MNB) aeration scheduling treatments: nonaerated control (CK), early aeration (AE), reproductive aeration (AR), late aeration (AL) and continuous aeration (AC). CT‐derived parameters included void ratio, pore morphology, nearest neighbour index (NNI), fractal dimension, absolute permeability and pore‐throat characteristics. AC produced the greatest improvements in the void ratio and pore area across both seasons. AR recorded the highest pore count in Season 1 (1.45 × 10 5 ) and NNI in Season 2 (6.9), indicating concentrated root–bubble interactions during peak oxygen demand. At the end of S1 and S2, the absolute permeability under AC was 8.6 and 18.9 μm 2 , respectively, compared with 4.3 and 0.7 μm 2 under CK. Because CT sampling was destructive and different soil blocks were collected at the end of each season, these values represent season‐specific cross‐sectional contrasts rather than longitudinal changes in the same soil core. Overall, growth‐stage MNB aeration was associated with distinct end‐of‐season rhizosphere pore‐network characteristics, supporting precision oxygen management in greenhouse SDI systems.

papers.title: Machine Learning and GIS-Integrated Framework for Irrigation Water Quality Index (IWQI) Mapping and Hydrochemical Clustering in an Algerian Semi-Arid Watershed
papers.summary: Abstract In the Ain Temouchent region, surface water is severely limited, leaving groundwater as the primary source for both domestic supply and agricultural irrigation. This study evaluates the suitability of El Melah watershed groundwater for irrigation by computing the Irrigation Water Quality Index (IWQI) following the Meireles approach, mapping its spatial distribution through GIS, and complementing the analysis with two machine learning methods: (i) a Random Forest (RF) model with Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) and SHAP explainability analysis to identify the dominant drivers of IWQI degradation; and (ii) K-means and hierarchical clustering to delineate hydrochemical facies and provide a statistically grounded alternative to the conventional Wilcox diagram. Salinity is elevated throughout the study area (EC: 1,034–5,010 µS cm⁻¹). The RF model achieved LOOCV R² = 0.61, with Na⁺ and EC confirmed as the dominant IWQI degradation drivers by SHAP analysis. Hierarchical clustering resolved three hydrochemical facies: a Ca²⁺-HCO₃⁻ continental group, a Na⁺-Cl⁻ evaporite-influenced group, and a seawater-intrusion group, all confirmed as statistically distinct by one-way ANOVA (p < 0.05). Overall, groundwater quality in the watershed ranges from moderate to severe restriction for irrigation use, with the northern sector most critically affected by marine infiltration.

papers.title: Erosion-resistance mechanisms of biopolymer-vegetation reinforced slopes under rainfall using experimental and coupled CFD-DEM methods
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced surface erosion poses persistent threats to the stability of highway slopes, causing significant economic losses and ecological degradation worldwide. This study investigates the combined effects of biopolymer (Xanthan gum) and vegetation (Festuca arundinacea) on rainfall-induced surface erosion through rainfall simulation experiments and CFD-DEM numerical simulations. Nine treatment combinations of biopolymer dosage (0-0.5%) and vegetation density (0-60 g·m-2) were tested under three rainfall intensities. Biopolymer and vegetation exerted opposing hydrological effects, with biopolymer increasing surface runoff by up to 17% while vegetation reduced it by 19%-42% through root-enhanced infiltration. Their combination reduced cumulative erosion by 93.1% relative to bare soil, and the relative contribution of biopolymer-vegetation interaction to erosion resistance rose from 13.9% to 24.1% with increasing rainfall intensity. Numerical simulations revealed that untreated slopes developed a positive feedback between porosity growth (0.44 to 0.58) and flow velocity increase (0.37 to 0.52 m·s⁻¹), driving progressive erosion escalation. Biopolymer bonding sustained inter-particle contact forces five times greater than untreated counterparts at stabilization, and the coordination number of the combined treatment reached 2.48 at stabilization, 34% higher than bare soil, confirming superior preservation of contact network integrity. These findings provide mechanistic insight into biopolymer-vegetation synergistic slope protection for transportation infrastructure.

papers.title: Integrating geoinformatics and high-resolution soil water retention data for fine-scale desertification sensitivity mapping of the Oued-Sakni sub-catchment, Cheliff-Zahrez hydrographic Basin, Algeria
papers.summary: Introduction This study presents a large-scale, quantitative assessment of desertification sensitivity in the Oued-Sakni sub-catchment (SCOS), a representative unit of the steppe belt of central Algeria. Although the region’s vulnerability to land degradation has been noted in earlier national-scale surveys, its spatial pattern had not previously been mapped at a resolution fine enough to support local management decisions. Methods Geoinformatics and remote-sensing techniques were combined within the MEDALUS (Mediterranean Desertification and Land Use) framework to delineate Environmentally Sensitive Areas (ESAs). The Environmental Sensitivity Area Index (ESAI) was computed as the geometric mean of four thematic indices — the Soil Quality Index (SQI), Climate Quality Index (CQI), Vegetation Quality Index (VQI) and Management Quality Index (MQI) — each built from natural and anthropogenic layers that together describe the land’s susceptibility to degradation. To offset the scarcity of local, high-resolution soil survey data, a methodological adaptation was introduced: soil depth and texture were substituted with high-resolution Volumetric Water Retention (VWR) data drawn from the World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) database. Land cover, the most dynamic of the four inputs, was mapped independently through a Random Forest (RF) classifier trained on Sentinel-2 imagery within Google Earth Engine, achieving an overall accuracy of 86.2% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.823, which gives the vegetation and management layers an empirical grounding rarely available in comparable steppe studies. Results and discussion The results show that the SCOS sub-catchment is highly vulnerable to desertification: critical areas cover 43.6% of the total surface, fragile areas 49.2%, and only 7.2% is classed as potentially sensitive. These figures place the SCOS among the more severely affected steppe catchments reported in the recent regional literature. The resulting ESA maps constitute a

papers.title: Post‐Mining Conservation Measures for Erosion Control: A Global Assessment of Their Effectiveness on Runoff and Soil Erosion Reduction
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Mining activities severely disturb land surfaces and hydrological processes, intensifying hillslope erosion and soil loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of post‐mining restoration measures and identify the factors regulating their performance, we compiled a global dataset of runoff and soil erosion yield from 58 studies spanning multiple mine types, climatic zones, and restoration practices, and conducted a weighted meta‐analysis using random‐effects models. Overall, restoration measures reduced runoff by 49.0% and soil erosion yield by 67.6%, with consistently greater reductions in soil erosion. Combined measures were most effective, whereas soil amendment alone showed the weakest runoff reduction (21.1%). Runoff reduction increased with restoration duration, while soil erosion control was strong initially but showed a transient decline before recovering. Restoration effectiveness also varied substantially among mine types and environmental conditions. Soil erosion reduction was more sensitive than runoff to climatic and topographic factors, with higher rainfall intensity and steeper slopes generally weakening both runoff and soil erosion control. Slopes longer than 15 m sharply reduced soil erosion control (56.9% vs. > 70% on shorter slopes). Vegetation cover further revealed contrasting responses: runoff reduction plateaued at approximately 40% cover, whereas soil erosion reduction continued to increase up to 80%–100% cover. These findings demonstrate that post‐mining restoration effectiveness is jointly regulated by restoration strategy, recovery duration, and site conditions, highlighting the need for context‐specific combinations of restoration measures, vegetation targets, and landform configurations.

papers.title: Enhancing Experimental Reliability Through Rainfall Simulator Calibration Under Intense Rainfall Rates
papers.summary: Acknowledging the benefit of Rainfall Simulators (RS) is continuously growing among researcher, mainly for laboratory-scale models where natural rainfall is either unavailable or inconsistent. RS put forward a reliable platform for replicating specific rainfall events under standardized set-up, making them invaluable for erosion, hydrology, and slope stability research needs. The present work offered a cost-effective Dripping Rainfall Simulator (DRS) for application on a 1.2 m² test plot area. After several standardizations, the DRS that produces replicable storms of rainfall (at 60 mm/hr and 120 mm/hr) demonstrated satisfactory spatial uniformity, with Christiansen’s uniformity coefficients (CUC) coverage ranging from 81.18–88.69% distribution across the monitoring plot. Additionally, the mean diameters (Dm ) and median volumetric drop diameters (D50), measured using a flour-pellet method, were found to extend from 3.8–4.4 mm and 2.7–3.1 mm independently which line up well with values reported in previous research. The relative terminal velocity (VT ) calculated was attained to range between 8.59–8.92 m/s with energy flux from 36.88 to 39.77 J/mm/m2 . These findings verify the RS capability to replicate natural rainfall with considerable accuracy let alone provide a strong foundation to be used in future applications in experimental modelling. From the basis of this study regarding RS, researchers will be able to create events-scale physical models in their relevant engineering areas.

papers.title: Effects of land‐use systems on macroaggregate pore structure, hydraulic conductivity, and physical protection capacity
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Reclamation of saline–alkali land relies on salt leaching and restoring soil fertility. However, the micro‐scale pore‐architectural changes associated with different land‐use systems remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in relation to their potential implications for water transport and fertility retention. This study selected natural land‐use systems (wasteland [WL] and degraded grassland [GL]) and artificial land‐use systems (upland field [UF] and paddy field [PF]) in Jilin, China, and scanned 5–7 mm macroaggregates for computed tomography imaging. Results showed that WL had a dense structure with low porosity (12.74%), while GL contained many elongated pores (21.74%). Porosity increased in the cultivated soils of UF (27.8%) and PF (22.48%). Network analysis indicated that UF had the highest hydraulic conductivity, whereas PF exhibited a hydraulically restrictive network. Using topological metrics, we identified critical pores within the macroaggregates. In natural systems (WL: two critical pores; GL: three critical pores), these pores resembled root systems. In contrast, the critical pores in UF (two critical pores) and PF (eight critical pores) were morphologically more uniform. Our analysis suggests that the two reclaimed agricultural systems are associated with divergent intra‐macroaggregate pore‐network configurations: UF was characterized by low‐tortuosity vertical pathways, suggesting a higher potential for rapid water transmission, whereas the more compartmentalized pore network in PF may restrict flow and increase the potential for physical protection of soil organic matter. These findings show that land‐use choice can redirect macroaggregate structural development during saline–alkali land reclamation, with implications for balancing salt leaching, hydraulic transport, and fertility retention.

papers.title: Geotechnical and Hydraulic Properties of Aeolian Kalahari Sands in Botswana
papers.summary: This literature review examines the geotechnical characteristics and engineering behavior of the Kalahari sands that cover approximately three-quarters of Botswana, extending from the southwest to the northeast with increasing thickness toward the western regions. These sandy soils originated mainly from Karoo Supergroup and Ghanzi Group sandstones and have been reworked by wind since deposition (aeolian), resulting in high quartz content. The sands are fine-grained, subrounded, poorly sorted, and display a collapsible fabric. The poor sorting also renders them susceptible to erosion. It is challenging to maximize strength by compaction due to the resistance and hardness of the quartz grains in these sands and their subrounded particle shape results in reduced shear strength. Previous studies reveal a notable plasticity achieved from the minus 0.075 mm fraction, despite conventional testing (on minus 0.425 mm) classifying them as non-plastic. The inherent plasticity and low natural moisture content yield significant suction strengths. Their fine composition lowers permeability, resulting in poor drainage and reduced groundwater potential, particularly in the western Botswana with a semi-arid environment. When utilizing these sands in construction dry compaction with high-energy equipment is a possible solution especially due to the water scarcity in large parts of Botswana. However, previous research indicates that hydrocompaction and differential settlement of these collapsible soils may result in structural damage and land degradation.

papers.title: Modeling Seasonal Shrink-Swell and Saturated Zone Deformation of Clay Underneath Buildings on Shallow Foundations
papers.summary: Increased damage reporting for residential buildings in the Netherlands following recent droughts has incentivized applied laboratory, field, and modeling investigations of the role of seasonal deformation of clay underneath buildings on shallow foundations. Here, a mathematical model is presented which simulates water transport, water content changes and deformation in the saturated and unsaturated zone at the building scale. The model provides a process-based framework to improve understanding of hydro-mechanical soil-foundation interaction in clay-rich settings, and to clarify factors that contribute to damage risk. Water loss and gain from evapotranspiration and rainfall drive the model and are applied adjacent to the building. Effects extend underneath the building and the (phreatic) water table movements are simulated rather than imposed. Shrink-swell and saturated zone deformation are modeled as a reversible process. A unique feature of the formulation lies in the extension of the van Genuchten retention model toward stress-dependent behavior, establishing formal continuity between unsaturated retention physics and the saturated compressibility framework conventionally employed in geotechnical practice. This allows exploring effects of the weight of the building. Laboratory-determined retention, hydraulic conductivity and shrinkage curves are used to model the differential vertical movements.

papers.title: Field Hydraulic Conductivity Test in Clayey Soils: Evaluation Aquifer Recharge Challenges
papers.summary: Climate change is altering rainfall patterns, leading to greater intensity and shorter duration of events. This generates significant surface runoff, causes flooding, and decreases natural aquifer recharge. Consequently, methods for artificial aquifer recharge must be evaluated, as groundwater extraction continues while natural infiltration declines. Baseline conditions must be investigated to evaluate phreatic levels, recharge areas, hydrogeochemistry, and isotopes, among other parameters. In Uruguay, the Raigón Aquifer is a vital groundwater resource utilized for agricultural and industrial activities, as well as drinking water. The Libertad Clay, an aquitard composed of clayey and silty-clayey soils, overlies the Raigón Aquifer. Regional piezometric levels indicate that recharge occurs through the Libertad Clay where its thickness ranges between 20 m and 35 m. In this study, field and laboratory tests were conducted to measure the hydraulic conductivity (HC) of the Libertad Clay and determined whether recharge through this aquitard is viable. In the field, 3 m deep wells were constructed for infiltration testing, and soil samples were collected every 0.5 m for laboratory classification and HC testing. Laboratory HC values were lower than 10-9 m/s, whereas field infiltration rates ranged from 10-6 m/s to 10-7 m/s. As a result, field infiltration rates were 100 to 1,000 times higher than laboratory measurements, finding that field testing provides a more representative evaluation of the hydraulic behavior of the Libertad Clay for aquifer recharge. Ongoing complementary research aims to identify the specific processes driving this recharge to inform future managed aquifer recharge strategies.

papers.title: A systematic review of sustainable pathways for balancing food production and environmental sustainability in Ethiopian agriculture
papers.summary: Between 2010 and 2026, Ethiopia faced the dual challenge of increasing agricultural production to meet growing food demand while safeguarding the natural resources that underpin long-term agricultural sustainability. Thus, the objectives of this review were to examine the interactions between food production and environmental sustainability in Ethiopian agriculture. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, evidence was synthesized from 130 peer-reviewed empirical studies and supporting grey literature identified through comprehensive searches of Scopus, Web of Science, Wiley Online Library, and Google Scholar. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist. The evidence indicates that agricultural expansion and conventional farming practices have contributed to widespread environmental degradation through soil erosion, nutrient depletion, deforestation, land degradation, and inefficient water use, threatening long-term agricultural productivity and ecosystem resilience. The review consistently identifies Climate-Smart Agriculture, agroforestry, sustainable intensification, and improved water management as the most effective pathways for enhancing agricultural productivity while improving soil health, water-use efficiency, biodiversity conservation, and climate resilience. However, their implementation remains constrained by socioeconomic limitations, weak institutional and extension support systems, insecure land tenure arrangements, knowledge gaps, population pressure, and climate-related risks. The review also identifies opportunities associated with supportive national policies, indigenous farming knowledge, climate financing mechanisms, and digital innovations. Nevertheless, the findings should be interpreted with caution because the review included only English-language studies conducted in Ethiopia and was limited by the methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. papers.title: Laboratory evaluation of capillary rise in silty sands with geotextile
papers.summary: Capillary rise of water in soil from a groundwater table is commonly observed in soils with fines. The capillary rise increases moisture in subgrade and base course with fines, thus affecting roadway performance. Fines content controls the level of capillary rise and geotextile may affect this level. Limited research has quantitatively evaluated capillary rise in unsaturated soils considering the influence of soil fines content and geotextiles. This paper presents a laboratory study evaluating capillary rise in silty sands with varying fines contents and the effects of wicking and non-wicking geotextiles. Soil columns consisting of upper and lower boxes were placed in a water tub to allow capillary rise, and volumetric moisture contents were monitored using moisture sensors over a 14-day period. At the end of each test, gravimetric moisture contents were measured to establish their relationship with the volumetric moisture contents. The test results indicate that capillary rise increased with the fines content. Existing methods were found to either under- or overestimate capillary rise in sands with fines. Non-wicking geotextiles acted as capillary barriers, restricting upward moisture migration above the interface, whereas wicking geotextiles were less effective in limiting upward capillary movement but enhanced horizontal drainage. Soil Water Characteristics Curves (SWCCs) and relative Hydraulic Conductivity Functions (HCFs) were also estimated and compared with the literature-based Geotextile Water Characteristics Curves (GWCCs). Analysis indicated that the non-wicking geotextile created a hydraulic discontinuity that reduced and delayed upward capillary water movement, particularly in soils with higher fines contents.

papers.title: Association of runoff risk with private well contamination in a fractured dolostone aquifer
papers.summary: In the United States, private well owners are responsible for monitoring and maintaining their drinking water but have little control over neighboring contamination sources and limited information about daily water quality. Potential for rapid contamination in karst settings exacerbates the challenge. The Runoff Risk Advisory Forecast (RRAF) is a real-time online tool available in five US states that helps nutrient applicators avoid times and locations of high runoff risk. We wanted to determine if RRAF could be repurposed in areas susceptible to groundwater contamination to inform well owners of conditions when contamination is likely. Private wells were repeatedly sampled on seven dates (32-36 wells per date) and analyzed for nitrate-nitrogen, total coliforms, and bovine manure markers. Three-day windows of RRAF risk prior to sampling were selected post hoc, ranging from 1 to 3 days prior for manure markers to 10-12 days prior for nitrate. Contaminants were associated with RRAF values of ≥75% within these windows based on observed weather. A hydrologic association between RRAF risk and groundwater depth was also apparent. Overall, results suggest the RRAF model anticipates conditions of elevated contamination risk for susceptible wells. For nitrate, between-well variation and delayed peak concentration suggested that well location and construction factors may be more informative than runoff events. Microbial contamination was rapid and distributed among wells, with one or more detections of coliforms in 31% of wells and bovine markers in 61% of wells. Thus, a warning system based on the RRAF model could help identify conditions of acute pathogen exposure.

papers.title: Numerical Modelling of the Stability of Rock Cliff
papers.summary: Rocky coastal cliffs are highly nonlinear systems in which geomechanical, hydraulic, marine and meteorological processes interact across very different spatial and temporal scales. Numerical modelling—nowadays mainly performed with FEM (Finite Element Method) and codes—is indispensable for estimating safety thresholds and forecasting collapse scenarios, yet its reliability is hindered by several critical issues. First, the uncertainty about strength parameters (cohesion, friction, tensile strength) which are often derived from few laboratory tests that may not be representative of the real heterogeneity of the rock mass. There are also uncertainties about piezometric levels conditioned by groundwater through fractures. Consequently, it is essential to embed the model within a systematic sensitivity analysis: controlled variation of input parameters makes it possible to identify those to the evaluation of factor of safety is most sensitive, isolating the “key parameter” governing stability. So, to guide targeted experimental campaigns to narrow its confidence range. Given the intrinsic complexity of the phenomenon, it is imperative to adopt advanced constitutive models that can accurately reproduce the tensile-deformation response of the rock mass in situ, incorporating the effects of anisotropy and the effect of weakness rocky levels and; and at the same time, the progressive erosion at the toe also in the light of the evolution of discontinuities. Such an advanced approach has been applied to the rock cliffs in weak sandstone layers yielding innovative failureprediction results that markedly improve the reliability of modelled failure mechanism obtained by numerical modelling, that are relevant in the light of reliable earlywarning assessments for this highrisk coastline stretches.

papers.title: Slope Geohazard Susceptibility Zonation Along a Mountainous Highway: A Case Study of the Sichuan-Tibet Highway, China
papers.summary: The Sichuan-Tibet Highway is considered the link between Tibet and eastern China, which is of strategic importance to China. The frequent occurrence of collapses/rockfalls and landslides in this region has attracted wide attention from geoengineering scholars. Various kinds of evaluation methods were employed for the susceptibility of geological hazards. Based on the analysis of the geological environment, seven main factors correlated with the development of slope geohazard were obtained, including lithology, tectonics, aspect, slope gradient, elevation, river system, and land use type. The susceptibility of slope geohazard in the region was predicted using the certainty factor method. The evaluation results were validated using the area under the curve method. The study area was divided into 5 levels based on the combination of the assessment results and field investigation. Very high susceptibility zones were distributed in Kawabaiqing Town, Lagen Town, and Yupu Town. High susceptibility zones were distributed in Tongmai-Guxiang Town, Songzong-Yupu Town, the area between Ranwu and Jida Town, and Baima Town. Moderate susceptibility zones were distributed in the west of Zhamu Town. Low susceptibility zones were distributed in the east of Gu Town and Ranwu Town. Very low susceptibility zones were distributed in Jida Town and the east of Zhamu Town.

papers.title: Groundwater Vulnerability Assessment of the Kingston Hydrological Basin in Jamaica Using the GIS ‐Based DRASTIC Model
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The Kingston Hydrological Basin (KHB) in Jamaica faces serious challenges in water security due to increased urbanisation, limited water resources and inadequate sewage treatment facilities. Nitrate contamination of the alluvial aquifer, coupled with a decrease in rainfall patterns, has resulted in the closure of many groundwater wells and a heavy reliance on surface water systems. This has created an increase in demand for potable water from inadequate surface water resources and water shortages during periods of drought within the KHB and adjoining basins. In this study, the Intrinsic DRASTIC Vulnerability Model, an overlay index method, was used to evaluate the aquifers' intrinsic and specific vulnerability to nitrate contamination. This model determines the vulnerability of aquifers based on seven hydrogeologic factors, including depth to the water table (D), aquifer recharge (R), aquifer media (A), soil media (S), topography (T), the impact of vadose zone (I) and hydraulic conductivity (C). To match the local hydrogeological context and incorporate the influence of human activities on the vulnerability, the model was modified to include ‘land cover’. To further improve the predictivity of the DRASTIC Model, logistic regression (LR) was applied to statistically identify the factors that influence the aquifer's vulnerability to nitrate contamination (concentration > 7.5 mg/L permissible limit accrued to local standard). The results showed that, based on the intrinsic parameters within the basin, areas with shallow water tables and very permeable and porous geology are classified as very high vulnerability. When the land cover is incorporated, the vulnerability is enhanced with the introduction of the source of contaminants. Most of the KHB is highly vulnerable to nitrate contamination, resulting in a higher chance of contaminants entering the system quickly, especially beneath urban areas.

papers.title: Hydrological Reorganisation in Mining-Subsided Lowlands: An Independently Validated Retention Potential Index
papers.summary: Mining-induced subsidence in low-relief landscapes does not automatically generate surface inundation. Its environmental consequences depend on how deformation reorganises near-surface hydrology through the formation of closed depressions, reduced hydraulic gradients, altered flow paths and modified groundwater persistence. Conventional threshold-based assessments and models trained directly on observed inundation inventories are limited in their ability to anticipate future activation, as they either oversimplify process linkages or rely on circular validation. This study reframes post-mining inundation as a problem of hydrological reorganisation and introduces a transparent, process-based Retention Potential Index (RPI). Six hydro-geomorphic predictors representing storage capacity, runoff impedance, flow convergence, substrate retention, deformation history, and groundwater state were integrated on a common 10 m grid. The 2025 inundation inventory was excluded from predictor construction, weighting, and threshold selection and was used exclusively for independent validation. Within the 119.98 km² Bogdanka mining domain, the morphology-dominant variant achieved AUC = 0.866. Spatial block validation retained skill (mean AUC = 0.822; median AUC = 0.805; Spearman r = 0.470, p = 0.0017). The final operational zonation comprised 4.04 km² of confirmed inundation, 2.69 km² of high-priority potential zones, 77.22 km² of observation/monitoring areas, and 36.03 km² of low-potential terrain. Results indicate that terrain morphology acts as the primary control on activation, while geology and groundwater modulate persistence. The framework provides a reproducible GIS-based screening tool for field verification, drainage management and spatial planning in actively deforming lowlands. Its process interpretation links landscape-scale terrain closure to pore-scale saturation, capillary storage, effective hydraulic conductivity and water-residence time.

papers.title: Internal Erosion in Colluvial Gravelly Soil Under Different Rainfall Intensities and Its Effects on Water Migration and Soil Structure
papers.summary: Rainfall infiltration commonly triggers shallow landslides by raising pore-water pressure and reducing shear strength. This mechanism, however, presupposes that the soil structure remains stable. In colluvial slopes composed of gravelly soils, rainfall infiltration may induce the migration of fine particles, a phenomenon known as internal erosion that alters the soil structure and consequently affects slope stability. To investigate internal erosion in colluvial gravelly soil under different rainfall intensities and its effects on water migration and soil structural characteristics, a series of laboratory soil column tests were conducted using a self-designed rainfall infiltration apparatus. The wetting front migration, soil moisture evolution, and fine-particle outflow under five rainfall intensities (30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 mm/h), together with the changes in grain-size distribution and pore structure before and after the tests, were systematically analyzed. The results indicate that rainfall intensity exerted a markedly layer-dependent influence on the infiltration process of colluvial gravelly soil: the steady-state moisture content increased most markedly in the upper layer and moderately in the lower layer but remained almost unchanged in the middle layer. Under the present test conditions, a rainfall intensity threshold of 30–60 mm/h was identified for the onset of fine-particle mobilization. Below this threshold, no particle washout occurred. Once it was exceeded, the effluent fine-particle concentration exhibited an initial peak followed by a later-stage decline, and the cumulative eroded mass increased with rainfall intensity. The vertical distribution of particle loss was closely aligned with the moisture content response across layers. The image-estimated porosity change rate at the front face of the soil column increased with rainfall intensity. papers.summary: No abstract available

papers.title: Drought modulates soil hydraulic, biological, and physicochemical responses to one-off tillage in a long-term cover-cropped Mediterranean vineyard
papers.summary: Sustainable soil management is a crucial factor to maintain soil health and long-term functionality in vineyards. In Mediterranean climates, cover crops have become a sustainable alternative to conventional tillage due to their positive effects on soil structure, water retention, and biological activity. Severe drought episodes are increasingly prompting growers to incorporate tillage to reduce water and nutrient competition between cover crops and grapevines. However, the immediate consequences of this practice on soil attributes remain poorly understood. To evaluate whether reintroducing tillage is a viable short-term strategy to relieve drought-induced water competition without compromising soil health, this study assessed the effects of a single tillage event on soil hydraulic properties (water retention curve, unsaturated hydraulic conductivity, Ku and field-saturated soil hydraulic conductivity, Kfs), physical and chemical properties (bulk density, total porosity, pore size distribution, total organic carbon, pH, CaCO 3 ) and biological properties (dehydrogenase and β-glucosidase activity) in a long-term cover-cropped organic vineyard of Vitis vinifera L. cv. Cabernet Sauvignon in Raïmat (Lleida, Spain), under commercial and survival water regimes. Soil water content dynamics were monitored, focusing on the April-June period when cover crop competition for water is greatest. Tillage reduced bulk density by 4.3% (1.35 ± 0.01 vs. 1.41 ± 0.02 g cm −3 , p = 0.020) and increased total porosity by 6.5% (0.49 ± 0.01 vs. 0.46 ± 0.01, p = 0.029) relative to cover crop, with no significant differences at field capacity (p = 0.352) or permanent wilting point (p = 0.264). Kfs was significantly higher under tillage regardless of water regime. Neither dehydrogenase nor β-glucosidase activity showed a significant reduction under tillage, suggesting that the measured biological indicators were not compromised by the one-off disturbance. papers.title: Recycling of coal mining waste geomaterials as a construction material
papers.summary: Much of the existing knowledge surrounding colliery discards dates back to the 1970s and 1980s, largely developed in response to the Aberfan disaster of 1966. However, the advancement of soil mechanics, both in theoretical frameworks and experimental methods, necessitates a renewed examination of these geomaterials. To fill this gap, samples of coal mine waste geomaterials (CMWG) were collected from the RH01 site located in Tylorstown, Wales. An experimental programme was designed to investigate physical, mineralogical, chemical, hydraulic, mechanical, and unsaturated properties of the CMWG. The main research objectives are: (a) examine the role of particle breakage, particularly initial breakage, on their mechanical response, (b) assess the effect of cementation on their properties and shearing response, (c) understand the instability and failure mechanisms of the geomaterials under a constant deviatoric shear (CDS) path (d) evaluate the suitability of the geomaterials as a construction material, particularly as a potential replacement for sand in construction, and (e) Assess feasibility of using produced concrete as a capillary barrier for mitigating geohazards during intense rainfall events. Key findings from this study can be summarised as: i) Tylorstown CMWG (TCMWG) is a highly crushable geomaterial, with particle breakage occurring during compaction, consolidation, and shearing. Initial breakage introduced during compaction influences both drained and undrained responses; however, addition of cement enhances its properties, such as stiffness (Young’s modulus) and shear strength, ii) onset of instability under a CDS path is strongly influenced by drainage conditions and unloading rate as well as initial breakage, (iii) TCMWG demonstrated to have the capacity to completely replace sand. papers.title: Grass Pavers
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Grass pavers provide a reliable way to strengthen lawn areas while preserving their natural appearance. Rather than installing concrete or relying on loose gravel that can shift, wash away, or develop ruts, these interlocking grids create a supportive foundation beneath the grass. Their open-cell design allows roots to grow naturally while the durable structure distributes weight across the surface. Our 24" x 24" permeable pavers are manufactured from recycled high-density plastic and feature an 87% porosity rating. This design allows rainwater to pass through the panels and soak into the ground, helping reduce standing water, muddy patches, and soil erosion. Each lightweight panel covers 4 square feet and weighs only 3.2 pounds. The convenient loop-to-peg connection system makes installation straightforward, allowing many homeowners to complete projects such as driveway extensions and additional parking spaces over a weekend.

papers.title: Dataset and R Code for "Biochar Increases Penetration Resistance Despite Acidity Relief and Greater Soil Moisture in Hardsetting Soils"
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This repository contains the experimental dataset and R analysis code supporting the research article “Biochar increases penetration resistance despite acidity relief and greater soil moisture in hardsetting soils” by Gholamahmadi et al. The study evaluates the chemical, hydrological, mechanical and vegetation responses of three Portuguese hardsetting pasture soils amended with wood-derived biochar. The experiment combined 18 sloping lysimeters and 18 accompanying pots, with monitoring across one growing season and nine natural rainfall events. The deposited materials support the statistical analyses of soil moisture, penetration resistance, bulk density, vegetation cover, aboveground biomass, runoff, estimated infiltration and soil erosion, including treatment contrasts and associated uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: Hydrological Attributes
papers.summary: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest tidal halophytic mangrove forest, spans 10,200 sq. km across India and Bangladesh, forming a dynamic interface between land and sea. It serves as a critical ecological buffer against cyclones and tidal surges while sustaining millions of people through its rich biodiversity and resources. Groundwater reserves, replenished by rainwater and river infiltration, are vital for drinking water and agricultural needs, though threatened by arsenic contamination and saline intrusion. This deltaic region, fed by the confluence of the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers, exhibits a complex hydrology shaped by tidal rhythms, freshwater inflows, and rainfall conditions. These unique hydrological processes create a fragile estuarine environment that is highly susceptible to climate change impacts, including sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion, and extreme weather events. Human interventions such as embankments, water diversions, and deforestation further exacerbate the vulnerability of this ecosystem. This chapter explores the intricate hydrological dynamics, challenges posed by environmental changes, and sustainable management strategies to preserve the Sundarbans’ ecological integrity and socio-economic stability.

papers.title: Assessment and Mapping of Soil Erosion Hotspots in the Himalayan Region Using RUSLE and Machine Learning Technique
papers.summary: Soil erosion is a major driver of land degradation, particularly in fragile and ecologically sensitive mountainous regions such as the Himalayas. This study assessed soil erosion risk and mapped erosion hotspots in the Bhagirathi watershed, Uttarkashi District, Uttarakhand, by integrating the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), remote sensing, GIS, field observations, and Random Forest (RF) machine learning. The assessment utilized 80 spatially distributed surface soil samples for estimating soil erodibility, ALOS PALSAR DEM (12.5 m) for terrain characterization and derivation of topographic factors, and Sentinel-2A multispectral data (10 m) for land use/land cover and spectral information. Rainfall, soil, topographic, vegetation, and management-related factors were integrated within the RUSLE framework to estimate soil loss, while terrain and spectral variables were subsequently used to develop the RF regression model. Areas experiencing estimated soil loss exceeding 40 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ were classified as erosion hotspots. The RUSLE-based erosion risk assessment showed good agreement with field observations, achieving an overall validation accuracy of 85%. The RF regression model demonstrated good predictive performance, with an R² of 0.72, RMSE of 0.31, and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency of 0.67. Slope, aspect and NDVI were found to be the most important predictors governing the model performance as well as spatial distribution of erosion hotspots. Erosion hotspots occupied approximately 9.34% of the watershed and were predominantly associated with steep slopes and areas with sparse or absent vegetation. These locations were also clearly identifiable in high-resolution satellite imagery. The findings demonstrate that integrating empirical erosion modelling with field observations, geospatial data, and machine learning can effectively assess erosion risk and identify priority hotspots in complex and inaccessible Himalayan terrain. The approach can support targeted

papers.title: Fuzzy multi criteria decision analysis for drinking water suitability in urban lake groundwater systems in Chennai India
papers.summary: Urban lake–groundwater systems in Chennai, India, face severe contamination challenges due to rapid urbanization, seawater intrusion, and anthropogenic inputs, while conventional water quality assessment approaches often fail to adequately account for uncertainty in ranking outcomes. To address this limitation, the present study applied fuzzy-based multi-criteria decision analysis techniques alongside conventional water quality index and classical multi-criteria decision-making approaches. A total of 30 water samples collected from three major lakes and adjacent groundwater sources were analyzed for physicochemical parameters using standard analytical procedures. The results indicate that lake waters generally comply with drinking water standards, reflecting the beneficial influence of rainfall recharge and dilution processes, whereas groundwater quality is considerably affected by seawater intrusion, prolonged water–rock interaction, and contamination from sewage infiltration and agricultural activities. Hydrogeochemical facies analysis revealed predominantly alkaline waters characterized by calcium–magnesium and sodium–chloride types, while hydrochemical interpretation suggested strong hydraulic connectivity between lakes and adjacent aquifers. Comparative evaluation demonstrated that fuzzy decision-making approaches produced more consistent and uncertainty-aware rankings than conventional methods, thereby providing a more reliable framework for drinking water suitability assessment. The proposed methodology offers a practical and reproducible approach for groundwater quality evaluation in data-limited urban environments and can be applied to similar lake–aquifer systems worldwide. The findings contribute to sustainable water resource management, urban resilience planning, and the achievement of global water sustainability objectives.

papers.title: Assessing Hydrological Impacts of Deforestation and Land Use Change in the Tel River Basin
papers.summary: Land use and land cover changes (LULCC) alter catchment hydrology by changing how water moves between the land surface and the atmosphere. This study examines how land use change between 1985 and 2015 affected the water balance of the Tel River basin, a sub-basin of the Mahanadi system in eastern India. Land cover maps for 1985, 1995, and 2005 were obtained from the national decadal LULC database, and a 2015 map was prepared from Landsat 8 imagery using a Random Forest classifier on Google Earth Engine (GEE) and later validated against NRSC data. The 2015 map reached an overall accuracy of 78.6 % (Kappa 0.68) against independent reference data. Forest and agriculture were mapped reliably, while the smaller classes of built-up land, bare land, and water body were combined into one less reliable category. Hydrological response was simulated with the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model for 1980 to 2018, using a one-factor-at-a-time design that holds climate constant so that only land use varies. Forest cover fell by 13.02% over the period, with most of the loss going to agriculture (about 1575 km2). With climate held fixed, lower evapotranspiration (about 16 mm/year, or 1.7%) was passed almost entirely into higher surface runoff (about 7 mm, 2.0%) and higher base flow (about 9 mm, 4.6%), while long-term soil water storage stayed essentially unchanged. A pixel-level analysis shows that runoff rises in some parts of the basin and falls in others, so the basin average understates the local change in flood and erosion risk. The results point to the value of catchment-scale water management that accounts for where land use is changing within the basin.

papers.title: Satellite and Reanalysis Soil Moisture Products for Irrigation Monitoring in Northern Algeria
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate estimation of soil moisture (SM) is a critical factor for sustainable irrigation management and food security, especially in semi‐arid agricultural regions where water availability is highly variable. Although reanalysis and satellite‐based products provide extensive spatial coverage, their reliability must be systematically validated against in situ measurements. This study establishes a multi‐product validation benchmark by evaluating and comparing several satellite and model‐based SM products over northern Algeria, including the Soil Water Index from the Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT), Sentinel‐1 (S1), the SM Active Passive (SMAP) mission, European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis v5‐Land (ERA5‐Land), and the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS). The analysis focuses on surface‐to‐near‐surface SM dynamics while accounting for site heterogeneity, product resolution, and sensing‐depth differences. The results reveal pronounced spatial variability linked to local pedoclimatic conditions, including soil properties, vegetation cover, and land‐use characteristics. Across the evaluated sites, ASCAT shows the highest average temporal consistency ( r ≈ 0.84; maximum 0.96 at Chiffa), whereas SMAP shows more balanced performance and Sentinel‐1 exhibits strongly site‐dependent behavior, with local failures discussed in the text. ERA5‐Land effectively reproduces temporal variability ( r up to 0.91), whereas the low unbiased root mean square error (ubRMSE) values obtained for GLDAS indicate a low random error component after bias removal rather than absolute accuracy. The bias profiles show that temporal agreement does not guarantee the absence of systematic error: At Chiffa, biases reach +12.75 percentage points in volumetric SM for ASCAT and +15.40 for ERA5‐Land, whereas the ASCAT bias reaches +14.00 at Oued Smar. The performance observed for ASCAT is specific to the evaluated sites and validation period; it does not cons

papers.title: A Planning Framework for Sustainable Stormwater Management Using Blue–Green Infrastructure in Lublin Streetscapes
papers.summary: Sustainable urban stormwater management requires planning tools that quantify local retention potential while accounting for limited street space and existing infrastructure. This study develops a planning-level framework for selecting and preliminarily sizing blue–green infrastructure (BGI) to support sustainable water and land management in existing streetscapes. A section of Henryka Wolińskiego Street in Lublin, Poland, was divided into 26 sub-catchments. Runoff was estimated from land cover, runoff coefficients, and a 15 min design rainfall depth of 16.13 mm with an annual exceedance probability of 20%, obtained from the PMAXTP model. Rain gardens, infiltration swales, stormwater curb extensions, and bioretention basins were allocated according to spatial, environmental, and infrastructure constraints. Calculated runoff was equivalent to 7.4 mm over the study area. The proposed facilities provided 6.8 mm of design storage and could accommodate 6.6 mm, or 89.4% of calculated runoff, under the adopted assumptions; 0.8 mm, or 10.6%, required sewer discharge. Unused storage coexisted with local deficits, demonstrating the importance of storage location and feasible hydraulic connections. The framework contributes a transparent decision-support procedure for assessing the water-management dimension of urban sustainability through runoff accommodation, residual sewer discharge, and BGI space requirements. These are design estimates, not measured environmental benefits or a comprehensive sustainability assessment. Application elsewhere requires local input data, field verification, and subsequent performance monitoring.

papers.title: Physical Structure Overrides Short‐Term Nitrogen Effects on Preferential Flow in Heterogeneous Rock‐Soil Media: Implications for Mountain Ecohydrology
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Mountainous critical zones, with heterogeneous rock‐soil structures, regulate water storage and flux through complex subsurface flow paths. Preferential flow, often triggered by textural contrasts, controls rapid water redistribution and eco‐hydrological connectivity. This study investigates the divergent infiltration dynamics between two dominant media—coarse, weathered clastic rock and finer brown soil—in the Taihang Mountains through controlled column experiments under varied nitrogen (N) concentrations (0–125 mg N L −1 ). A quantitative multi‐criteria framework was applied to discriminate matrix flow from preferential flow, including volume‐balance closure via the piston displacement index ( ν ), velocity ratio, flux‐capacity ratio, wetting‐front morphology with Monte Carlo noise calibration, and Green–Ampt consistency. Brown soil was matrix‐dominated ( ν * = 0.93–1.12; smooth wetting fronts) and retained significantly more water, with cumulative infiltration of 18.1–21.8 cm and effective storage capacity of 19.4 cm over the 45‐cm profile. Clastic rock exhibited strong bypass behaviour ( ν * = 1.35–1.53; p = 0.005), with 26%–35% of infiltrated water moving beyond the visible wetting front, despite its late‐time flux remaining below the matrix saturated conductivity. Cumulative infiltration in clastic rock was significantly lower (13.3–15.2 cm; p = 0.005), and its leaching risk index was medium‐to‐high (0.44–0.88) compared with low values in brown soil (0.08–0.24; p = 0.002). Wetting front velocity was significantly higher in clastic rock in all phases (), but morphology remained near‐piston‐like (), indicating that rapid infiltration was a matrix‐capacity and storage‐capacity effect rather than finger‐like preferential flow. Nitrogen addition, applied as a short‐term chemical perturbation, did not significantly alter these physical controls across the tested range. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for understanding water partitioning, retentio

papers.title: GIS-Based Multi-Criteria Analysis for Identifying Suitable Rainwater Harvesting Sites to Enhance Groundwater Recharge: A Case Study of the Western Wellfield in Thaqban Area, Sana’a, Yemen
papers.source: مجلة جامعة صنعاء للعلوم التطبيقية والتكنولوجيا
papers.summary: Groundwater depletion in the Sana’a Basin, Yemen, has intensified due to over-abstraction, rapid urbanization, and limited natural recharge. The Western Wellfield, which supplies a significant portion of Sana’a City’s domestic water demand, has experienced substantial groundwater level declines, highlighting the need for sustainable recharge interventions. This study evaluates the potential of rainwater harvesting (RWH) for enhancing groundwater recharge in the Thaqban area using a Geographic Information System (GIS)-based Multi Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) integrated with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Ten thematic criteria were considered, including rainfall, runoff depth, slope, geological media, soil texture, land use/land cover, drainage density, distance to wadis, distance to groundwater wells, and groundwater depth. The criteria were weighted using AHP and combined through a weighted linear combination (WLC) approach to generate an RWH suitability map. The results show that 1.34% of the study area is highly suitable for RWH implementation, 37.60% is moderately suitable, 58.21% is marginally suitable, and 2.85% is unsuitable. Highly suitable areas are mainly associated with permeable geological formations, favorable topography, and proximity to production wells. This study demonstrates the usefulness of GIS-MCDA techniques for identifying priority recharge zones and supporting sustainable groundwater management in arid environments.

papers.title: Knowledge-graph reasoning for temporal lag effects and mechanism inversion of heavy-rainfall-induced landslide events: case study on Hong Kong
papers.summary: Heavy rainfall can sustain landslide activity for several days after a storm, but daily event inventories often obscure this delayed response and provide little information on the evidence used to infer failure processes. We developed a knowledge-graph workflow that links 2,961 Hong Kong landslide records from 2001 to 2021 with daily rainfall, slope attributes, spatial relations, and 57 investigation reports. Lag analysis was possible for 2,950 records, mechanism analysis for 2,940 records, and 43 events had traceable report anchors. Daily incidence rates and threshold–window tests identified a high-hazard stage on days 0–3 and an extended-hazard stage on days 4–7. With a 50 mm threshold and a 7 days look-back window, 42.2% of events occurred on a qualifying rainfall day and 30.1% occurred during the following week. A nearest-station test using 21 gauges produced 89.4% agreement with the baseline stage classification. The graph combined storm, slope-form, neighborhood, and regional evidence to estimate five mechanism classes. Pore-pressure-dominated soil slides and channelized debris flows accounted for 78.9%–84.4% of classifications across lag stages, while posterior uncertainty increased with lag. Leakage-controlled leave-one-out testing yielded Top-1 and Top-2 accuracies of 0.163 and 0.349. These results support storm-cluster interpretation and investigation prioritization, while event-specific causes still require field evidence.

papers.title: Migration and transformation characteristics and potential risk assessment of heavy metals under different rainfall conditions in contaminated soil
papers.summary: Abstract Contaminated mining soils cause heavy metal environmental pollution such as the soil, river, groundwater and plants under rainfall conditions. In this work, the copper, zinc, lead and chromium leaching characteristics, leaching efficiency, fractions variation, binding intensity, mobility and potential environmental risks were investigated under different rainfall conditions. Results demonstrated that Zn obtained a high leaching concentration under the 19.6, 13.1 and 6.5 mL.min −1 , which concentrations were 180.3, 154.7 and 123.5 μg.L −1 , respectively. On the surface soil particles, Cu, Zn, Pb and Cr migrated into the water with the rainwater runoff, indicating a sustainable increase with rainfall intensity raising and obtained a high solubility and mobility, promoting heavy metals to migrate via the soil surface rainwater runoff. Exchangeable and reducible fractions of Pb and Cr have decreased and transformed into the metal ions, which migrated into the outflow, whereas the oxidizable and residual fractions have increased under the rainfall conditions. Cu and Pb obtained more stable fractions, such as the oxidizable and residual fractions. Cu, Zn, Pb and Cr I R values were affected by their concentration and fractions under the rainfall conditions. Heavy metal mobility order was Zn > Pb > Cr > Cu, with M F values of 4.34%, 3.52%, 2.67% and 2.45%, respectively. These results can provide significant support for the mining soils of efficient remediation methods to promote the mines' ecological environmental improvement.

papers.title: Urban Tree Soil Moisture Dynamics Across Central European Cities: A Multi-Site Approach Showing Links Between Hydrology, Tree and Site Characteristics
papers.summary: Abstract. Urban trees face intensifying drought stress, and soil water storage and its dynamics are important for the drought resilience of urban trees. Existing evidence is based on process-based growth and ecosystem-service models, on water-balance studies of urban green spaces and irrigation, and on single-city monitoring campaigns, while multi-city in-situ observations under a consistent methodology are missing. We present a continuously growing database of 555 urban tree sites in 41 Central European locations, each instrumented with soil moisture sensors and paired with meteorological data, topographic, sun exposure and groundwater descriptors, manually digitised land use around the tree and tree characteristics. An event-based workflow detects rain and irrigation events and extracts two response metrics, the normalised soil moisture increase and the drying time. Random Forest models are built for all combinations of target (soil moisture increase, drying time), event type (rain, irrigation) and measurement depth (30, 60, 90 cm). The models explain up to 69 % of the variance of the moisture increase after irrigation and 40 to 55 % for the other combinations in cross-validation. Grouped cross-validation shows that the rain models transfer to unseen sites within 0.03 in R2 while the irrigation models lose 0.21 to 0.37, therefore encoding a site signature of the few heavily irrigating cities. Rain and irrigation responses differ markedly. The mean air temperature during the event and the pre-event rainfall dominate the rain responses, whereas the pre-event soil moisture and the storage capacity of the substrate control the irrigation responses and how long their effect persists. The unsealed, vegetated area around the tree is the only consistently relevant site characteristic, whereas depth to groundwater shows no effect. The database and workflow are openly available and turn the assessment of planting sites and the verification of irrigation into measurable quan

papers.title: Integrated subsurface screening for bioengineering suitability and erosion control on a tropical cut slope
papers.summary: Tropical cut slopes are highly susceptible to erosion and shallow landslides because intense rainfall interacts with deeply weathered residual soils, yet bioengineering interventions are frequently designed without adequate subsurface characterization.This study aimed to conduct an integrated geological, geophysical, and geotechnical characterization of a tropical cut slope on the Kenny Hill Formation, Selangor, Malaysia, in order to evaluate its suitability for bioengineering.Field reconnaissance and weathering grade classification were combined with a two-dimensional electrical resistivity survey, soil penetration resistance, near-surface moisture content, and erosion rate measurements collected across three vegetation coverage plots over 24 months.The slope was classified as Grade III to IV weathered metasedimentary rock with a sandy clay loam surface texture.Resistivity imaging identified a high resistivity, coarse-textured near-surface layer of 20,000 to 360,000 Ωm at 0 to 5 m depth, overlying a low resistivity, moisture-affected zone of 300 to 800 Ωm at 5 to 14.8 m depth.Penetration resistance increased significantly under vegetation cover, reaching 4.4 kPa in the densely vegetated plot compared with 2.9 kPa in the control, while nearsurface moisture content and hydraulic conductivity rose progressively, and erosion rate declined by up to 74.04% relative to the initial condition.These results indicate that the near-surface zone provides mechanically, hydrologically, and ecologically favorable conditions for root establishment, whereas the deeper zone offers limited support for root anchorage.The corresponding reduction in erosion rate confirms that the subsurface conditions identified through this integrated approach translate into measurable improvement in slope performance.Overall, combining weathering grade classification, resistivity zonation, and penetration resistance testing provides a reliable, fielddeployable framework for screening tropical cut slope

papers.title: Hydrological modelling of land use land cover change effects on urban stormwater runoff in Hyderabad, Pakistan for 2017, 2021, and 2024
papers.summary: Pakistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, which points to the need for resilient urban infrastructure and effective stormwater management. This study investigates changes in land use and land cover (LULC) and urban stormwater runoff in Qasimabad, Hyderabad, Pakistan. LULC analysis was conducted with ArcGIS Pro 3.1.5, while hydrological simulation used HEC-HMS 4.11. Changes in LULC were assessed for 2017, 2021, and 2024; hydrological characteristics were examined through flow direction analysis and sub-basin modelling. Across the study period, the spatial distribution of built-up areas, vegetation, water bodies, and bare land changed substantially. Built-up land made up 64.3% of the classified area in 2017. That share was 36.8% in 2021 and 46.2% in 2024, reflecting changes in the mapped land-cover extent alongside continued urban development. Over the same period, population density rose from 8,708 persons per km² in 2017 to 9,963 persons per km² in 2024. Using the HEC-HMS model, seven sub-basins were identified, and peak discharge, runoff timing, and flow characteristics were quantified across the drainage network. When LULC, flow direction, and hydrological modelling were considered together, the analysis showed where runoff was concentrated and where drainage constraints might occur, especially in densely developed areas. These findings can guide urban planners and water resource managers in planning targeted stormwater drainage, protecting natural drainage pathways, and managing flood risk in rapidly developing urban areas.

papers.title: Engineering Geological Assessment and Landslide Hazard Zonation Using the Slope Stability Susceptibility Evaluation Parameter Method Around Gidole Town, Southern Ethiopia
papers.summary: Gidole Town and its surrounding areas have experienced repeated landslide events that have damaged roads, farmland, and settlements, yet detailed engineering geological investigations and quantitative hazard assessments remain limited. This study investigates the engineering geological factors controlling slope instability and develops a landslide hazard zonation map using the Slope Stability Susceptibility Evaluation Parameter (SSEP) method. The research integrates detailed geological and geomorphological mapping, structural discontinuity measurements, landslide inventory mapping, laboratory testing of representative soil samples, and Geographic Information System (GIS)-based spatial analysis. The results show that highly weathered basalt, unconsolidated colluvial deposits, steep slopes, groundwater seepage, and intense seasonal rainfall are the primary controls on landslide occurrence in the study area. The hazard zonation model classified 67.7% of the area as high hazard, 29.0% as moderate hazard, and 3.4% as low hazard. Model validation using the mapped landslide inventory indicated that approximately 74% of documented landslides fall within the predicted high-hazard zones, demonstrating the robustness and reliability of the SSEP approach. The resulting hazard map provides a scientific basis for land-use planning, infrastructure development, slope stabilization, and disaster risk reduction in southern Ethiopia. The findings further demonstrate that the SSEP method is an effective and practical tool for landslide hazard assessment in data-constrained mountainous regions.

papers.title: Influence of groundwater seasonality on suspended sediment dynamics, in a 20 km 2 Mediterranean mountainous catchment
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the interplay between groundwater and surface runoff in controlling suspended sediment dynamics within the Galabre catchment, a 20 km² Mediterranean mountainous catchment characterized by extensive badland areas. Using an End-Member Mixing Analyzing framework that accounts for event-specific variability in end-member chemistry, the study quantifies surface runoff and groundwater contributions during 86 flood events spanning three hydrological years. Hydrological analyses reveal clear seasonal contrasts in the generation of surface runoff and groundwater flow rates. Surface runoff contributions during floods vary from 0 to 50 % of the instantaneous flow rate, with higher proportions during the dry spring/summer season (May–September) and lower values in autumn/winter. Surface runoff and groundwater flow rates are strongly correlated with event rainfall accumulation, while groundwater-related variables also show sensitivity to antecedent rainfall over 15 days, highlighting their dependence on long-term hydrological connectivity. Results further demonstrate that suspended sediment concentrations correlate more strongly with surface runoff flow rate than with flow rate, emphasizing the dominant role of surface runoff in sediment detachment and transport on hillslopes. Marked seasonal differences in hydrosedimentary processes were observed. Spring/summer floods, driven by short and intense rainfall, produce low-flow responses with high surface runoff contribution, high suspended sediment concentration, and exhibit anticlockwise flow concentration hysteresis loops. This suggests that high amounts of fine sediments are mobilized on hillslopes during these floods, leading to high suspended sediment concentrations and moderate flow rates in the river network, associated with sediment deposition. Conversely, autumn/winter floods, governed by prolonged low-intensity rainfall, and characterized by enhanced groundwater contributions, produce hig
