papers.title: Hydraulic behavior and solute redistribution of saline-alkali black soil: Implications for stormwater source control
papers.summary: Study Region Daqing, northeastern China, has saline-alkali soils, strong evaporation, and shallow groundwater that constrain infiltration-based stormwater source control. Study Focus We examined hydraulic behavior and water and solute redistribution in black soil amended with 0, 0.5, and 2.0% Na 2 CO 3 . Saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K s ) was measured after 0~4 wetting-drying cycles. Soil water retention was determined by the filter paper method, and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity ( K u ) was estimated with the van Genuchten-Mualem model. A complementary column experiment applied sequential rainfall depths of 10, 20, 40, and 70 mm to track soil moisture, electrical conductivity (EC), and gravel layer water EC. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Na 2 CO 3 addition reduced initial Kₛ from 3.31 × 10 −6 m/s at 0% to 2.49 × 10 −7 and 3.02 × 10 −8 m/s at 0.5% and 2.0%. Wetting-drying caused further declines, while estimated Kᵤ remained lower in Na 2 CO 3 -amended soils over most of the modeled suction range. During sequential rainfall, the 2.0% treatment accumulated more water near the surface and responded more slowly at depth. EC decreased in the upper 20 cm but increased at 20~40 cm, while gravel layer water EC increased by only 8.9%. Low hydraulic conductivity therefore restricted vertical water transmission and promoted solute accumulation within the soil profile.

papers.title: Debris flow susceptibility assessment along the G55 expressway in Guangdong Province, China
papers.summary: Western Guangdong Province in China is frequently affected by intense rainfall and related geological hazards, yet studies on debris flow disasters in this area remain limited. In June 2025, four consecutive debris flow events occurred along the Lianzhou-Sanshui section of the G55 Erenhot-Guangzhou Expressway, attracting significant attention. To better understand the spatial distribution and controlling factors of these hazards, this study conducted a debris flow susceptibility assessment for this section. Based on regional topographic, meteorological, and geological conditions, combined with historical disaster data, an evaluation index system and database were established. Four machine learning algorithms, Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were applied and systematically compared. Algorithm performance was assessed using 3-fold spatially independent validation. Among the tested algorithms, XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.923, recall of 0.879, F1-score of 0.794, and ROC-AUC of 0.927. The debris flow susceptibility was classified into low, medium, and high levels. Medium and high susceptibility areas exhibited clear spatial clustering, mainly in the northern section of the expressway, while the southern section showed generally low susceptibility. Debris flows along the expressway were primarily triggered by shallow surface collapses and landslides that formed cascading hazard chains, while the slipperiness of surface weathering products showed an observed association with debris-flow occurrence and may represent a potential conditioning factor. These findings provide a scientific basis for debris flow risk identification and mitigation and offer insights for improving susceptibility assessment methodologies.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping for Railway Slopes Using Comparative Models and InSAR-Based Validation
papers.summary: Abstract We evaluated landslide susceptibility along the Carajás Railway in Brazil using five approaches: Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting, Multilayer Perceptron, Support Vector Machine, and Weight of Evidence. The models integrated an inventory of 148 landslide events with geomorphological, hydrological, and land-use conditioning factors. We assessed predictive performance using receiver operating characteristic curves and the area under the curve. Random Forest performed best (0.859), followed by Extreme Gradient Boosting (0.850), Multilayer Perceptron (0.687), Weight of Evidence (0.669), and Support Vector Machine (0.459). We independently evaluated susceptibility predictions using ground-deformation time series derived from Sentinel-1 interferometric synthetic aperture radar data processed with the Small Baseline Subset approach. Deformation rates increased progressively across susceptibility classes, with the highest magnitudes concentrated in areas classified as highly susceptible. Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting showed the strongest agreement between susceptibility patterns and observed deformation. The results indicated that interferometric deformation provided an independent physical assessment of susceptibility predictions and strengthened the interpretation of model outputs. The integrated approach improved the reliability of susceptibility assessment and supported risk-informed management of railway slopes.

papers.title: InSAR observations from multiple tracks reveal rainfall modulation of post-failure reactivation of the Xiongwadashan landslide
papers.summary: Large mountain landslides may remain active after major movement, yet the migration of dominant deformation zones, internal post-failure partitioning, and rainfall modulation remain insufficiently understood. We investigate the Xiongwadashan (XW) landslide on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau using Sentinel-1 LOS observations from selected pre- and post-event periods between 2017 and 2025, terrain-constrained three-dimensional displacement estimates for 2022–2024, CHIRPS rainfall data, and field observations. Before the September 2018 event, deformation was concentrated mainly in the middle–lower slope. After failure, the dominant deformation zone shifted to the middle–upper slope and later extended partially downslope toward the middle slope. Movement was dominated by horizontal, near-downslope displacement, with a peak cumulative east–west displacement of ~ 210 mm at XW1-3. Integrated LOS deformation, three-dimensional displacement, time series, and geomorphic evidence delineated high-deformation, transitional, and low-deformation kinematic zones. The high-deformation zone showed stronger displacement increases following concentrated rainfall, while deformation persisted during relatively low-rainfall periods. These results indicate that rainfall mainly modulated stage-wise acceleration rather than controlling long-term activity, and demonstrate the value of integrating temporal deformation-zone migration with internal kinematic zonation for post-failure landslide monitoring.

papers.title: SAMBHV: A Unified Open-Source Platform for Multi-Hazard Early Warning and Situational Awareness in Northeastern India
papers.summary: Abstract The North Eastern Region (NER) of India is one of the areas of the country that suffers from landslides, flash floods and isolation of roads as a result of the extreme mon- soon rainfall, fragile topography and lack of planning for hill cutting. All of these dangers have led to hundreds of fatalities, isolation of remote villages for weeks and the damage of critical infrastructure that connected people together from 2020-2025. Existing monitoring system is reactive and manual; not predictive, resulting in loss of life which could have been saved if there was a warning ahead of time. This paper presents a full-featured end to end open-source platform, SAMBHV (Situational Awareness & Multi-hazard Bharat Helper) which consists of various sub-systems namely: multi-source telemetry ingestion, two-stage hybrid predictive modeling, multi-channel alert dissemination system covering LoRa mesh system for network dead zones, real time GIS visualization and a zero-hallucination conversational AI layer to establish an end-to-end platform. It sends data from the IoT sensors, IMD weather APIs, Doppler radar, satellites, and citizen reports to the system that is processed by an XGBoost spatial regressor (F1 ≥ 0.85), ConvLSTM nowcaster, graph neural network for village separation, HEC-RAS 2D hydraulic solver, and LSTM flood stage forecaster. The ensemble decision gate needs to agree on 2 out of 3 physics, AI/ML and ground-truth gates and false alarms are kept below 10%. SAMBHV provides support in 11 Indian languages via IndicBART translation, offline mode with 72+ hours runtime on edge devices and alerts via 6 redundant channels. When the routes are obstructed, the platform calculates alternative safe routes in real-time with pgRouting. The entire architecture, mathematical models, empirical testing over 311 disaster test cases, and deployment of the system with F1 scores of ≥0.87 and lead time of >15 minutes is described.

papers.title: Surrogate modelling approach for modelling peak discharge in rainwater harvesting tanks: case study in Quito, Ecuador
papers.summary: Urbanisation increases surface runoff and recurrent flooding in cities, mainly by reducing infiltration capacity and shortening times of concentration. Rainwater harvesting tanks can store water to mitigate peak flows from urban development and support sustainable planning for new buildings. This study presents a hydrological routing approach for rainwater harvesting tanks, solved using the Rosenbrock method, combined with Monte Carlo analysis to generate a sufficiently large, representative set of hydrological scenarios. Based on these simulations, we developed multiple machine learning (ML) models to provide a simplified, efficient predictive framework. A total of 200 scenarios were generated using Latin Hypercube Sampling by varying key input parameters, including rainfall intensity, pipe length, internal pipe diameter, and tank surface area. In total, 28 ML regression models were evaluated to estimate peak outflow discharge. The Cubic Support Vector Machine (SVM) exhibited the best performance, achieving coefficients of determination ( $${R}^{2}$$ ) of 0.984 and 0.985 for the validation and testing stages, respectively. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the internal pipe diameter is the most influential parameter controlling peak discharge. The proposed methodology offers a computationally efficient, reliable tool for predicting the hydraulic performance of rainwater harvesting tanks, supporting decision-making for urban planners and local authorities in flood mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Eco-Compatible Stabilization of Loess Mine Slopes Using a PDADMAC-Based Polymer–Mineral Composite: Hydraulic, Mechanical, and Ecological Performance
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced surface erosion of aeolian loess slopes in open-pit coal mines threatens slope stability and ecological reclamation, whereas conventional rigid protection and ordinary soil stabilizers can hardly reconcile soil reinforcement, impermeabilization, and vegetation compatibility. Here, poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) was compounded with nano-SiO2, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium bentonite, and sodium lignosulfonate into a modified PDADMAC-based composite (MPDC). An L18(37) orthogonal array optimized the mix proportion (0.80, 0.50, 0.15, 1.60, and 0.10 wt.% of dry soil for PDADMAC, nano-SiO2, CMC, bentonite, and lignosulfonate, respectively), which was evaluated by shear and permeability tests, scanning electron microscopy, a 480 min rainfall test on a 38° slope model, and six-month field monitoring. The optimum mixture raised cohesion from 18.5 to 41.8 kPa and the friction angle from 26.8° to 32.7°, and cut saturated hydraulic conductivity by 74.3%. Under 480 min of rainfall, sediment loss and erosion ratio were 142.3 g m−2 and 4.7%, i.e., 88.7% and 88.8% below untreated loess, and cumulative infiltration fell by 85.4%. After six months, the treated 0–5 cm layer retained 46.6 kPa cohesion and a 2.2% fissure ratio (versus 20.8%); after 48 h of scouring, soil loss and sliding area were only 5.3 kg m−2 and 1.5 m2 per 100 m2, with Medicago sativa survival above 91.3%. MPDC thus couples soil reinforcement, seepage control, and ecological restoration.

papers.title: Study on the degradation mechanism of petroglyph carrier surfaces in Baiyin: Under water-temperature-salt coupling effects
papers.summary: The Baiyin petroglyph cluster in Gansu, China, stands as a significant piece of evidence for early human cultural exchange, showcasing distinct regional cultural traits and anthropological art value. However, the sandstone carrier of the petroglyphs has formed a composite degradation pattern characterized by crack development, void formation, and flaking peeling due to the freeze-thaw and chemical coupling weathering, driven by thermodynamic cycles and aqueous chemical processes, leading to the preservation crisis of some petroglyphs. Based on selected environmental characteristics relevant to the Baiyin petroglyph sites, laboratory freeze–thaw tests were conducted with controlled top-down infiltration of water or salt solutions to represent episodic precipitation/snowmelt infiltration and subsequent lateral moisture migration along exposed sandstone surfaces. Mass, hardness, and P-wave velocity were measured at 5-cycle intervals, while surface morphology, pore characteristics, microstructure, mineralogy, and chemical composition were characterized at 10-cycle intervals. The results show that freeze–thaw cycling progressively deteriorated the physical properties and pore structure of the sandstone, while the degradation response varied markedly with solution chemistry. Na 2 SO 4 produced the strongest macroscopic and pore-structural deterioration, whereas (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 caused faster mineralogical changes, indicating that salt type controls not only the magnitude of deterioration but also the dominant surface-degradation pathway. A surface-porosity-based damage model was further used to quantify the damage evolution under the tested conditions.

papers.title: Experimental Investigation of Pervious-Impervious Concrete Layered System for Airport Runway Drainage
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Severe operational hazards, including dynamic hydroplaning and reduced visibility is caused by the accumulation of surface water on airfield pavements, while it also places significant strain on conventional airport drainage infrastructure. This research presents an experimental investigation into the use of pervious concrete as a Sustainable Drainage System for pavements of airport. Pervious concrete creates an interconnected microporous network that facilitates rapid surface runoff infiltration by intentionally reducing and omitting the fine aggregates. As the mechanical strength of Conventional Pavement Quality concrete is higher so its application in aviation environment is traditionally limited. This study evaluates the structural and hydraulic performance of various pervious concrete mix proportion by varying water-cement ratio, aggregate sizes and aggregate to cement ratio. Laboratory tests such as compressive strength and hydraulic conductivity are conducted at 7-day and 28-day curing interval. The primary goal is to optimize the mix design to get a viable balance between drainage performance and structural load-bearing capacity to ultimately determine the feasibility of deploying pervious concrete in specific airfield zones such as runway shoulders, taxiway edges and apron margins. Building upon these structural and hydraulic assessments, the research explores the broader operational impacts of replacing traditional impermeable surfaces. By preventing water pooling, the optimized porous matrix serves as an active safety intervention, preserving friction to the pavement and drastically cutting down aquaplaning risks during heavy rainfall. Additionally, adopting this decentralized storm water related pollutants such as unburnt hydrocarbons and heavy metal runoffs before infiltrate local water tables. papers.title: Research on damage characteristics and slope instability mechanism of loess under the wet-dry-freeze-thaw coupling cycles
papers.summary: Abstract In recent years, the alternating changes in extreme climate have frequently caused loess to undergo the combined effects of wet-dry (WD) cycles and freeze-thaw (FT) cycles, leading to an increasing occurrence of overall instability and sliding in loess slopes. To reveal the damage mechanism of loess materials under the coupled wet-dry and freeze-thaw (WDFT) action and the evolutionary mechanism of landslides induced thereby, this study conducted a series of WD cycles, FT cycles, and WDFT coupling cycles tests. Multiple testing methods, including P-wave velocity, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, scanning electron microscopy and direct shear tests, were combined to systematically evaluate the evolution patterns of loess in terms of macroscopic physical-mechanical properties and microstructure. The results indicate that physical-mechanical properties attenuate nonlinearly with increasing cycles, driven by rising porosity and microstructural complexity, while the stress-strain behavior transitions from strong to weak strain softening. Due to distinct core mechanisms of cycle modes, their damage effects exhibit significant temporal and severity differences. In the early stages of cycling, the deterioration capability of FT action is greater than that of WD action; as the number of cycles increases, WD action becomes more significant. The damage to loess from the coupled WD and FT effects is not merely an additive combination of their individual effects but represents a more complex accelerating deterioration. For example, at 50 kPa, the final degradation rate of shear strength caused by WD, FT, and WDFT cycle modes are 0.64, 0.61, and 0.76, respectively. The WD cycles generate directional crack networks, FT cycles induce porous structures, and WDFT coupling combines both into a more complex interconnected damage system. papers.title: The Invisible Depletion: Compound Drought, Groundwater Collapse, and Maladaptation in the Middle East and Southwest Asia
papers.summary: The Middle East and Southwest Asia (MESWA) region is experiencing severe hydro-climatic non-stationarity, transitioning from cyclical precipitation deficits and surpluses to a state of structural water bankruptcy. This review synthesizes the compounding atmospheric and anthropogenic drivers of this crisis, highlighting the region’s shift towards a regime defined by frequent, concurrent extremes of drought and heat ("Hot Drought" regime). While fundamental ocean-basin teleconnections (e.g., El Niño Southern Oscillation) to MESWA remain intact, their hydrological impacts have become asymmetric, with the impact of drought-causing La Niña events remaining robust even while the wetter-than-normal conditions associated with El Niño have become less reliable. This asymmetry has emerged because (1) expected moisture delivery to MESWA has been frequently deflected by persistent atmospheric blocking and (2) escalating temperatures and extreme evaporative demand have reduced snow water storage and the ability of precipitation events to recharge surface moisture and water resources. To compensate for these losses in surface water availability, the region has increasingly relied on unregulated groundwater extraction. This dynamic has created a Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystems (WEFE) maladaptation trap where governments are forced to liquidate future aquifer reserves to prevent immediate food system collapse. This anthropogenic depletion, combined with the ongoing cryospheric buffer failure, has pushed regional basins past thresholds of historical elasticity—manifesting as irreversible physical degradation such as land subsidence, and coastal salinization—locking the corridor into a state where climatic variability alone is no longer sufficient to recharge water resources. We argue that operational Early Warning Systems (EWS) must expand beyond traditional, precipitation-centric meteorological forecasting by additionally tracking absolute systemic limits using Terrestrial Water Stora

papers.title: A study on surface runoff prediction in Guangzhou using the SCS-CN model
papers.source: International Conference on Advances in Energy and Environmental Engineering (AEEE)
papers.summary: With the acceleration of urbanization, the impervious surface area in Guangzhou has expanded, leading to an increase in surface runoff and a rising frequency of urban waterlogging events. This study established localized CN parameters for Guangzhou based on the SCS-CN model, fitted rainfall amounts for different return periods, simulated surface runoff, and conducted sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. The simulation results were then spatially correlated with waterlogging risk hotspots. The results show that under low return periods, risks are concentrated in low-lying areas of built-up zones, while under high return periods, risks rapidly spread to surrounding areas and the northern region, with waterlogging evolving from point-scale ponding to regional inundation. This study can provide scientific support for urban flood drainage planning and waterlogging risk early warning.

papers.title: Upper bound solution under rainfall-earthquake coupling for curvilinear shallow landslides considering progressive failure mechanism
papers.source: International Conference on Advances in Energy and Environmental Engineering (AEEE)
papers.summary: The shallow landslides are mostly triggered by rainfall and earthquakes. Shallow slopes usually exhibit curved profiles, and obvious multi-stage characteristics are showed in their progressive failure process due to the coupling effect of rainfall and earthquake. Based on the improved upper bound method of limit analysis theory, the stability of curved shallow slopes was analyzed under different coupling conditions of rainfall and earthquakes. A logarithmic spiral sliding surface was proposed for the typical terrain features of steep terrain, and pseudo static seismic effects were corrected to use acceleration amplification coefficients. By the strength and pore water pressure power, the expression was derived for the evolution of the wetting front. Then the energy balance equation was established, four stages of progressive failure mechanisms were revealed. The critical wetting front depth and sliding body length were solved by constructing an allowable velocity field and establishing a variational optimization framework based upon the Euler Lagrange equation. The stability influence of shallow slopes was analyzed depended on effective cohesion, static soil pressure coefficient, and maximum central slope angle. The results indicated that effective cohesion played a key controlling role in the depth of the critical wetting front. The sliding scale was mostly impacted on the static soil pressure coefficient. The maximum central slope angle does not decouple the infiltration process excepted with mainly adjusts the sliding range. These results are good with agree with the values of finite elements method. This study provides a scientific basis for the stability analysis and disaster prevention of curved slopes in mountainous areas.

papers.summary: _ This article, written by JPT Technology Editor Chris Carpenter, contains highlights of paper SPE 228528, “Application of an Innovative Degradable Particulate-Diverter Technology for Effective Acid Diversion in High-Water-Cut, High-Permeability-Contrast Reservoirs: A Case Study From Offshore Malaysia,” by Muhamad R. Bacho, SPE, Saurabh Anand, SPE, and Haydn B. Sinanan, SPE, Petronas, et al. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. _ This paper presents the application of degradable particulate-diverter technology to improve oil production by effectively diverting stimulation treatment fluids away from high-water-cut, high-permeability, high-temperature producing intervals or zones. This paper presents the application of degradable-particulate-diverter (DPD) technology, an engineered pill system consisting of proprietary degradable particles suspended in a viscoelastic carrier fluid, to improve oil production by effectively diverting stimulation-treatment fluids away from high-water-cut, high-permeability, high-temperature producing intervals or zones. The DPD technology was deployed to achieve temporary zonal isolation in high-water-cut intervals without the need for mechanical isolation tools or coiled tubing intervention. The same high-permeability intervals of Zone I also could be found at the adjacent water injectors. Both Well 1 and Well 2 were producing at water cuts exceeding 80%, with a marked decline in oil rate despite sustained total liquid production. papers.title: Quantifying macroporosity and preferential flow variations in soil under rice and wheat cultivation
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Soil macropores play a vital role in movement of water in agricultural fields, yet their spatial and structural dynamics under intensive crop rotation systems remain poorly quantified. This study investigates the contrasting effects of rice‐wheat cultivation on soil hydraulic properties, macropore function, and preferential flow dynamics. Field experiments were conducted post‐harvest of rice and wheat crops at an agricultural plot in IIT Kanpur. Dye‐tracer experiments were performed for visual confirmation of preferential flow. Tension disc and double ring infiltrometer measurements were taken at six different locations at 3 depths (10, 25, and 50 cm). The parameters for matrix ( and ) and macropore ( ) domains were estimated. Wheat soil exhibited significant difference depth‐wise in infiltration rate (). Critically, the steady‐state flux at 25 cm was 77.53% greater, indicating the sporadic activation of deep, high‐capacity macropores within a restrictive layer. No significant depth‐wise variation was observed in parameters under rice cropping (). Matrix parameters were significantly higher under wheat when compared to rice (mean: cm h −1 , cm −1 for rice; 24.26 cm h −1 , for wheat) and showed significant depth‐wise variation at 25 and 50 cm. This trend confirms the restorative and deep‐reaching effect of the wheat root system on pore continuity and subsoil structural stability. The findings emphasize that preferential flow under rice and wheat cultivation is dynamic and crop‐dependent, governed by alternating phases of structural degradation and recovery.

papers.title: Embedding Probabilistic Pore Occupancy into Soil Hydraulic Models
papers.summary: Conventional soil hydraulic models describe unsaturated water retention and conductivity by assuming that water occupies the smallest pores, i.e., lower-energy pores. The author introduces a statistical pore occupancy framework to quantify the pore states by a pore distribution, retrieved from the retention function, allowing statistical inference of pore state conditions. The framework introduces a parameter b, which represents the water pore occupancy distribution, impacting the behavior of the retention and conductivity functions. The approach uses an effective energy formulation to facilitate the calculations, allowing direct integration into traditional soil-water dynamic simulators. As a second step, a back transformation is introduced for a direct physical interpretation of the pore-filling condition, leading to the probability of pores being filled or not filled with water. The framework introduces a modified closed-form formulation of the Van Genuchten-Mualem model. The new model can quantify hysteretic behavior of the retention function and simultaneously predict the hydraulic conductivity behavior. Root mean square differences (RMSD) ranged from 0.007 to 0.021 m3 m-3, for the retention data, predicting both drying and wetting experiment scenarios; and from 0.117 to 0.216 for the conductivity, expressed as log10⁡(K). The embedded statistical mechanic can also assist in quantifying the solute transport. The respective shapes of the solute breakthrough curves (BTC) were reproduced, leading to a calibration RMSD of 0.018 and 0.016 [–]. A discussion regarding the back-transformation showed how the framework can be used to infer the configuration of pores filled with water in the soil, considering the model assumptions.

papers.title: Shear-generated stratification: A diagnostic indicator of laminar sandy debris flow processes in apparently massive submarine fan sandstones
papers.summary: Subtle stratification is locally observed within otherwise massive sandstone beds in submarine fan deposits. The genetic mechanism and process significance of this stratification, however, remain unclear. This study investigates the origin of this stratification and its implications through a detailed analysis of outcrops of the Middle Triassic Baifeng Formation in the Baise area, southern China. We identify three principal lithofacies based on their distinct sedimentary fabrics and structures: (1) laminated siltstone (LSl), (2) graded sandstone (GS), and (3) massive sandstone (MS). These lithofacies are organized into vertical successions or are individually present—namely, MS → GS → LSl, and more commonly, MS, MS → LSl, MS → GS, and GS → LSl. These successions are partly analogous to the Bouma Sequence, which is characterized by MS → GS → LSl. Massive sandstones are characterized by sharp, flat bases and uneven tops and contain floating gravel clasts and mudclasts. Basal dish and water-escape structures are present, and locally, subtle, often deformed stratification with convolute structures occurs within otherwise massive intervals. These sedimentary characteristics of the massive sandstones, combined with the prevalence of incomplete vertical successions, indicate deposition from cohesive, laminar, plastic gravity flows that underwent en masse freezing, consistent with the mechanics of sandy debris flows. Therefore, we interpret the subtle stratification as a primary syn-sedimentary structure generated by internal shearing within sandy debris flows, and propose it as a key diagnostic indicator for such processes. This study refines the understanding of gravity flow processes in submarine fan systems and offers new criteria for identifying sandy debris flow deposits in the sedimentary record.

papers.title: Data Fusion for Modelling the Bed Topography of Rock Glacier
papers.summary: The methodology presented in this study was applied to the Bonnard rock glacier, located in southwestern Switzerland between 3000 and 3200 m a.s.l., corresponding to the regional lower limit of permafrost occurrence. The terminal part of the rock glacier constitutes a major source area for recurrent debris flows affecting the downstream Pétérey and Tracuit torrents. To reconstruct the geometry of the stable bedrock surface beneath the rock glacier, several complementary datasets were integrated, including high-resolution LiDAR and photogrammetric topography, seismic refraction surveys, destructive boreholes, geomorphological mapping, and GNSS displacement measurements. All datasets were integrated within a common 3D reference framework using AdHoc-3D software, allowing the generation of a coherent set of georeferenced control points. The resulting dataset was processed using geostatistical interpolation with kriging and external drift to produce a digital elevation model of the bedrock surface. The reconstructed geometry allowed the estimation of the thickness and volume of the active layer, together with associated uncertainties. The results provide quantitative constraints on the potentially mobilizable sediment volumes contributing to debris-flow initiation and therefore constitute a useful tool for hazard assessment and climate-change adaptation in high-alpine periglacial environments.

papers.title: Assessing the Feasibility of Crowdsourced Pavement Roughness as a Proxy for Landslide Impacts on Roads in Italy
papers.summary: Monitoring landslide impacts on transport infrastructure remains challenging at national scale, where systematic damage surveys and high-resolution monitoring are rarely feasible. This study explores the potential of using crowdsourced road pavement roughness data as a proxy indicator of landslide-related road degradation across Italy, with particular emphasis on the contrast between national- and regional-scale analyses under heterogeneous data conditions. Vehicle-based pavement roughness observations from the SmartRoadSense platform were spatially intersected with the Italian Landslide Inventory (IFFI) and analyzed at both national and regional scales. Pavement roughness distributions inside and outside mapped landslide polygons were compared using descriptive statistics and nonparametric approaches. Results show that at national scale, median pavement roughness values inside and outside landslide areas are comparable, with substantial overlap between distributions, limiting the interpretability of roughness as a uniform proxy. In contrast, regional-scale analyses reveal highly variable behaviour: several regions exhibit higher roughness within landslides, others show weak contrasts, and in some cases higher roughness occurs outside mapped landslides. These differences reflect regional variability in landslide inventory completeness, roughness data coverage, and spatial correspondence between mapped landslides and deformation zones. These findings highlight both the potential and the limitations of crowdsourced pavement roughness for large-scale screening of landslide–road interactions. While national-scale aggregation tends to obscure landslide-related signals, regional analyses provide more informative results where data conditions are favourable. This emphasises the need for scale-aware interpretation when integrating crowdsourced infrastructure proxies into landslide risk frameworks, particularly for early-warning applications.

papers.title: Risk Assessment of Bridges Affected by Landslides
papers.summary: Following the collapse of the Morandi Bridge in 2018, the Italian National Guidelines introduced a multi-level procedure for the classification, safety assessment, and monitoring of existing bridges, identifying landslide risk as one of the main risks (along with structural seismic and hydraulic risks) affecting the safety of the infrastructure. Within this framework, the MARIE project (Methodological Approaches for RIsk assessment in the framework of landslide-bridge IntEraction), promoted within the Consorzio FABRE, aims to improve and standardise the operational assessment of bridge-landslide interaction, with particular reference to Special Inspections and Level 4 detailed assessments. The project addresses the main uncertainties that emerged during the application of the Guidelines, including incomplete inventory data, poorly constrained landslide geometry and kinematics, suspected or non-inventoried phenomena, and the definition of appropriate investigation and monitoring strategies. Preliminary results highlight the need to place preliminary geological and geotechnical models at the core of the assessment process, as a link between risk classification and accurate safety verification. These models support the identification of interaction scenarios, the optimisation of investigation campaigns, and the integration of monitoring data, remote sensing and physically based analyses for rainfall-induced processes. The proposed methodology provides a more coherent and reproducible pathway for landslide risk management of existing bridges. It contributes to reducing decision-making uncertainty, supporting future refinements of the Guidelines and improving the safety, resilience and durability of critical infrastructure exposed to evolving geomorphological and climatic conditions.

papers.title: Erosion Mechanisms of Landslides: Granular Column Collapse Experiment on Erodible Beds and DEM Insights
papers.summary: Dynamic erosion and entrainment of loose path materials can fundamentally reshape the mobility, kinematic stages, and deposition morphology of rapid granular landslides. However, it remains challenging to isolate controlling factors because erosion results from coupled momentum transfer, bed deformation, and local mass exchange at the particle scale. This paper investigates erosion development during granular column collapse over erodible beds through laboratory experiments and three-dimensional discrete element method (DEM) simulations. A transparent flume (120 cm long, 80 cm high, 20 cm wide) was used to release granular columns onto a 5 cm-thick erodible layer, enabling systematic comparisons across material combinations and initial aspect ratios while minimizing wall effects by ensuring a sufficiently large flume-width-to-particle-size ratio. Experiments were repeated three times for each condition to ensure reproducibility. Three distinct regimes were identified from synchronized observations of free-surface evolution, erosion-interface migration, and front kinematics: (i) non-erosion, (ii) overriding (covering) erosion, and (iii) plunging (penetrating) erosion. Front-position evolution exhibits a characteristic S-shaped trajectory with acceleration, quasi-steady propagation, and deceleration stages. Erosion significantly prolongs the initial acceleration and final deceleration stages while shortening the quasi-steady stage, yet the total flow duration remains proportional to the free-fall timescale. DEM results reproduce these trends and reveal that the particle density ratio between the column and bed governs regime transitions, whereas particle size ratio and initial aspect ratio play secondary roles.

papers.title: A review of partial saturation in liquefaction assessment: theory, laboratory studies, and field case histories
papers.summary: Abstract Liquefaction triggering analyses commonly assume that soils below the groundwater table (GWT) are fully saturated. In loose, granular soil deposits, this assumption suggests an increased potential for liquefaction. However, soil deposits below the GWT may be only partially saturated due to the presence of entrapped air in the pore water, which can significantly alter liquefaction resistance. Laboratory studies have shown that liquefaction resistance increases as the degree of saturation (S r ) decreases. P-wave velocity (V P ) is a reliable parameter for assessing saturation conditions in both laboratory and field settings. In fully saturated soils, compression waves propagate at velocities comparable to that of water, (~ 1500 m/s), whereas V P values below this threshold indicate partial saturation. Laboratory results show a strong, nearly exponential empirical relationship between V P and liquefaction resistance, with resistance increasing significantly as V P decreases. This relationship enables the development of partial saturation correction factors that can be applied to the factor of safety against liquefaction triggering, thereby improving prediction accuracy by accounting for the additional liquefaction resistance associated with partial saturation. This paper provides researchers and practitioners with a consolidated basis for understanding and accounting for partial saturation in liquefaction assessment, progressing from its theoretical and experimental basis to field identification and application. The review consolidates findings dispersed across individual studies and provides a new synthesis of field case histories within a common framework, enabling consistent comparison and a unified interpretation of the influence of partial saturation on liquefaction response. The findings highlight how accounting for partial saturation can support more representative liquefaction hazard and risk assessment.

papers.title: Wetting-Drying Cycles and Cone Penetration Tests in Clay - How Does Seasonal Drought and Vegetation-Induced Suction Affect Clay Strength?
papers.summary: The increasing frequency and duration of droughts over the last decade raise concerns about the behaviour of clay soils that support shallow foundations. This study investigates the response of clay strength to repeated wetting–drying cycles using mini‑cone penetration tests (mini-CPTs). A laboratory procedure was developed to subject clay samples to controlled and reproducible realistic wetting-drying cycles. Tests were conducted on two clay types: a homogeneous, artificially prepared Vingerling clay, and a natural clay obtained from the eastern Netherlands. The resulting mini-CPT results show a clear relationship between water content and cone penetration force. For the Vingerling clay, this relationship follows an almost perfect logarithmic trend. The natural clay, which is considerably stronger, shows the same logarithmic trend, although with greater scatter, likely due to the clay’s heterogeneity. No systematic trend was observed between the number of wetting–drying cycles and the cone penetration force..

papers.title: A calculation method for the ultimate support pressure of a shield tunnel excavation face accounting for fault dip angle
papers.summary: Abstract This study investigated the influence of fault dip angle on tunnel excavation-face stability. Starting from the conventional wedge instability model for homogeneous strata, an associated flow rule was introduced to improve the wedge model, and a modified wedge calculation model that accounts for the fault dip angle is proposed. Then, by establishing the compatibility relationship between the rupture angles of the upper and lower strata, an analytical formula for the ultimate support pressure of the excavation face under inclined fault conditions is derived using the limit equilibrium method, along with the corresponding calculation procedure. Three-dimensional numerical simulations are performed to evaluate the theoretical model, and the results reveal that the trends in the theoretical predictions and numerical simulations are consistent, with relative errors ranging from 3.2% to 15% across all working conditions, indicating good agreement between the theoretical and numerical results. The calculation results reveal that stratum strength parameters and fault dip angle are the key factors controlling ultimate support pressure. The proposed calculation method for the ultimate support force of the excavation face considering fault dip angle can quantitatively estimate ultimate support pressure in faulted strata, providing a theoretical basis for assessing support parameters and evaluating excavation-face stability during slurry-shield tunneling through fault fracture zones.

papers.title: Characterizing gas diffusivity, air permeability, and extracellular enzyme activity in an early‐stage comparison of conventional and regenerative pasture
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Regenerative pasture is an emerging agricultural framework characterized by high forage diversity, adaptive grazing, and reduced external inputs. However, early‐stage soil structural transitions and associated microbial activities remain unclear, particularly given the higher spatial variability expected in these systems. We compared regenerative and conventional pastures after 3 years of management at an experimental site in Canterbury, New Zealand, evaluating soil‐water retention, diffusion‐controlled aeration, and macropore‐dependent properties, alongside extracellular enzyme activities as an early biological indicator. Twenty undisturbed cores were analyzed for soil‐water retention (−1 to −1500 kPa), soil‐gas diffusivity ( D p / D o ) and air permeability ( k a ) (−1 to −10 kPa), bulk density ( ρ b), and saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K s ). Additional cores were used to measure eight hydrolytic and oxidative enzyme activities and compare spatial heterogeneity. Regenerative soils showed modestly lower ρ b (1.29 g cm − 3 ) than conventional soils (1.33 g cm − 3 ) and consistently higher water retention, giving 9.8% more plant‐available water. Derived pore‐size distributions indicated emerging micropore connectivity despite minimal change in total porosity. The D p / D o slope coefficient ( A ) was ∼30% higher in regenerative soils, allowing well‐aerated conditions ( D p / D o > 0.01) at field capacity, whereas conventional soils remained largely hypoxic. In contrast, macropore‐sensitive indicators ( k a and K s ) were highly variable and lower in regenerative soils, suggesting early reorganization favors functional macropore connectivity rather than increased pore volume. Mean enzyme activities did not differ between systems, but within‐plot variability was higher in regenerative plots. Functionally meaningful responses are therefore not yet clearly evident, and longer term monitoring is required to detect statistically distinguishable outcomes.

papers.title: A novel soil-water characteristic curve prediction model for unsaturated soil considering pore structure characteristics
papers.summary: The soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) graphically describes the significant hydraulic characteristics of unsaturated soil seepage. Several factors influence the SWCC of unsaturated soil, including temperature, void ratio, pore characteristics, particle composition, and load, with soil pore structure exerting a pivotal influence on SWCC. This study aimed to analyze the influence of pore structure on the SWCC of loess. The results showed that the shape of SWCC of loess is similar with varying pore structures under a fixed void ratio, with discrepancies in the air entry value(AEV) and decline sections. The void ratio of macro pores of intact loess exceeded that of remolded loess, in turn resulting in a larger AEV. There were fewer small pores and middle pores in the intact loess sample, whereas the remolded loess showed a greater decline rate after transitioning into an the unsaturated state. On the other hand, an increase in the size of the pores was observed in the loess following the drying-wetting cycles, whereas the number of smaller and middle-sized pores decreased. Similarly, there was an increase in AEV of loess following the drying-wetting cycles, with the gradual deceleration in the rate of decline in the unsaturated stage. The pore state parameters and fractal dimension of pore size distribution(PSD) were introduced into the V-G model based on the experimental results, with deriving a modified V-G model. The intact loess was predicted by remolded loess, and the loess after the drying-wetting cycles were predicted by loess before the drying-wetting cycles. The results showed that the modified V-G model is more effective in predicting the SWCC of intact loess and loess after the drying-wetting cycles.

papers.title: Spatial Distribution and Hydrogeological Controls On Hydrocarbon Contamination in Groundwater in Ogale, Niger Delta, Nigeria
papers.summary: Groundwater contamination by petroleum hydrocarbons is an environmental concern in the Niger Delta, where oil-related activities threaten groundwater resources used by surrounding communities. This study investigated the spatial distribution of total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylenes (BTEX) in groundwater in Ogale, Rivers State, Nigeria, and examined their relationships with selected hydrogeological parameters. Fifty-six groundwater sampling locations were assessed using hydrocarbon concentration data, hydraulic-head measurements, hydraulic-conductivity estimates, and geospatial analysis. Descriptive statistics showed substantial spatial variability in contaminant concentrations. TPH ranged from 0 to 1,680,625 µg/L, with a mean of 108,024.36 µg/L and a median of 8,255.50 µg/L. PAHs ranged from 0 to 12,454 µg/L, while BTEX ranged from 0 to 25,469 µg/L. Hydraulic head ranged from 4.640 to 16.120 m, and hydraulic conductivity varied from 1.220 × 10⁻⁸ to 2.610 × 10⁻³ m/s. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis identified a positive association between TPH concentration and depth to water (ρ = 0.301, p = 0.024). No statistically significant associations were observed between the other hydrocarbon groups and the examined hydrogeological parameters. The findings demonstrate heterogeneous groundwater contamination and indicate that depth to water may be associated with TPH distribution. However, the observational design and limited statistical associations do not establish causal transport mechanisms. The study highlights the importance of integrating contaminant mapping with hydrogeological characterisation to guide targeted groundwater monitoring, delineation of contamination, and remediation planning in Ogale.

papers.title: Research on the Residual Strength Characteristics of Landslide Slip Zone Soil in Reservoir Areas Based on Ring Shear Testing
papers.summary: The sliding zone soil constitutes a critical stratum governing landslide stability, rendering it essential for investigating the initiation mechanisms and conducting stability assessments of reservoir-induced landslides. Nevertheless, existing research on the residual shear strength of sliding zone soils in such landslides remains limited. To address this gap, this study focuses on the sliding zone soil sampled from the Xuwa landslide and employs ring shear testing to systematically characterize its residual strength behavior under varying moisture conditions. Test results reveal that specimen failure is consistently manifested as concentric circular scratches centered on the annular shear surface. Specifically, at low moisture contents, the scratches are deeper, and the failure surface exhibits pronounced roughness, abundant asperities, and thin, fragmented material; conversely, at high moisture contents, the scratches become shallower, the failure surface smoothens significantly, asperities diminish, and fragments become thicker and more cohesive. Furthermore, an evident transition in deformation behavior is observed, from strain-softening to strain-hardening, with increasing moisture content. These findings contribute valuable experimental insights and serve as a reference for advancing the understanding and modeling of residual strength in reservoir landslide sliding zone soils.

papers.title: Temperature Evolution in Sandy Soil Under Large-Displacement Shear
papers.summary: Granular material within the sliding zone of a landslide can undergo large-displacement shearing during its motion. The mechanical behaviour of the material under such shear process significantly affects the basal friction of a landslide and therefore governs its mobility. Both field observations and laboratory experiments have provided evidence that this shear process is companied by significant temperature generation. The generated heat can dynamically modify the shear strength of the material by degrading organic matter or influencing pore pressure. Although the effects of shear-induced temperature rise have been discussed in previous studies, it remains difficult to directly record the temperature evolution during large-displacement shearing. In this study, a direct temperature measurement unit integrated with a ring-shear apparatus is developed to record the complete temperature evolution process, from heating to cooling. Ring-shear tests were conducted on silica sand samples with two different grain sizes. The results indicate that the temperature evolution curve exhibits an initial increase followed by a steady rising phase once the specimen reaches the critical state. With continued shearing, the temperature generation rate gradually decreases, which is attributed to grain crushing occurring within the shear zone. The measurements further reveal a pronounced spatial heterogeneity in temperature distribution along the shear zone, with the temperature at the centre being approximately four times higher than that near the boundary. These obtained data are expected to be valuable for calibrating parameters in thermal-mechanically coupled numerical analyses of landslide dynamics.

papers.title: Analytical Analysis of VOC Remediation by Horizontal Permeable Reactive Barriers for Time-Dependent Source
papers.source: Boletim da Sociedade Paranaense de Matemática
papers.summary: Various natural and man-made objects, like industrial waste buried beneath soil emit many harmful gases known as Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) are hazardous for living beings. If released in environment VOCs can contaminate air, soil, and groundwater, causing health risks like dizziness, organ damage, and cancer. Their migration through unsaturated soil occurs via diffusion, advection and dispersion. Horizontal Permeable Reactive Barriers (HPRBs) are an effective in situ method to remediate and oxidize VOCs in the vadose zone. The degradation of an HPRB due to long-term interaction with VOCs occurs over several years; therefore, mathematical modeling is an effective and necessary tool for predicting its long-term behavior, as conducting experiments over such extended timescales in real life is impractical. In this study, an analytical diffusion-reaction model is presented to investigate VOC transport from a subsurface source, through the unsaturated soil layer, and into a HPRB. The model accounts for time-dependent conditions and the transport process is analyzed separately under the effects of various parameters involved. The obtained simulation through graph shows good agreement with the behavior observed in experiment. This study provides insight into the long-term performance and durability of the HPRB, which will help in barrier design and lifetime assessment.

papers.title: SHEAR RESPONSE OF UNSATURATED CLAY–GEOTEXTILE INTERFACE UNDER A WIDE RANGE OF SUCTIONS
papers.source: Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (University of Maryland College Park)
papers.summary: Soil–geotextile interface behavior governs the performance of many geotechnical systems, including mechanically stabilized earth walls, reinforced slopes, pavements, embankments, and landfill cover systems. Although the behavior of these interfaces has been widely investigated under saturated conditions, their response under unsaturated conditions remains insufficiently understood, particularly at medium- to high-suction levels encountered in compacted fine-grained soils. Most previous studies have been limited to low matric suctions (<100–300 kPa), leaving a gap in understanding interface behavior under higher suction conditions representative of many field environments.This research investigates the shear behavior of unsaturated low-plasticity clay–geotextile interfaces over a suction range of 1 to 8 MPa using two low-plasticity clay soils and two polypropylene geotextiles (woven and nonwoven). The experimental program included soil-water retention curve (SWRC) testing using the osmotic method, suction measurements using the filter paper method, and direct shear testing conducted under normal stresses of 50, 100, and 200 kPa. The study evaluates the influence of suction, normal stress, soil type, and geotextile type on the peak and post-peak interface shear behavior. The experimental results show that interface shear strength increases with increasing suction; however, the relationship is nonlinear and cannot be adequately represented by conventional linear extensions of the Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion. The increase in shear strength is primarily attributed to suction-induced adhesion, while the interface friction angle remains nearly constant throughout the investigated suction range. Nonwoven geotextiles consistently mobilized greater suction-dependent interface resistance than woven geotextiles because of their greater contact area and enhanced soil–fiber interaction. The results also demonstrate that suction influences both peak and residual interface behav

papers.title: Synergistic valorization of oil palm empty fruit bunch and pome sludge for balanced erosion control and runoff quality
papers.summary: The palm oil sector confronts significant sustainability challenges due to massive biomass waste generation, particularly Oil Palm Empty Fruit Bunches (OPEFB) and Palm Oil Mill Effluent (POME). This study aimed to valorize OPEFB-POME materials into biodegradable soil pellets in three distinct ratios to determine the optimum sludge ratio and evaluate their efficacy in mitigating soil erosion, surface runoff quality, and environmental sustainability. Rainfall simulation experiments were conducted on loamy sand, utilizing standardized soil characterization within erosion control plots at five application rates (T1, T2, T3, T4, and T5 g/ft 2 ) to evaluate the balance between physical protection and runoff quality. The results revealed that Pellet II (40:60 OPEFB-to-sludge ratio) exhibited the optimal dimensional stability, while application rate T2 provided the best balance between erosion control and runoff quality. Despite maximal pellet coverage (T5) decreasing turbidity by 97.80%, it exceeded the environmental thresholds for chemical oxygen demand (192 mg/L) and phosphorus (4.59 mg/L). Despite this rate reducing the nutrient load relative to higher application rates, it still introduced phosphorus levels exceeding eutrophication thresholds, marking it as a best-compromise solution rather than a completely benign intervention and providing the highest degree of balanced performance between physical protection and chemical runoff loading. This study highlights that OPEFB-POME pellets reflect an effective by-product valorization pathway, providing an integrated option for enhancing resource recovery in the palm oil sector by balancing soil conservation with aquatic environmental protection.

papers.title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil
papers.summary: This work proposes a hyper-reduced order model for coupled hydro-mechanical simulations of elastoplastic deformation and water flow in partially saturated soils. These simulations are used to monitor and assess the safety of geotechnical structures such as earthfill dams, where calibration, uncertainty quantification and scenario analysis require solving the same transient model many times for different parameter values. The displacement and the pore pressure are approximated in a field-split reduced basis obtained by proper orthogonal decomposition, and the Galerkin-projected equations are integrated with decomposed cubature rules, one per balance equation, built with the energy-conserving sampling and weighting (ECSW) method. Each residual is split into an affine part and a nonlinear correction: the affine part is computed exactly, at negligible online cost, so that the cubature rule only needs to approximate the correction, which is localized in space. The construction is independent of the constitutive model choices and is implemented in FEniCSx by assembling the original variational forms on the small set of elements selected by ECSW. The method is tested on two- and three-dimensional dams retaining tailings and water, simulating a raise of the dam and the subsequent consolidation phase, with the friction angle, stiffness and hydraulic conductivity of the dam material and the height of the raise as varying parameters. The hyper-reduced model reproduces the displacement and pressure fields with errors below $0.5\%$ with respect to the finite element solution, achieving speed-ups of up to $43\times$ in two dimensions and $77\times$ in three. These performance gains grow with the extent of the plastic yielding, and the selected elements concentrate in the plastified and unsaturated zones, whose size is set by the physics rather than by the mesh resolution.

papers.title: Unsaturated Soil Behavior Under Repeated Traffic Loading in Arid Climates: A Scenario-Based Numerical Study of Road Subgrade Performance Under Assumed Climate-Analogue Suction Pathways
papers.summary: Road subgrade response in arid regions is governed by the unsaturated state of the soil, yet pavement design frameworks represent moisture mainly through empirical, largely equilibrium environmental adjustments rather than through the explicit evolution of matric suction during wetting and drying. Climate influence is represented by a two-suction concept that separates the annual-average drying trend from the critical post-rainfall wetted state. The suction pathways are not derived from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) output: their end-of-life values (140 and 55 kPa) are prescribed, and they are labelled Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 analogues only because their direction and ordering are qualitatively consistent with the projections of the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) for arid regions. They are treated throughout as assumed scenario parameters. All soil, traffic and deformation parameters are representative literature-based values; no measured retention, resilient modulus or rutting data are used, so every result is a conditional model output and not a validated prediction. Under the assumed high-emission analogue the computed year-20 subgrade rut depth is 22.0 mm (parameter-perturbation range 12-31 mm), reaching the 20 mm rut-depth threshold adopted here between years 19 and 20, against 6.5 mm for the constant-climate baseline and 11.1 mm for the moderate analogue. A one-at-a-time sensitivity screening ranks the assumed pathway shift (+15.5 mm) first, followed by design suction (+4.6/-1.8 mm), the initial-strain (ε0) scaling and the exponent β, with traffic growth least influential.

papers.title: Python Scripting for PLAXIS
papers.summary: Python Scripting for PLAXIS is a comprehensive guide to developing Python-based workflows for automating PLAXIS analyses, enabling increased productivity, reduced errors and more efficient use of engineering effort in geotechnical modeling. PLAXIS is a widely used finite element software for analyzing safety, stability, deformation, consolidation and groundwater flow problems in geotechnical engineering. It is routinely applied to complex projects such as foundations, dams, embankments, ground improvement, and both surface and underground excavations. While most users rely on the graphical user interface (GUI), PLAXIS also provides powerful scripting capabilities through its command-line interface and Python API. This book demonstrates how these capabilities can be leveraged to automate repetitive modeling and analysis tasks, streamline workflows and enhance consistency in model definition and execution. Written for researchers, academics and practicing engineers alike, the book is ideal for both new and experienced PLAXIS users seeking to integrate scripting into their daily workflows and unlock the full potential of the software.

papers.title: Effects of sequential hydration on water retention and shrinkage of cement-stabilized unsaturated soil
papers.summary: Early-age shrinkage cracking often compromises the durability of infrastructures constructed with cement–stabilized soils (CSS). This study evaluates a sequential hydration (SH) strategy designed to curb shrinkage while sustaining hydraulic response (e.g., degree of saturation) and mechanical performance pertinent to seepage control and serviceability limit-state design. Three hydration paths were examined: OH-100, one-time hydration at 100 % OMC; SH-80 and SH-60, compaction at 80 % and 60 % OMC respectively, followed by second-stage wetting. Soil-water retention curves (SWRCs) were measured under zero-stress and vertical stress using a stress-controllable pressure-plate apparatus and drying–wetting shrinkage was tracked over three cycles for a CSS. The results show that SH significantly reduces early-age free shrinkage while modifying water-retention behavior, hysteresis, and stress-dependent hydraulic response. Among the investigated treatments, SH at 80 % OMC produced the most favorable balance between shrinkage mitigation and hydraulic performance. SEM/EDX analyses suggest that staged hydration promotes pore-throat refinement and changes hydration-product distribution, particularly A-S-H formation. These findings indicate that SH may serve as a construction-stage strategy for reducing shrinkage cracking in cement-treated pavement bases while maintaining adequate hydraulic performance.

papers.title: Scalable and locally mass-conservative simulation of basin-scale variably saturated groundwater flow
papers.summary: Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km^2, contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. papers.title: FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems. 1. Theory and applications with intercode benchmarking
papers.summary: Abstract FLOWS (FLOws of Water and Solutes in soils) is a dynamic physically-based model to simulate water flow and solute transport in the soil–plant–atmosphere system. The numerical code was written in MATLAB. One-dimensional vertical transient water flow is simulated by numerically solving the 1D form of the Richards equation (RE) using an implicit, backward, finite differences scheme with explicit linearization. As for the solutes, the code solves the 1D Advection Dispersion equation (ADE) by an explicit, central difference scheme, allowing for a relatively easy inclusion of non-linear adsorption and other non-linear processes. The model produces information on the time evolution of (among many other outputs): soil water contents and pressure potentials in the soil profile; solute (tracers, adsorbed, volatile and reactive solutes) concentrations in the soil profile; water and solute uptake and actual evapotranspiration for simulated crops; deep percolation water and solute fluxes; root uptake of water and solutes, also in presence of water and osmotic stresses; water fluxes and related solute fluxes to runoff; drainage water fluxes and related solute fluxes; irrigation fluxes computed by the model; and temperature in the soil profile. Compared to other existing models, some specificities of FLOWS model are: (1) integrated simulation of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus transformations and transport contextually to the simulation of water contents and fluxes; (2) macroscopic root uptake; (3) irrigation management, by allowing to optimize the time scheduling and volumes according to some criterion based on the average pressure head in the root zone; (4) the possibility of running multi-site simulations, which may be especially important for spatially distributed simulations; and (5) an interactive graphical user interface, allowing the user to easily handle even large input files and seeing the simulation results by graphical display of the main output variables.

papers.title: Evidence for temporal decoupling of olivine weathering and inorganic carbon removal in unsaturated soil columns
papers.summary: Introduction Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a nature-based carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal technology that speeds the natural weathering process of rocks by applying finely ground silicate rocks over the land surface. It has been proposed that ERW can remove between 0.5 and 2 Gt CO 2 year −1 when deployed at scale. To investigate how soil porewater responds to the dissolution of silicate dust during enhanced rock weathering, we conducted unsaturated soil column experiments amended with olivine (Mg 2 SiO 4 ). Methods Since the main principle of ERW-based carbon removal is the reaction of atmospheric CO 2 dissolved in rainwater with silicate rocks, leading to release of base cations and bicarbonate ions, we measured cations, anions, pH, alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the leached effluent. Complementary solid-phase soil measurements of exchangeable cations, pH, total inorganic carbon (TIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) were performed to improve understanding of weathering product transport and retention, while aqueous speciation calculations provided saturation state information of relevant secondary mineral phases. Results We demonstrate that measurable olivine weathering can occur without proportional short-term export of bicarbonate or DIC, and estimates of potential CO 2 removal based on weathering-derived cation release exceeded realized inorganic CO 2 removal quantified from bicarbonate and DIC export. Furthermore, the observed increase in DOC export and decrease in surface-soil organic carbon suggest that enhanced weathering may alter soil organic carbon dynamics. Discussion The discrepancy between weathering-derived cation release and inorganic carbon export is consistent with temporal decoupling between weathering and realized carbon removal, likely caused by retention of weathering-derived products within the soil. papers.title: The 7 April 2026 Reactivation of the Petacciato Landslide (Adriatic Coast, Italy): Field Evidence, Ground Deformation, and Rainfall-Triggering Conditions
papers.summary: The Petacciato landslide is a well-known, very large landslide located along the Adriatic coast of central–southern Italy and involving Plio-Pleistocene marine clay sequences with sandy intercalations. Reactivations have been documented since the early twentieth century and have occurred predominantly after prolonged rainfall periods. On 7 April 2026, a new reactivation event provided an opportunity to investigate this complex landslide system further. Displacements affected the A14 motorway and the Adriatic railway and led to the declaration of a national state of emergency. This study integrates geological, geomorphological, and hydrological information with recent European Ground Motion Service (EGMS) remote-sensing data and precipitation analyses to improve the understanding of the phenomenon. The findings indicate that the Apennine thrust front acts as a structural predisposing factor for the deep-seated landslide, whereas prolonged rainfall triggers reactivation. The analysis highlights the role of long-term cumulative rainfall as a primary driver of reactivation and the value of InSAR monitoring for evaluating continuous ground deformation, including during apparently dormant periods. The results emphasise how reactivation events can improve understanding of landslide behaviour and inform risk-management strategies.

papers.title: From Rainfall to Absolute Landslide Probability: A Machine Learning–Based Approach
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors. papers.title: Landslide‐Channel Coupling Controls Asymmetric Flash Flood—Debris Flow Transitions: Insights From an Extreme Rainfall‐Induced Hazard Chain in Yuzhong of China in 2025
papers.summary: Abstract Extreme rainfall‐triggered landslide–flash flood–debris flow hazard chains (LFFDF) are increasingly responsible for hydroclimatic losses worldwide. Although dynamics of individual hazards are established, transition mechanisms within LFFDF governed by coupled landslide–channel responses remain unresolved. Taking a catastrophic LFFDF event in northwestern China in 2025, we reconstructed the transition dynamics of the hazard chain using satellite data, seismic records, and numerical modeling. The results show that the LFFDF cascade operates as asymmetric transition processes, in which the dominant controls are state‐dependent. Rainfall‐induced landslides supplied one‐third of the mobilized sediment; their interaction with flash floods increased channel‐flow Shields stress by more than an order of magnitude, prematurely initiating debris flows in headwater channels. The downstream reversion from debris flow to flash flood is mainly controlled by the thickness and saturation state of channel sediments. Finally, we suggest a cascade‐based paradigm for risk assessment to enhance community resilience to LFFDF risks.

papers.title: From Fragmented Plans to a Public Regulatory Knowledge Infrastructure: Harmonizing Flood and Landslide Risk Planning in the Central Apennine River Basin District, Italy
papers.summary: Italy’s transition to river basin district governance within the framework of Directive 2000/60/EC unified institutional responsibilities while leaving existing flood and landslide plans in force. District authorities therefore had to integrate instruments with different knowledge bases, classifications and land-use rules. This article examines the integration of nine Hydrogeological Setting Plans (PAIs) into two coordinated plans for the Central Apennine district (42,275 km2), adopted in final form in May 2026. Document analysis compared classifications, intervention conditions and assessment responsibilities, examining 175 public submissions and 118 first-round regional determinations. Geographic information system analysis quantified current classification correspondences and coverage: approximately 1860 km2 within the fluvial planning framework, including safeguard proposals, and 107,045 landslide phenomena occupying approximately 4970 km2. Initial flood transposition retained inherited boundaries, while landslide classification followed a common type–activity matrix. Regulatory comparisons identified conditional extensions of admissibility alongside more selective urban restructuring rules; the plans also established formal updating procedures. Institutional review connected technical choices with regulatory decisions, producing amendments while leaving some precautionary disagreements unresolved. The framework coordinated inherited knowledge without eliminating differences in detail or completeness. The article offers a procedural and regulatory reference for other authorities facing fragmented planning systems; implementation and risk-reduction outcomes require subsequent evaluation.

papers.title: Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.
